- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`; (5) `claude plugin eval` (writing and running plugin eval suites, its JSON/report, sandbox, CI, early-access enablement) and the `/skill-doctor` report. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Glob, Grep, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- Explore: Fast read-only search agent for locating code. Use it to find files by pattern (eg. "src/components/**/*.tsx"), grep for symbols or keywords (eg. "API endpoints"), or answer "where is X defined / which files reference Y." Do NOT use it for code review, design-doc auditing, cross-file consistency checks, or open-ended analysis — it reads excerpts rather than whole files and will miss content past its read window. When calling, specify search breadth: "quick" for a single targeted lookup, "medium" for moderate exploration, or "very thorough" to search across multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

## 4bdddc46-3b80-45ec-bc37-523e74d4fda6
The official Figma MCP server. Use this server whenever the user wants to create, generate, edit, implement, or sync any design, UI, screen, component, mockup, or visual — in Figma, FigJam, Figma Make, or Figma Slides — and whenever the user mentions Figma or provides a figma.com URL.

This server bridges code and design in both directions, and supports designing from scratch using existing design systems and codebases.

CAPABILITIES:
- Read designs FROM Figma into code (get_design_context, get_screenshot, get_metadata, get_figjam)
- Write designs INTO Figma from code, intent, or existing components (use_figma, generate_figma_design, create_new_file, upload_assets)
- Bridge code and design via Code Connect (get_code_connect_map, add_code_connect_map)
- Create diagrams and FigJam content (generate_diagram, get_figjam)

WHEN TO USE THESE TOOLS:
- The user wants to create, mock up, or generate any UI, screen, component, or design — even if Figma isn't named
- The user wants to implement a design as code (design-to-code)
- The user wants to push a page, view, or component into Figma (code-to-design)
- The user wants to update, sync, or edit an existing Figma file
- The user shares a figma.com URL
- The user wants to build or extend a design system, design tokens, or component library
- The user wants to create a diagram in FigJam

SKILLS (Prefer the skills shipped with the Figma plugin on the agent being used. If no Figma plugin is installed, use the skills served by the Figma MCP resource):
- /figma-use — MANDATORY before calling use_figma; fallback: skill://figma/figma-use/SKILL.md
- /figma-generate-design — for translating an app page or layout into Figma; fallback: skill://figma/figma-generate-design/SKILL.md
- /figma-generate-library — for building a design system in Figma from code; fallback: skill://figma/figma-generate-library/SKILL.md
- /figma-code-connect — for mapping Figma components to codebase components; fallback: skill://figma/figma-code-connect/SKILL.md
- /figma-use-figjam — for FigJam-specific use_f

- hyperframes: Mandatory entry point: read this first for any request to make, create, edit, animate, or render a video, animation, or motion graphic, including a promo, explainer, captioned clip, title card, overlay, slideshow or interactive deck, Remotion port, or any HyperFrames HTML composition. Also use it to inspect, diagnose, validate, preview, publish, or batch-render an existing HyperFrames project. Inputs may be a website URL, GitHub PR, Figma design or URL, text or brief, existing footage, or music. It resumes project state, captures intent when applicable, selects and installs the owning workflow, and routes domain capabilities. HyperFrames is the default output framework unless the user explicitly chooses another framework for the deliverable or asks only to record a browser session.
- hyperframes-animation: All animation knowledge for HyperFrames — atomic motion rules, multi-phase scene blueprints, scene transitions, broader motion-design techniques, AND the seven runtime adapters (GSAP default, plus Lottie, Three.js, Anime.js, CSS keyframes, Web Animations API, TypeGPU). Use for any motion or animation task: pick 2-4 rules and compose, or load a blueprint, or look up runtime-specific API (e.g. GSAP eases / Lottie player / Three.js mixer). Also covers auditing an existing composition's choreography (animation map) and 24 named text-animation effects. HyperFrames-native: single paused timeline, seek-safe, deterministic.
- hyperframes-audio: Use when audio already placed in a HyperFrames composition needs to be mixed: fade-in/fade-out, crossfade, track gain or volume, volume automation, ducking, a music bed that fights a voiceover (voiceover carve), effects on a track (EQ, compressor, limiter, gate, saturation, delay, reverb, chorus, phaser, bitcrush), or automation envelopes drawn on a track's volume or any effect parameter. Don't use for sourcing or generating audio — finding BGM, SFX, or making a voiceover is `/media-use`. Don't use for clip timing or track layout, which is `/hyperframes-core`.
- hyperframes-cli: Use the HyperFrames CLI development loop: init, add, catalog, capture, lint, check, snapshot, compare, grade-compare, preview, play, present, beats, keyframes, single or batch render, publish, cloud, cloudrun, feedback, lambda, doctor, browser, info, upgrade, skills, compositions, docs, benchmark, telemetry, transcribe, auth, tts, and remove-background. Also use when diagnosing build or render failures. validate, inspect, and layout are deprecated aliases; use check. Covers local, HeyGen-hosted cloud, AWS Lambda, and Google Cloud Run rendering.
- hyperframes-core: The HyperFrames composition contract — build one renderable project. Use for composition structure, the `data-*` timing attributes, `class="clip"`, tracks, sub-compositions, variables, framework-owned media playback, deterministic-render rules, and validation. Also covers Tailwind projects and the STORYBOARD.md / SCRIPT.md plan formats. Read before writing composition HTML.
- hyperframes-creative: Non-animation creative direction for HyperFrames videos. Use for design spec (frame.md / design.md) handling, palettes, typography, narration, beat planning, audio-reactive visuals, composition patterns, and brand / style decisions. For atomic motion patterns and scene blueprints, use `hyperframes-animation`.
- hyperframes-keyframes: Use when a HyperFrames composition needs a punch-in, punch-out, zoom, reframe, Ken Burns treatment, camera move, visual match/whip handoff, or other seek-safe 2D/3D keyframes; also for GSAP, CSS keyframes, Anime.js, WAAPI, FLIP, paths, masks, SVG morph/draw, text trails, 3D depth, or `hyperframes keyframes` diagnostics. Don't use for broad scene strategy, brand design, media sourcing, captions, or general video planning.
- hyperframes-registry: Install, discover, and wire registry blocks and components into HyperFrames compositions. Use when running hyperframes add or hyperframes catalog, installing one item or every block matching a tag, wiring an installed item into index.html, or working with hyperframes.json. Covers discovery, install locations, block sub-composition wiring, component snippet merging, and authoring a new block or component to contribute upstream (idea → scaffold → validate → PR).
- media-use: Agent Media OS, the single skill for every media need in a HyperFrames project. Resolve BGM, SFX, image, icon, brand logo, voice, color grade, or LUT into a frozen local file or paste-ready block + ledger record (one verb, `resolve`); generate via TTS / music / image models when the catalog misses; produce voiceover, transcription, captions, and background removal through one shared audio engine; operate on media (cut / reframe / transform); and reuse assets across projects. Also use for vague feedback that real footage looks dark, flat, boring, should feel retro/camcorder/print/ASCII, needs privacy, or needs a media reveal.
- motion-graphics: A short, design-led motion graphic where motion is the message — kinetic typography, stat count-up, chart/data-viz hit, logo sting / brand lockup, lower-third / callout / social overlay, animated map (highlight regions, connect places, zoom to a location), animated tweet / news-article / headline, webpage / UI animation (scroll, cursor, callouts), or fusing a real image's geometry into a chart. Usually under 10s (up to ~30s), no narration or live-action subject; renders to MP4 or transparent overlay. Longer / narrated / multi-scene → /general-video. Unclear → /hyperframes.
- figma:figma-code-connect: Creates and maintains Figma Code Connect template files that map Figma components to code snippets. Use when the user mentions Code Connect, Figma component mapping, design-to-code translation, or asks to create/update .figma.ts or .figma.js files.
- figma:figma-create-new-file: **MANDATORY prerequisite** — you MUST invoke this skill BEFORE every `create_new_file` tool call. NEVER call `create_new_file` directly without loading this skill first. Trigger whenever the user wants a new blank Figma file — a new design, FigJam, or Slides file — or when you need a fresh file before calling `use_figma`. Usage — /figma-create-new-file [editorType] [fileName] (e.g. /figma-create-new-file figjam My Whiteboard, /figma-create-new-file slides Q3 Review)
- figma:figma-design-to-code: **MANDATORY prerequisite** — you MUST invoke this skill BEFORE calling the `get_design_context` Figma MCP tool. You MUST trigger this skill whenever the user wants to implement, build, port, or code up a Figma design as code. Example prompts (not exhaustive) are 'implement this Figma design', 'build this screen from Figma', 'turn this Figma into code', 'design to code'. This skill provides critical instructions and steps to the agent on how to correctly implement Figma designs in code and must NOT be skipped.
- figma:figma-generate-design: Use this skill alongside figma-use when the task involves translating an application page, view, or multi-section layout into Figma. Triggers: 'write to Figma', 'create in Figma from code', 'push page to Figma', 'take this app/page and build it in Figma', 'create a screen', 'build a landing page in Figma', 'update the Figma screen to match code', 'convert this modal/dialog/drawer/panel to Figma'. This is the preferred workflow skill whenever the user wants to build or update a full page, modal, dialog, drawer, sidebar, panel, or any composed multi-section view in Figma from code or a description. Discovers design system components, variables, and styles from Code Connect files, existing screens, and library search, then imports them and assembles views incrementally section-by-section using design system tokens instead of hardcoded values.
- figma:figma-generate-diagram: MANDATORY prerequisite — load this skill BEFORE every `generate_diagram` tool call. NEVER call `generate_diagram` directly without loading this skill first. Trigger whenever the user asks to create, generate, draw, render, sketch, or build a diagram — flowchart, architecture diagram, sequence diagram, ERD or entity-relationship diagram, state diagram or state machine, gantt chart, or timeline. Also trigger when the user mentions Mermaid syntax or wants a system architecture, decision tree, dependency graph, API call flow, auth handshake, schema, or pipeline visualized in FigJam. Routes to type-specific guidance, sets universal Mermaid constraints, and tells you when to use a different diagram type or skip the tool entirely (mindmaps, pie charts, class diagrams, etc.).
- figma:figma-generate-library: Build or update a professional-grade design system in Figma from a codebase. Use when the user wants to create variables/tokens, build component libraries, create individual components with proper variant sets and variable bindings, set up theming (light/dark modes), document foundations, or reconcile gaps between code and Figma. Also use when the user asks to create or generate any component in Figma — even a single one — since components require proper variable foundations, variant states, and design token bindings to be production-quality. This skill teaches WHAT to build and in WHAT ORDER — it complements the `figma-use` skill which teaches HOW to call the Plugin API. Both skills should be loaded together.
- figma:figma-implement-motion: Translates Figma motion and animations into production-ready application code. Use when implementing animation/motion from a Figma design — user mentions "implement this motion", "add animation from Figma", "animate this component", provides a Figma URL whose node is animated, or when `get_design_context` returns motion data or instructs you to call `get_motion_context`.
- figma:figma-swiftui: SwiftUI ↔ Figma translation. Use whenever the user mentions Swift, SwiftUI, iOS, iPhone, or iPad — in EITHER direction — translating a Figma design into SwiftUI (design → code), or pushing SwiftUI views / screens / tokens back into a Figma file (code → design). Triggers on phrases like 'implement this Figma design in SwiftUI', 'build this screen in Swift', 'push this SwiftUI view to Figma', 'mirror my Swift code in a Figma file', or whenever a Figma URL appears alongside `.swift` files / an `.xcodeproj`. Routes to a direction-specific reference doc; loads alongside `figma-use` for the code → design path.
- figma:figma-use: **MANDATORY prerequisite** — you MUST invoke this skill BEFORE every `use_figma` tool call. NEVER call `use_figma` directly without loading this skill first. Skipping it causes common, hard-to-debug failures. Trigger whenever the user wants to perform a write action or a unique read action that requires JavaScript execution in the Figma file context — e.g. create/edit/delete nodes, set up variables or tokens, build components and variants, modify auto-layout or fills, bind variables to properties, or inspect file structure programmatically.
- figma:figma-use-figjam: This skill helps agents use Figma's use_figma MCP tool in the FigJam context. Can be used alongside figma-use which has foundational context for using the use_figma tool.
- figma:figma-use-motion: Motion / animation context for the `use_figma` MCP tool — animating Figma nodes via manual keyframes, animation styles, easing, and timeline duration. Load alongside figma-use whenever a task involves adding, editing, or inspecting animation on a node.
- figma:figma-use-slides: This skill helps agents use Figma's use_figma MCP tool in the Slides context. Can be used alongside figma-use which has foundational context for using the use_figma tool.
- anthropic-skills:consolidate-memory: Reflective pass over your memory files — merge duplicates, fix stale facts, prune the index.
- anthropic-skills:docx: Use this skill whenever the user wants to create, read, edit, or manipulate Word documents (.docx files) or Word templates (.dotx files). Triggers include: any mention of 'Word doc', 'word document', '.docx', '.dotx', or requests to produce professional documents with formatting like tables of contents, headings, page numbers, or letterheads. Also use when extracting or reorganizing content from .docx or .dotx files, inserting or replacing images in documents, performing find-and-replace in Word files, working with tracked changes or comments, or converting content into a polished Word document. If the user asks for a 'report', 'memo', 'letter', 'template', or similar deliverable as a Word or .docx file, use this skill. Do NOT use for PDFs, spreadsheets, Google Docs, or general coding tasks unrelated to document generation.
- anthropic-skills:explain-usage: Explain where this session's tokens went, with one simple chart in plain language. Use when the user says things like "explain my usage", "where did my tokens go", or asks for a usage breakdown.
- anthropic-skills:morning: Render the user's morning brief as a styled HTML artifact, or set it up as a recurring weekday task. Use only when the user explicitly asks to run, see, or set up their morning brief, or if they invoke /morning by name. A question about their day, schedule, or calendar is not by itself a request for the brief; answer it directly instead.
- anthropic-skills:pdf: Use this skill whenever the user wants to do anything with PDF files. This includes reading or extracting text/tables from PDFs, combining or merging multiple PDFs into one, splitting PDFs apart, rotating pages, adding watermarks, creating new PDFs, filling PDF forms, encrypting/decrypting PDFs, extracting images, and OCR on scanned PDFs to make them searchable. If the user mentions a .pdf file or asks to produce one, use this skill.
- anthropic-skills:pptx: Use this skill any time a .pptx or .potx file is involved in any way — as input, output, or both. This includes: creating slide decks, pitch decks, or presentations; reading, parsing, or extracting text from any .pptx or .potx file (even if the extracted content will be used elsewhere, like in an email or summary); editing, modifying, or updating existing presentations; combining or splitting slide files; working with templates (.potx), layouts, speaker notes, or comments. Trigger whenever the user mentions "deck," "slides," "presentation," or references a .pptx or .potx filename, regardless of what they plan to do with the content afterward. If a .pptx or .potx file needs to be opened, created, or touched, use this skill.
- anthropic-skills:schedule: Create or update a scheduled task that runs automatically. Use when the user says things like "every day", "each morning", "remind me in an hour", "run this at noon", or wants to reschedule an existing task.
- anthropic-skills:setup-cowork: Guided Cowork setup — install role-matched plugins, connect your tools, try a skill.
- anthropic-skills:skill-creator: Create new skills, modify and improve existing skills, and measure skill performance. Use when users want to create a skill from scratch, edit, or optimize an existing skill, run evals to test a skill, benchmark skill performance with variance analysis, or optimize a skill's description for better triggering accuracy.
- anthropic-skills:xlsx: Use this skill any time a spreadsheet file is the primary input or output. This means any task where the user wants to: open, read, edit, or fix an existing .xlsx, .xlsm, .xltx, .csv, or .tsv file (e.g., adding columns, computing formulas, formatting, charting, cleaning messy data); create a new spreadsheet from scratch or from other data sources; or convert between tabular file formats. Trigger especially when the user references a spreadsheet file by name or path — even casually (like "the xlsx in my downloads") — and wants something done to it or produced from it. Also trigger for cleaning or restructuring messy tabular data files (malformed rows, misplaced headers, junk data) into proper spreadsheets. The deliverable must be a spreadsheet file. Do NOT trigger when the primary deliverable is a Word document, HTML report, standalone Python script, database pipeline, or Google Sheets API integration, even if tabular data is involved.
- design: Create a design canvas — a multi-artboard visual design published as an Artifact that runs Claude Design's canvas editor (an early preview of Claude Design inside Claude Code). You DRAFT the design as .dc.html artboards laid out on one pan/zoom canvas; where saving is enabled for the user's account they refine every element visually (click-to-select, a properties panel, inline text editing, undo/redo) and Save publishes a new version for everyone, otherwise they get a view-and-export (PNG/PDF) preview of your draft. Good for UI mockups and screen flows, landing pages, marketing and social graphics, and print pieces — posters, flyers, brochures as single-page artboards; memos and reports as one flowing artboard. Use when someone wants a design, mockup, wireframe, UI or screen design, landing page, poster, flyer, brochure, banner, card, one-pager, or any visual layout they would rather tweak by hand than in code. Only for CREATING or re-seeding a canvas; an existing one is edited in its published Artifact.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including Markdown ones — format is part of the design pass, never a speed shortcut.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts — when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, keeping state shared across viewers, handing the viewer a file to save, or updating and republishing itself. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).

# Running this locally

## 1. Prerequisites

- Node.js 18+ (https://nodejs.org)
- PostgreSQL running locally, with a database created for this project:
  ```sql
  CREATE DATABASE kodely_personal;
  ```

## 2. Configure

Copy `.env.example` to `.env` and fill in your local Postgres connection
string (username/password/port depend on how you installed Postgres —
pgAdmin or the installer's setup step will have shown you the password
you set for the `postgres` user).

## 3. Install and set up the database

```bash
npm install
npx prisma db push
```

## 4. Log in with your Claude subscription (one-time)

```bash
node_modules/@anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk-win32-x64/claude.exe setup-token
```

(On macOS/Linux, drop the `.exe` and use the matching
`claude-agent-sdk-darwin-x64` / `claude-agent-sdk-linux-x64` folder instead
— `npm install` only downloads the one for your actual OS, so check
`node_modules/@anthropic-ai/` to see which one you have.)

This opens a real browser on your own machine and logs in normally —
requires a Claude Pro/Max subscription, won't work on a free account.
One-time only; the login persists after this.

## 5. Build and run

```bash
npm run build
npm run dev
```

Open http://localhost:3000, sign up with any email (this is your own
private local database), and start building. Every generation runs on
your Claude subscription, not an API key — no metered cost.

Publishing a project locally serves it from this same local server
(http://localhost:3000/api/site/<slug>) rather than a real kodely.site
URL — that domain belongs to the real, separately-hosted product and
isn't reachable from here, so this instance never mints a URL that looks
like it's live on Kodely's real hosting.

## What this is (and isn't)

This is the real Kodely product's UI (editor, chat, live preview) with one
deliberate change: `lib/agent.ts` uses the Claude Agent SDK authenticated
via your subscription instead of the Anthropic API + API key. It's a
personal, single-user copy — not connected to the real kodely.me database,
not deployed anywhere, and it should stay that way. `skills/kodely-house-
style/SKILL.md` is the prompt driving generation quality; refine it as you
build real sites, and bring proven improvements back to the real product's
`lib/agent.ts` when ready (a separate, deliberate step — this local copy
never becomes "live" on its own).

That rm failure at the end is likely an EBUSY error on Windows, probably because a lingering subprocess handle, file watcher, or antivirus scan is still holding the directory open right after it was used as a cwd. Actually, I think the real bug is in the try/finally structure: since this is a generator function, if rm throws inside the finally block, it overrides the successful completion and propagates out as the reported error, even though the site generation itself already finished fine. The fix should wrap the rm call in try/catch so cleanup failures don't mask success, and add retry options like maxRetries and retryDelay to handle Windows' transient directory locks.

content.text: Found it — [lib/agent.ts:154-156](lib/agent.ts:154). The `rm(workDir, ...)` cleanup runs in a `finally` block, and on Windows a lingering process handle can transiently lock the directory right after the agent's Bash tool exits (EBUSY). Since it's a generator function, an exception thrown in `finally` overrides the successful result — so even though generation likely completed fine, the cleanup failure gets reported to the user as if the whole build failed. Let's fix it: add Node's built-in retry for exactly this Windows timing issue, and never let cleanup errors mask a successful generation.

content.text:
No comments/attachments on any card — confirmed this is all the detail there is (matches the seed data exactly). Here's my assessment of all 19 cards, grouped by how tractable they are for me to actually implement locally:

## Phase A — Pre-GA critical

| Card | Assessment |
|---|---|
| Off-site backups + disaster recovery | **Large / infra-only.** No cloud infra exists for this local instance to back up to. Not actionable in this codebase. |
| Anthropic multi-key pool + spend caps | **Large.** Doesn't apply here — this local instance runs on your subscription via `claude setup-token`, not a pooled API key. Not applicable to this personal copy. |
| Service-key rotation runbook | **Doc-only, small.** I can write a rotation runbook/checklist as a markdown doc. Real key rotation itself is a manual action you'd take on the actual service dashboards. |
| Kodely tier numbers — names, prices, credits | **Decision, not code.** This needs a business decision from you (names/prices/credit amounts) before any Stripe wiring can be finished. I can implement once you give me numbers. |
| Pre-GA security review | **Medium, code-actionable.** I can run a real review pass over the build/publish path in this codebase (`/security-review` or manual audit) and report findings. |

## Phase B — Product

| Card | Assessment |
|---|---|
| Click-to-edit visual editing | **Large feature.** Real scoped feature work — multi-day even for a real team. Could start a first slice (e.g. click-to-select an element) if you want. |
| Asset / image upload | **Medium, actionable.** Concrete: upload endpoint + storage + UI. Buildable here. |

Now I have the full picture, so I'm planning the fixes: adding a manual theme toggle with localStorage persistence so users can force light mode regardless of OS settings, and updating globals.css to support class-based overrides alongside the media query default. I also need to make sure the board stays self-contained on one screen without vertical scrolling per column.

For the board layout, I'm fixing the issue where columns grow unbounded with many cards by making each column a fixed-height flex container with internal overflow-y-auto scrolling, constraining the overall page height with h-screen and flex-col.

For the broken voice-to-text, I'm investigating possible causes — browser support for the Web Speech API, permission issues, or a bug where interim and final transcription results get mixed together and garbled. I'm checking how speech recognition support is detected in the code to narrow down the actual failure point.

Localhost should count as a secure context so that shouldn't be the blocker. More likely culprits are unhandled exceptions when starting recognition without mic permission granted, or error handlers that silently fail without surfacing anything to the user, making it seem broken when it's actually erroring out quietly.

I should also look at other UX gaps: clicking directly into the description to edit it instead of requiring an Edit button click, and improving drag-and-drop since the current implementation only supports column-level dragging without reordering, visual feedback, or placeholders.

For smoother drag and drop, I'm leaning toward using framer-motion's layout animations on card elements since it's already a dependency, combined with tracking drag-over state to compute insertion indices and enable reordering within the same column.

Now I'm mapping out the concrete implementation plan. For the theme toggle, I'll mirror the existing pattern from the main app — a class-based dark mode toggle with a no-flash script and localStorage persistence under the same kodely-theme key, rather than inventing a new system.

For the single-screen layout, I'm restructuring the page into a fixed-height flex container so the header stays put and each column scrolls independently within its own bounded area, with the add-card input pinned below the scrollable list rather than floating away with it.

Next I need to dig into why voice-to-text isn't working.

For the description editing, I want clicking directly on the rendered text to trigger edit mode immediately, autofocusing the textarea and saving on blur the same way the title field behaves, rather than forcing users through a separate Edit button.

For drag and drop, I'm planning to bring in @dnd-kit to get smooth sortable animations with insertion indicators, plus a trash-icon drop zone that appears during dragging so cards can be deleted by dropping them there.

Finally, I want to add a search input in the header that filters cards by title.

With only 4 columns currently, equal-width CSS grid columns solve both the scrolling and spacing issues together, falling back to horizontal scroll only if there were many more columns. Given the scope of changes across multiple files—main layout, global styles, a new theme toggle, the card modal, voice input, and the drag-and-drop library—I'm planning to work through this methodically, starting by reproducing the current setup.

My plan: fix the voice-to-text bug first since it's quick, then install dnd-kit, rewrite the main page with a grid layout that fits the screen with per-column scrolling, add the theme toggle and search bar, and wire up drag-and-drop with a trash dropzone. After that I'll update the card modal so clicking the description edits it directly, build out the theme system across the CSS and layout files, and finally test everything in the browser—type-checking, hot reload, theme persistence, board fit, search filtering, drag reordering, drag-to-delete, and voice input.

Since this is an automation browser rather than the user's actual Chrome/Edge, I can't reliably reproduce the exact bug they're seeing, so I should focus on inspecting the code for known issues instead. Looking at useVoiceInput.ts, I'm checking whether the onresult handler correctly distinguishes interim from final results when iterating through the results array.

The real suspect seems to be that start() is asynchronous and can fail either synchronously on permission denial or asynchronously via onerror, and while onerror resets listening to false, it doesn't surface any feedback to the user about what went wrong.

This matches the likely bug: if microphone permission was denied or blocked (common on Windows Chrome), recognition fails completely silently with no prompt or error message, so the user just sees nothing happen. There's also a minor gap where recognitionRef.current isn't cleared on natural end, though that's less likely the core issue.

Since I can't get the exact repro, the right move is to harden the implementation: surface errors from onerror (not-allowed, no-speech, audio-capture, network) via a toast or inline message, wrap rec.start() in try/catch to handle synchronous exceptions, guard against double-start InvalidStateError, reset the UI on error so the button doesn't stay stuck in listening state, and consider proactively requesting mic permission via getUserMedia for clearer feedback.

I'm also planning to add a visible error state to the mic button itself—red styling plus tooltip text—so failures are obvious rather than silent, which means adding an error state to the hook and surfacing it through title/aria-label and a brief inline toast.

Given the scope, I'm now mapping out the full set of files to change: updating globals.css to add class-based dark/light theming matching the main app's approach while keeping prefers-color-scheme as a fallback, plus board-specific grid and scrollbar styles; and updating layout.tsx to add a no-flash theme script using its own localStorage key to avoid colliding with the main app's.

I'm keeping the naming consistent as "kodely-board-theme" even though collision isn't really a risk given different origins. I'm also planning a new ThemeToggle component using simple inline SVG icons rather than adding lucide-react as a dependency, since the board app keeps its dependency footprint low. Beyond that, I need to harden error handling in the voice input hook, surface that error state in the mic button, and rework the main page layout to use a full-height flex column with a CSS grid board area sized to fit the column count without page scrolling.

I'm also planning narrower columns with their own internal vertical scroll, a search input to filter cards by title, description, or labels, and dnd-kit integration for smooth drag reordering plus a drag-to-delete trash zone. The card modal needs click-to-edit for descriptions without a separate edit button, and I'll need to add the dnd-kit packages to package.json. Given the scope, I'll tackle this in stages, testing with tsc and the browser after each major change, starting by installing the dnd-kit dependencies.

content.thinking:
I realize clicking a link inside the description while not editing would trigger edit mode instead of navigating, since the outer div's onClick handles that — but that's an acceptable tradeoff given the request to click straight into editing. Now I need to handle the onBlur save behavior for the description field.

Thinking through the event order: clicking "Done" triggers blur on the textarea before the click registers, so saveDescription already runs and exits edit mode via blur, making the Done button's own click handler essentially redundant since the button disappears from the DOM before its click can fire.

I'll keep the Done button anyway since it's harmless and helps with clarity, especially since blur also covers keyboard tabbing and Escape cases.

Now I'm shifting focus to the main page.tsx — designing a self-contained single-screen board with search, narrower fit-to-width columns, smooth dnd-kit drag-and-drop, and drag-to-delete. I'm planning the layout: a full-height flex container with no page scroll, a fixed header with search and theme toggle, and a board area using CSS Grid that fills the remaining height so columns can scroll internally.

I'm reconsidering the approach to use flexbox instead, where each column flexes to share width evenly and shrinks as more columns are added, only falling back to horizontal scroll once there are too many columns to fit comfortably — this solves both the "can't see all stages" and "columns too wide" complaints. Writing flex container styles...

Inside each column I'm planning a fixed header, a scrollable card list, and an add-card input pinned at the bottom, so each column scrolls independently and the board itself stays pinned to the screen height rather than growing with hundreds of cards. For drag and drop I'm setting up dnd-kit with a DndContext and pointer sensor wrapping the board.

Each column uses a SortableContext for its cards, with useSortable enabling reordering within and across columns using the standard multi-container pattern, and I'm adding a droppable trash zone that appears during dragging so cards can be deleted by dropping them there instead of moved.

I'll keep the cards array as the source of truth, updating it optimistically during onDragOver so the UI reflects live reordering as the user drags, then finalize positions on drop, plus use a DragOverlay for a smooth floating preview card to avoid layout jumps.

On onDragEnd, I need to persist the final ordering via PATCH calls, but checking the existing API route, it only updates columnId/position on the single moved card without shifting siblings -- so I need to handle position conflicts myself since the original moveCard logic always appended to the end of a column rather than supporting mid-column insertion.

I'll design the reorder logic to renumber positions sequentially within affected columns after a drag, then fire off individual PATCH calls per changed card -- fine for a local sqlite app with reasonable column sizes. Now I'm working out the onDragEnd handler, starting with determining the source column at drag start...

I'll follow dnd-kit's standard multi-container sortable pattern: handleDragStart tracks the active id, handleDragOver moves cards between columns live for visual feedback, and handleDragEnd finalizes ordering with arrayMove and reassigns positions before persisting.

For empty columns, I need each column container to act as a droppable zone (merging useDroppable with the sortable context) so cards can be dropped even when the list is empty, and I'll resolve the destination column by checking whether `over.id` matches a card (use its columnId) or a column directly.

I'm also adding a floating trash dropzone that appears only while dragging, using useDroppable with id 'trash' — dropping a card there deletes it, which is safer and more discoverable than inferring deletion from dragging off the board entirely.

I'll reuse existing API helpers like updateCard, moveCard, deleteCard, addCard, addColumn, renameColumn, deleteColumn, and createBoard, plus add a reorderCards helper that optimistically updates local state and persists position changes via PATCH calls after drag end. I'm structuring the rendering into a SortableCard component using useSortable and a Column component combining useDroppable with SortableContext.

For the multi-container drag setup, I'll wrap each column's content in useDroppable alongside its SortableContext so empty columns can still receive dropped cards, following dnd-kit's standard multi-container pattern. I'll also add a search bar that filters cards by title and description.

There's an actual console error here unlike the main Kodely app, even though both render a script tag inside head the same way. I should check whether the main app ever actually had this warning but went unnoticed, and figure out what's different about Next.js 16's handling here.

This is likely React 19's newer behavior flagging manually placed `<script>` tags that aren't hoisted through `next/script`, since plain inline scripts without async/precedence attributes can trigger hydration identity warnings. The fix is to switch the theme script in layout.tsx to use Next's `Script` component with `strategy="beforeInteractive"`, which is built exactly for this no-flash-theme pattern and is hydration-safe.

content.text: That's a real warning — React 19/Next 16 wants inline scripts via `next/script`, not a raw `<script>` tag. Let's fix it properly.

Structure confirmed correct: 2 glow layers (both rings behind, correctly inset), composer at 95% opacity sitting above them, text visible. Both fixes are in place and verified as far as this environment allows.

## Summary

**Root causes found and fixed** in [PromptHero.tsx](components/marketing/PromptHero.tsx):

1. **Glow washing over the text** — not actually a z-index bug; the composer box was translucent (`bg-white/45`, `dark:bg-white/[0.06]`) with backdrop-blur, so the intense glow sitting directly behind bled straight through the glass onto the text. Fixed by making the composer 95% opaque (`bg-white/95` / `dark:bg-neutral-950/95`) so the glow only ever reads as a halo outside the box edges.
2. **Glow "disappearing"** — rebuilt as two counter-rotating conic-gradient rings (matching the Gemini reference you sent) at a fixed, always-visible opacity — nothing cycles down toward invisible, and it no longer depends on any JS animation ticker that could stall.

Found it — this is a fundamentally different bug than I diagnosed before, and it explains every previous failure. I was rotating the entire rectangular ring shape with `transform: rotate()`. A wide, non-square rectangle rotated around its center swings its corners way outside its own footprint at angles like 30°–60° (that's the giant diamond in your screenshot), then swings back into alignment near 0°/90°/180°/270° — which is exactly what reads as "appears, then disappears" as it cycles. That's the real root cause across every attempt so far.

The correct technique (and what Gemini's actual effect does) is: **never rotate the ring's shape at all** — keep it perfectly static, and instead rotate the gradient's color angle *inside* the fixed ring using an animatable CSS custom property (`@property`). The ring geometry never moves; only the color chases around it.

content.text:
Confirmed by the DOM — this is the bug, and the evidence is unambiguous:

1. The root page div (`relative min-h-screen bg-white …`) has an **opaque background** (`lab(2.75381 0 0)`), with `z-index: auto`, `opacity: 1`, no transform — so it does **not** create a stacking context.
2. That means any descendant at `z-index: -10` paints **behind that opaque background** → invisible.
3. The only reason the glow was *ever* visible: the `<Reveal>` wrapper directly above it shows `opacity: 0` **and `transform: true`** — both of which create a temporary stacking context that trapped the `-z-10` layers inside it, keeping them visible *while the reveal animated*. When the reveal finishes, Framer Motion sets opacity to 1 and clears the transform — the stacking context evaporates, and the glow drops behind the page background.

That is precisely *"appears for a few milliseconds, then no more glow after that"* — and it's why swapping between `@property`, CSS masks, conic gradients, Framer Motion, and clip+rotate never mattered. Every one of those was painting correctly; all of them were being hidden behind the page background a moment later.

Now verified fixed: `glowZIndex: "auto"` (paints above the page background) and `composerZIndex: "10"` (still above the glow, so text stays clean).

Both changes verified:

**Focus glow removed** — `shadowIdenticalOnFocus: true`, so clicking in no longer adds a second glow fighting the ring. Focus is still signalled (required for keyboard users) via a quiet border-color shift instead.

**Liquid-glass drip added** — droplets bead on the bottom edge and fall as you type:
- `backdrop-filter: blur(3px) saturate(1.6)` — real refraction of what's behind them, which is what makes it read as glass rather than a colored dot
- Organic asymmetric `border-radius`, a bright inset top highlight, and a brand-tinted underside
- The fall animation squashes the blob at the edge, **necks** as it detaches (narrow + tall), then thins as it falls — that stretch is what sells "liquid"
- Slight random sideways drift so they don't fall dead straight
- Throttled to ~1 per 170ms (verified: 40 rapid keystrokes → 3 droplets, not 40)
- Each removes itself on `animationend` — no timers, so the list can't leak
- Rendered as siblings of the composer, since it's `overflow-hidden` and would otherwise clip them exactly at the edge they need to fall past

One thing worth flagging: I hit the same class of bug as earlier — `backdrop-filter` written in `globals.css` was being stripped by Lightning CSS down to only the `-webkit-` prefix and computed to `none`. I moved it to an inline style (which bypasses that transform) and left a note in both files explaining why, so it doesn't get "cleaned up" back into the stylesheet later.

Now I'm investigating why the HeroMock wrapped in Reveal isn't showing a scroll entrance animation—since it uses whileInView with a shrunk viewport margin, and the HeroMock is already partially visible on page load, the animation likely never triggers because it's considered already in view.

I'm checking whether HeroMock's perspective and rotation transforms could be conflicting with Reveal's own transform animation, but they're on separate elements so that shouldn't be the issue. It's possible the animation does fire but is too subtle for this large mockup, so I want to empirically verify by checking the element's opacity state before and after scrolling into view using the IntersectionObserver behavior that whileInView relies on.

I realize the sandbox freezes animations, so Reveal-wrapped elements show opacity 0 there even though they clearly animate fine in the user's actual browser for other content like the headline and text. The real question is why HeroMock specifically wouldn't animate for them — and I'm now wondering if it's simply because HeroMock is already visible on initial page load, so by the time they scroll, there's nothing left to reveal.

Given the hero section's padding and typical viewport heights, HeroMock's top edge likely sits right at or just below the fold, meaning on taller windows it's already in view when the page loads and animates immediately rather than on scroll. ########## Shipped — Live in Prod (17) ##########

1. Phase 1 core loop is LIVE at kodely.me (2026-08-17)
   Auth (signup/login, scrypt password hashing, hashed session tokens) + credit ledger (250 free signup credits, 1 credit ≈ $0.002 real spend) + the codegen agent loop (Claude Sonnet 5, effort tuned high-on-create/medium-on-edit, tool-based write_file/delete_file, cache_control on the system prompt) + a chat-rail + live-preview editor + one-click Publish to a real *.kodely.site subdomain. Every new signup gets a seeded, genuinely-designed onboarding project (a coffee-shop site) instead of an empty dashboard. A build that fails is recorded but never charged — the anti-bill-shock promise is enforced in code (app/api/generate/route.ts), not just copy. Verified end-to-end on prod: signup → seeded project → generate → preview → publish → public serving, all over HTTPS.

2. Publish-time secret-leak scan (shipped)
   lib/secret-scan.ts blocks Publish (not generation) if a draft file contains something that looks like a real credential (AWS keys, Stripe/OpenAI/Anthropic-shaped keys, Google API keys, PEM private keys, JWTs) — because *.kodely.site serves published files to the public internet with no auth. Verified live on prod by injecting a fake Stripe key into a draft and confirming publish returns 400 and does not go live.

3. Read-only admin cost/margin dashboard (shipped, /admin)
   Owner-only (role=ADMIN gate) view of every Build row: real cost (from metered token usage), credits charged, derived gross margin $ and %, recent-build table with status. Unit economics is Kodely's #1 existential risk per the research — this gives visibility from day one instead of flying blind. No promotion path to ADMIN role exists yet (deliberately out of scope for this wave).

4. Stripe credit top-ups wired, INERT until real keys are set (shipped, gated)
   Full money-path: fixed server-side credit packs ($9/500, $40/2500, $90/6000 — client only ever sends a pack id, never an amount), Stripe Checkout session creation, and a signature-verified webhook that grants credits ONLY on confirmed payment (never the client-side success redirect) with a StripeEvent claim-row guarding against double-grant on webhook retries. Currently returns a clean 503 'Billing isn't set up yet' everywhere — needs real STRIPE_SECRET_KEY + STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET before it does anything. OWNER ACTION: create a Stripe account/keys when ready to accept real payment.

5. ✅ RESOLVED — *.kodely.site nginx fix applied (2026-08-17)
   Found + diagnosed 2026-08-17: the Kodely VM's internal nginx (/etc/nginx/sites-enabled/kodely) still routes kodely.site and *.kodely.site to a leftover static placeholder directory from initial provisioning (root /var/www/kodely-site-router), never updated to proxy into the Next.js app like the kodely.me block does. Effect: Publish succeeds and returns a URL, but visiting it shows a generic Cloudflare/nginx error page instead of the real site — the one-click-deploy feature is currently broken end-to-end on the serving side. FIX IS READY, blocked only on sudo (harness classifier gates system-config edits from chat regardless of approval): swap that block's `root ...; index ...;` for the same `proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:3000;` block already used by kodely.me. ########## Builder / Editor UX (30) ##########
1. Editor workspace: chat + live preview
   The core canvas — an AI chat/command rail beside a live, interactive preview of the running site. This IS the product; everything else orbits it. Fast, resizable, keyboar…
2. Click-to-edit on the canvas
   Select any element in the preview and edit it directly (text, color, spacing, swap image) — by clicking or by telling the AI 'make this bigger'. The difference between a …
3. Visual inspector / property panel
   A panel to tweak the selected element's typography, color, spacing, and layout without prompts — for users who want direct control. Writes back to the same code.
4. Version history, checkpoints & rollback
   Every AI change and manual edit is a saved checkpoint; one-click restore to any prior state. Removes the fear of 'the AI broke my site' — a top competitor complaint.
5. Undo / redo across AI + manual edits
   A unified history stack so undo works the same whether the last change came from a prompt or a click. Table stakes users assume exists.
6. Code view + inline editing + export
   Show the real generated code, let advanced users edit it inline, and export/download or push to GitHub. Backs the 'you own the code' ownership moat.
7. Responsive preview (device frames)
   Preview desktop / tablet / mobile and fix responsive issues per breakpoint. Generated sites must look right on phones or they're worthless.
8. Comments / annotations on the preview
   Pin comments to elements for feedback/review (client ↔ agency). A cheap retention + collaboration lever.
9. Multi-page & file management
   Create/manage multiple pages and assets in one project, with navigation wiring. Real sites aren't one page.
10. Streaming generation UX (stop / regenerate / branch)
   Watch the build stream in, stop it, regenerate a section, or branch an alternative — reuse Nxeon's Build-with-AI streaming + graceful-degrade UX.
11. Plan-before-spend mode
   Before a costly build, show the plan + a credit estimate for the user to approve/edit. The core anti-bill-shock lever, in the editor.
12. Error-recovery UX (auto-fix loop, visible)
   When a build fails or errors, show the diagnosis and the AI's fix attempts inline instead of dumping a stack trace. Reliability people can see is reliability they trust.
13. Visual database / schema editor
   Create tables, fields and relations visually (or by prompt) — 'add a bookings table'. The backend-depth wedge vs frontend-only builders.
14. Auth builder (roles, providers, protected pages)
   'Add login' produces working auth with roles and protected routes — no config. Backend that actually works, not a screenshot.
15. Secrets & env-var vault
   A place to store API keys/secrets that are injected server-side and never shipped to the client bundle. Security-by-default; prevents the #1 leak class.
16. Payments builder (Stripe from a prompt)
   'Add a subscription/paywall' wires real Stripe checkout + webhooks. Monetizable backend from one sentence.
17. Publish flow: draft → live + preview links
   Explicit publish with shareable preview URLs and draft/prod separation, so editing never breaks the live site.
18. Custom domain connect + guided DNS (Nxeon bridge UX)
   The go-live UI: attach yourdomain.com, guided DNS records, verification, SSL — powered by the Nxeon partner API. The monetization handoff, made usable.
19. Deployment history + rollback to any live version
   List past deploys and roll production back instantly. Ops-grade safety for non-ops users.
20. Asset & media management (upload, logo, stock, AI images)
   Image/logo/video upload + a stock-image library + AI image generation, with hosting/optimization. Real sites need real photos; every competitor has this and it's currentl…
21. Seed / sample-data generation for previews & QA
   Auto-populate generated DB tables with realistic demo data so a bookings/CRM/store app looks alive in preview and can be QA'd. You can't demo (or trust) a data app agains…
22. Forms + submission handling
   Contact/lead/booking forms that route submissions to an inbox + email/notification. Table-stakes for the SMB/business-owner buyer; currently nowhere on the board.
23. i18n / multi-language for generated sites
   A localization story for generated output (and multi-currency, reusing Nxeon geo work) — a real gap and a differentiator for the global SMB/agency audience.
24. Post-launch content/CMS editing for non-devs
   A structured way to edit products/blog posts/menu items after launch without prompting (beyond click-to-edit text). Post-launch editing is under-served and drives retenti…
25. User-facing SEO / meta panel
   Per-page title/meta/OG-image/slug editing in the editor. Auto-SEO handles generation; this is the surface to edit it. Complements the generated-site auto-SEO card.
26. Accessibility checker surfaced in the editor
   Surface a11y issues inline like the security-scan banner ('Accessibility: 3 issues → fix'). The engine has an a11y budget but nothing shows the user.
27. Command palette / keyboard shortcuts
   'Keyboard-friendly' is asserted but never carded — a power-user/perf lever; complements slash-commands.
28. Connection-loss / sandbox-death recovery UX
   Explicit reconnect / 'build resumed' / 'hibernated project rehydrating' states in the editor. Project persistence exists in Tech, but the user-facing offline/error state …
29. Data / CSV import into a generated app
   Import a spreadsheet to seed an internal tool / CRM (a real JTBD from the Market column). The Import card covers Figma/URL/repo only.
30. Builder UI accessibility (WCAG / screen reader)
   The Kodely editor itself must be accessible, distinct from the a11y of generated output. Broadens the addressable audience.

I've read both boards end to end — 724 cards. Here's what actually needs doing.

## Your own direct requests ("manual stuff" — 3 cards)

| Card | Status |
|---|---|
| **prompt box glow bug** — *"appear around the border, not overtop"* | ✅ **Done this session** — should be moved to Done |
| **button hover effect** — *"emulate Nxeon; hover effect only, not a constant glow running in the background"* | ❌ **Not started** — actionable right now |
| **pilates picture** | ⚠️ **Empty description** — I can't act on it; what did you want here? |

## The real blockers (Phase 0 — everything else is gated behind these)

1. **Funded Anthropic key + multi-key pool + hard spend caps** — flagged as *LAUNCH BLOCKER*; single key, no failover, already caused one cost scare.
2. **Rotate exposed service keys** — the board itself records that **two live keys were pasted in plaintext**. This is the most urgent item on either board, and there's still no rotation runbook.
3. **Off-site backups + DR** — no snapshot, no RTO/RPO, no restore drill. "Flagged repeatedly, still nothing built."
4. **Tier numbers (names/prices/credits)** — Stripe is fully wired but returns 503 until you decide these. *You said you'd send these and haven't yet — this is the single cheapest unblock on the board.*
5. **Pre-GA security review** — no pen test on the build/publish path.

## Security debt cluster (highest risk, given you *host* generated sites)

No content moderation on publish, sandbox not hardened (Firecracker deferred), no secret-scan-on-generate (only on publish), no disclosure policy. The Risks column is blunt: Kodely **becomes the host** of any phishing site it generates → IP-blocklisting/depeering exposure.

## The actual deploy path (from your board)

Prod deploys from GitHub, not from here:

```bash
git clone git@github.com:santino1233/kodely.git
```

# Kodely service-key rotation runbook

Owner: Kodely operator (single-operator today).
Covers **Kodely's own service credentials** — not end-user passwords or the
secrets inside generated sites.

Board cards this closes: *"Service-key rotation runbook"* (My Roadmap, Phase A)
and *"Service-key rotation runbook (Anthropic / Stripe / Nxeon / Cloudflare)"*
(Trust, Legal & Compliance).

## Why this exists

Two live keys were pasted in plaintext into a board card. A one-off "change the
key" is not a fix — a credential with no rotation process is a credential you
cannot reason about. This defines a standing process so exposure is a routine
event, not a crisis.

**Assume any secret that has ever appeared in chat, a board card, a ticket, a
screenshot, or a file on the Desktop is compromised and must be rotated.**

---

## 1. Standing rules

1. **Secrets live in exactly two places:** the issuing provider's console, and
   `/opt/kodely/.env` + `/opt/kodely-staging/.env` on VM 110. Nowhere else.
2. **`.env` is gitignored and never leaves the VM.** Do not copy it to your
   laptop, do not paste it into a chat, do not commit it. The VM is the source
   of truth (same rule as `package-lock.json`).
3. **Never paste a secret into a Kanban card, chat message, or commit message** —
   including "temporarily". Reference the *name* (`ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`), never
   the value.
4. **Prod and staging get separate credentials** wherever the provider allows
   it, so a staging leak can't touch production or real money.
5. **Rotate forward, then revoke.** Create the new credential, deploy it, verify
   it works, and only then revoke the old one. Revoking first causes an outage.
6. Any secret file that must exist on disk temporarily gets `chmod 600` and is
   deleted immediately after use — not left on the Desktop.

---

## 2. Secret inventory

| Secret | Used by | Lives in | If leaked | Rotate |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` | Codegen agent (every build) | prod + staging `.env` | Unbounded spend on your account; the #1 cost risk on the board | Quarterly + on exposure |
| `STRIPE_SECRET_KEY` | Checkout session creation | prod `.env` | Real money movement, refunds, customer data | Quarterly + on exposure |
| `STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET` | Webhook signature verification | prod `.env` | Forged webhooks → **free credits granted without payment** | Quarterly + on exposure |
| `DATABASE_URL` (Postgres role `kodely`) | Prisma, both envs | prod + staging `.env` | Full read/write of all user accounts, projects, credit ledger | Semi-annually + on exposure |
| `GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET` | Google OAuth sign-in | prod `.env` | Account takeover via forged OAuth flow | Semi-annually + on exposure |
| GitHub deploy key (`~/.ssh/kodely_github`) | VM → GitHub, write access | VM 110, `kodely` user | **Supply chain**: attacker pushes to `main`, which deploys | Semi-annually + on exposure |
| Host → VM SSH key (`/root/.ssh/id_rsa`) | Proxmox host → VM 110 | Proxmox host root | Full VM control | Semi-annually + on exposure |
| Cloudflare API / tunnel token | DNS + edge for kodely.me / kodely.site | Cloudflare + VM | DNS hijack of your domains; traffic interception | Semi-annually + on exposure |
| Nxeon partner API signing key | Kodely ↔ Nxeon bridge | both sides | Cross-product trust boundary breach | Semi-annually + on exposure |

**Session tokens** need no rotation entry: they're random and stored
`scrypt`-hashed (`lib/auth.ts`), with no standalone signing secret. To
invalidate all sessions, delete the session rows.

---

## 3. Routine rotation (quarterly)

Do these one at a time. Verify each before starting the next.

### Anthropic

1. Anthropic Console → API keys → **Create key** (`kodely-prod-<YYYYMM>`).
2. On VM 110, edit `/opt/kodely/.env`, replace the value, then:
   ```bash
   sudo systemctl restart kodely
   ```
3. Verify with a **real generation** (health check alone won't exercise the key):
   sign in to kodely.me, create a project, confirm the build succeeds.
4. Repeat for staging with a separate key, restarting `kodely-staging`.
5. Only now: revoke the old key in the console.

> Prod **and** staging `.env` were both missing `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` once and it
> wasn't noticed until a real generation was attempted. A green `/api/health`
> does not prove the codegen path works.

### Stripe

1. Stripe Dashboard → Developers → API keys → **Roll** the secret key. Choose a
   grace period rather than immediate expiry.
2. Update `STRIPE_SECRET_KEY` in prod `.env`, restart `kodely`.
3. Webhook secret: Developers → Webhooks → endpoint → **Roll signing secret**.
   Update `STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET`, restart.
4. Verify: send a test event from the Stripe dashboard and confirm it is
   accepted (a bad `STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET` fails *closed* — credits silently
   stop being granted, which is easy to miss).
5. Let the old key expire.

### Postgres role

```bash
sudo -u postgres psql -c "ALTER ROLE kodely WITH PASSWORD 'NEW_PASSWORD';"
```
Update `DATABASE_URL` in **both** `/opt/kodely/.env` and
`/opt/kodely-staging/.env` (URL-encode any special characters), then:
```bash
sudo systemctl restart kodely kodely-staging
```
Verify: load a page that reads the DB (dashboard or `/blog`).

### Google OAuth

1. Google Cloud Console → Credentials → the OAuth client → add a new secret.
2. Update `GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET` in prod `.env`, restart.
3. Verify a real Google sign-in end to end.
4. Delete the old secret.

### GitHub deploy key

```bash
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -f ~/.ssh/kodely_github_new -C "kodely-app@10.20.0.30"
```
Add the new public key to `github.com/santino1233/kodely` → Deploy keys (allow
write). Point `~/.ssh/config` at the new file, then verify:
```bash
git -C /opt/kodely fetch origin
```
Only once that succeeds: delete the old deploy key on GitHub and remove the old
private key from the VM.

---

## 4. Emergency rotation (suspected exposure)

Work top to bottom. Do **not** wait for a maintenance window.

1. **Contain first.** Revoke immediately — before any tidy-up — if the exposure
   is public or the key can move money or spend:
   - Anthropic: delete the key in the console.
   - Stripe: roll with **immediate** expiry.
   - GitHub deploy key: delete it (this also stops attacker-triggered deploys).
2. **Rotate** using the routine procedure above; a short outage is acceptable
   here, unlike routine rotation.
3. **Assess blast radius:**
   - Anthropic → Console usage graph for unexpected spend.
   - Stripe → recent payments/refunds; check the `StripeEvent` claim rows for
     credit grants without matching payments.
   - Postgres → unexpected `User` / credit-ledger rows.
   - GitHub → repo Audit log for pushes you didn't make; diff `main` against the
     last commit you recognise.
   - VM → `last`, `journalctl -u ssh`.
4. **Scrub the exposure** (board card, chat, file) — *after* rotating. Deleting
   the card first does not un-leak the key and loses the audit trail.
5. **Write it down**: what leaked, where, when, when it was rotated, what the
   usage review showed.

---

## 5. Immediate action items

These are known, currently-outstanding exposures.

- [ ] **Rotate the two keys pasted into the board card.** Still recorded as
      unrotated. Then edit the card to remove the values.
- [ ] **Three plaintext credential files on the Desktop** —
      `anthropic api key.txt`, `stripe_backup_code.txt`, `claude_code.pem`.
      A Desktop inside a synced OneDrive folder means these are also in cloud
      storage and version history. Rotate what they contain, then delete them
      and purge OneDrive's version history.
- [ ] **Check whether OneDrive has synced any `.env`.** `.gitignore` stops git,
      not file sync.
- [ ] Set a recurring quarterly reminder for §3.

---

## 6. Verification checklist

After **any** rotation:

```bash
curl -s https://kodely.me/api/health
curl -s https://staging.kodely.me/api/health
```

- [ ] Both return `{"ok":true}`
- [ ] A **real generation** completes (proves `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` and the DB)
- [ ] A publish serves on `*.kodely.site`
- [ ] Stripe test event accepted (if Stripe was rotated)
- [ ] Old credential confirmed revoked at the provider
- [ ] If a deploy was involved, `BUILD_ID` is newer than the deploy:
      ```bash
      ls -l /opt/kodely/.next/BUILD_ID
      ```
      `systemctl` reporting *active* proves the process is up — not that it is
      running the new code.

content.text:
You're right, and I contributed to it by building in the local copy. Let me name the actual problem and fix it properly.

## Why it's a mess

You have **four** places holding code, none of them authoritative:

| Location | State |
|---|---|
| `Desktop/Kodely` (local) | **Not a git repo** — no history, no diff, no branches |
| `santino1233/kodely` | The real repo, but behind staging |
| `/opt/kodely-staging` on VM | Has unpushed edits; `deploy.sh` will destroy them |
| `santino1233/kodelylocal` | One orphan commit, unclear role |

Because local isn't version-controlled, every port is what we just did by hand: diff two folders, decide file-by-file what's safe, hope nothing slipped. That doesn't scale, and it's exactly how `lib/agent.ts` eventually gets copied across and makes every prod build free.

## Two rules that fix most of it

**1. Never edit files on the VM.** That's what turned staging into an un-deployable trap. The VM should only ever run `deploy.sh`. Code changes happen in a repo and flow *to* it.

**2. Only one thing is authoritative: `origin/main` on GitHub.** Everything else is a checkout of it.

## The structural fix: one repo, a `personal` branch

The divergences are only **five files** — `lib/agent.ts`, the publish route, `package.json`, `.gitignore`, `tsconfig.json`. That's small enough to live as a *branch*, not a separate folder-fork.

Make `Desktop/Kodely` a real checkout of `santino1233/kodely` on a long-lived `personal` branch, with those five files as a single commit on top of `main`.

Day to day that gives you:

```bash
git log main..personal
```

— *exactly* what's personal, always visible. Then:

- **Port work up:** `git cherry-pick` the commit onto a branch off `main` → push → PR. No folder diffing, no manual file lists, no risk of `agent.ts` sneaking through.
- **Pull prod changes down:** `git rebase main` on `personal`.
- **Real history** on the local app for the first time — you can see what changed and undo things.

I'd also add a `.gitattributes` with `* text=auto eol=lf` to kill the CRLF noise, and delete or archive `kodelylocal` so there's one repo, not two.

## Later, if you want the branch to disappear entirely

Put the divergences behind env flags (`KODELY_ENGINE=sdk|api`, `KODELY_PROD_HOST`) so both code paths live in `main` and the local instance is just a different `.env`. Then there's no fork at all. That means touching `agent.ts`, so it's a deliberate follow-up — not today.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# ship.sh — take a commit from the local `personal` branch all the way to
# kodely.me: cherry-pick onto main, push, merge, deploy staging, verify,
# deploy prod, verify.
#
#   ./ship.sh                  ship the tip commit of `personal`
#   ./ship.sh <sha>            ship a specific commit
#   ./ship.sh <sha> --staging  stop after staging (don't touch prod)
#
# Refuses to run if the commit touches a personal-instance file (see
# FORBIDDEN below) — that guard is the whole point: lib/agent.ts reports
# zero token usage, so shipping it would make every prod build free.
set -euo pipefail

HOST=root@51.79.162.96          # Proxmox host
VM=kodely@10.20.0.30            # Kodely app VM
REPO=santino1233/kodely
GH="/c/Program Files/GitHub CLI/gh.exe"

# Files that must never leave the personal branch.
FORBIDDEN='^(lib/agent\.ts|app/api/projects/\[id\]/publish/route\.ts|package\.json|package-lock\.json|tsconfig\.json|\.gitignore|LOCAL-SETUP\.md|ship\.sh|skills/|AGENTS\.md|CLAUDE\.md)'

SHA="${1:-personal}"
STAGING_ONLY="${2:-}"

say() { printf '\n\033[1m== %s\033[0m\n' "$*"; }
die() { printf '\n\033[31mABORT: %s\033[0m\n' "$*" >&2; exit 1; }
vm()  { ssh -o BatchMode=yes -o ConnectTimeout=15 "$HOST" "ssh -o BatchMode=yes $VM \"$1\""; }

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- checks
say "Pre-flight"
[ -z "$(git status --porcelain)" ] || die "working tree is dirty — commit or stash first"
git fetch -q origin main
SHA_FULL=$(git rev-parse "$SHA")
SUBJECT=$(git log -1 --format=%s "$SHA_FULL")
echo "shipping: $(git rev-parse --short "$SHA_FULL")  $SUBJECT"

TOUCHED=$(git show --name-only --format= "$SHA_FULL")
echo "$TOUCHED" | sed '/^$/d' | sed 's/^/  /'

if echo "$TOUCHED" | grep -qE "$FORBIDDEN"; then
  echo
  echo "$TOUCHED" | grep -E "$FORBIDDEN" | sed 's/^/  !! /'
  die "commit touches personal-instance files (listed above). Split the commit."
fi

# ------------------------------------------------------------ branch+PR
BR="ship/$(git rev-parse --short "$SHA_FULL")"
say "Cherry-picking onto a branch off origin/main ($BR)"
ORIG_BRANCH=$(git rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD)
cleanup() { git cherry-pick --abort 2>/dev/null || true; git checkout -q "$ORIG_BRANCH" 2>/dev/null || true; }
trap cleanup ERR

git checkout -q -B "$BR" origin/main
git cherry-pick "$SHA_FULL" || die "cherry-pick conflicted — resolve manually"

say "Pushing $BR and merging into main"
git push -q -u origin "$BR"
git checkout -q main 2>/dev/null || git checkout -q -B main origin/main
git merge --ff-only "$BR" -q
git push -q origin main
NEW=$(git rev-parse --short main)
trap - ERR
git checkout -q "$ORIG_BRANCH"
echo "main is now $NEW"

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- deploy
ROLLBACK=$(vm 'cd /opt/kodely && git rev-parse --short HEAD')
say "Rollback point (current prod): $ROLLBACK"

deploy_and_verify() {
  local env="$1" url="$2" dir="$3"
  say "Deploying $env"
  vm "/home/kodely/deploy.sh $env 2>&1 | tail -3"

  say "Verifying $env"
  local head build behind
  head=$(vm "cd $dir && git rev-parse --short HEAD")
  behind=$(vm "cd $dir && git rev-list --count HEAD..origin/main")
  build=$(vm "stat -c %y $dir/.next/BUILD_ID | cut -d. -f1")
  echo "  HEAD=$head  behind_main=$behind  BUILD_ID=$build"
  [ "$head" = "$NEW" ] || die "$env HEAD ($head) != main ($NEW)"
  [ "$behind" = "0" ]  || die "$env is $behind commits behind main"

  local code
  for path in /api/health / /pricing /blog; do
    code=$(curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' -m 25 "$url$path")
    printf '  %-14s %s\n' "$path" "$code"
    [ "$code" = "200" ] || die "$env $path returned $code"
  done
}

deploy_and_verify staging https://staging.kodely.me /opt/kodely-staging

if [ "$STAGING_ONLY" = "--staging" ]; then
  say "Stopped after staging (--staging). Prod untouched."
  echo "When ready:  ssh $HOST 'ssh $VM \"/home/kodely/deploy.sh prod\"'"
  exit 0
fi

deploy_and_verify prod https://kodely.me /opt/kodely

say "Shipped"
echo "  main:     $NEW"
echo "  live:     https://kodely.me"
echo "  rollback: $ROLLBACK   (deploy.sh after 'git reset --hard $ROLLBACK')"

I deliberately did **not** ask you to paste SMTP credentials into chat; that's the exact practice the runbook we just wrote forbids. Add them directly on the VM instead.

You'll need a mailbox on your Mailcow (`mail.nxeon.cloud`) that's allowed to send as `kodely.me` — e.g. `noreply@kodely.me`, or reuse `hello@kodely.me`.

```bash
SMTP_HOST=mail.nxeon.cloud
SMTP_PORT=587
SMTP_USER=noreply@kodely.me
SMTP_PASS=the-mailbox-password
MAIL_FROM=Kodely <noreply@kodely.me>
```

Then:

```bash
sudo systemctl restart kodely-staging
```

Tell me when that's done and I'll send a real test message through staging, confirm it lands in `hello@kodely.me`, and only then deploy prod.

| | |
|---|---|
| **Transport** | Your existing Nxeon mail server — no new vendor, no cost. `kodely.me`'s MX already points at `mail.nxeon.cloud` and SPF includes `nxeon.cloud`, so mail passes authentication with no new DNS. |

| **Header injection blocked** | CR/LF stripped from anything reaching a header — otherwise `"\r\nBcc: ..."` in the name field turns this into an open relay. |
| **Honeypot** | Returns `200 {ok:true}` so bots think they succeeded and don't retry. |
| **Throttle** | 5/hour per IP — verified: 5 through, 6th returns 429. |
| **Errors** | SMTP details logged server-side, never returned to callers. |
