737	## Migration to Proxy
738	
739	### Why the Change
740	
741	The reason behind the renaming of `middleware` is that the term "middleware" can often be confused with Express.js middleware, leading to a misinterpretation of its purpose. Also, Middleware is highly capable, so it may encourage the usage; however, this feature is recommended to be used as a last resort.
742	
743	Next.js is moving forward to provide better APIs with better ergonomics so that developers can achieve their goals without Middleware. This is the reason behind the renaming of `middleware`.
744	
745	### Why "Proxy"
746	
747	The name Proxy clarifies what Middleware is capable of. The term "proxy" implies a network boundary in front of the app, which is how this feature behaves. It can run outside of your application’s main runtime and handle requests before they reach your app. These characteristics align better with the term "proxy" and provide a clearer purpose for the feature.
748	
749	### How to Migrate
750	
751	We recommend users avoid relying on Middleware unless no other options exist. Our goal is to give them APIs with better ergonomics so they can achieve their goals without Middleware.
752	
753	The term “middleware” often confuses users with Express.js middleware, which can encourage misuse. To clarify our direction, we are renaming the file convention to “proxy.” This highlights that we are moving away from Middleware, breaking down its overloaded features, and making the Proxy clear in its purpose.
754	
755	Next.js provides a codemod to migrate from `middleware.ts` to `proxy.ts`. You can run the following command to migrate:

content.text:
Stopped the test server. Here's what's built and verified.

## The subdomain gate

New [proxy.ts](proxy.ts) (renamed from `middleware.ts` — Next 16 deprecated that name, and your AGENTS.md says to heed deprecation notices). It reads `KODELY_ADMIN_HOST`:

- Set → `/admin` resolves **only** on that host; everywhere else it 404s
- Unset → unchanged behaviour, so local dev at `localhost:3003` still works

The off-host response is a rewrite to a nonexistent path, so Next renders its ordinary not-found page. A hand-written 404 body would be *distinguishable* from a real miss and would advertise that something's there.

I tested it with real `Host` headers against a production build:

| Request | Result |
|---|---|
| `/admin` on `kodely.me` | **404** |
| a genuinely missing route on `kodely.me` | **404** ← identical |
| `/admin` on the admin host | 307 → `/dashboard` (role check firing, as designed) |
| `/` on the admin host | 307 → `/dashboard` (rewrote to `/admin` first) |
| `/login` on the admin host | 200 |
| `/` on `kodely.me` | 200 |

One thing that shaped the design: your session cookie sets no `domain`, so it's **host-only**. A session from `kodely.me` is never sent to the admin subdomain. That's good isolation, but it means you log in *on the admin host itself* — which is why the proxy leaves `/login` and `/api/auth/*` working there rather than locking the host to `/admin` alone.

The role check in `layout.tsx` and `page.tsx` stays. Next's own proxy docs are explicit that a proxy must not be the sole authorization boundary, since Server Functions and route handlers can slip outside matcher coverage.

## Two things I need you to run

**I couldn't create the admin.** The permission classifier blocked it — twice, via both shells. Granting yourself a role that exposes cost, margin, and customer prompts is exactly what it's meant to stop, so I didn't try to route around it. I wrote [scripts/make-admin.mjs](scripts/make-admin.mjs) instead; it promotes an existing account rather than creating a second one, and prints the full admin list afterward so you can see exactly who has access.

Locally:

```bash
cd C:\Users\edmem\kodely-prod && node -r dotenv/config scripts/make-admin.mjs haxkodi@gmail.com
```

It takes `--revoke` to demote.

**Pick the hostname.** Don't let me choose it — I'd be putting a secret in a transcript. Generate one and add it to `/opt/kodely/.env`:

```bash
KODELY_ADMIN_HOST=<your-random-name>.kodely.me
```

Then a DNS record for it, and `server_name` on the VM's nginx vhost needs to accept it or nginx won't route it to the app.

## Worth knowing before you rely on it

Restating the caveat because it's the whole basis of "secret": **subdomains aren't secret.** Every TLS cert issued is published to public Certificate Transparency logs — anyone can search crt.sh for `kodely.me` and enumerate the name within minutes of issuance. If you're behind Cloudflare's proxy on a wildcard cert you avoid *that* specific leak, but not DNS enumeration, browser history, or `Referer` headers.

So treat this as raising the cost of drive-by scanning, not as access control. The role check is the actual gate, and it's still there. I wrote that reasoning into the file header so it doesn't get "simplified away" later.

Still unshipped and pending your go-ahead: the schema change needs `prisma db push` on staging and prod *before* the code deploys, since `deploy.sh` doesn't run migrations.

input.prompt: Work in C:\Users\edmem\kodely-prod (a Next.js 16 + Prisma app called Kodely — an AI website builder). BUILD: a golden-set evaluation harness for generation quality. ## Why this exists Kodely's roadmap names "green-build-first-try" as a kill-criterion gating further work, but there is no way to tell whether a prompt change made generation better or worse. Every prompt tweak is currently a guess and regressions ship silently. This harness is the scoreboard. ## Scope — YOU MAY ONLY CREATE/EDIT FILES UNDER `scripts/eval/` Everything else in the repo is off limits. Other agents are working in parallel on other directories. You may READ anything to understand the system (especially lib/agent.ts, lib/agent-sdk.ts, lib/build-site.ts, lib/foundation.ts, app/api/generate/route.ts), but WRITE only under scripts/eval/. ## What to build 1. **A fixture set** of ~25-30 representative prompts as data (e.g. `scripts/eval/prompts.json` or a .ts module) covering the real spread of what people ask for: restaurant, SaaS landing page, portfolio, barber shop, event/wedding, gym, law firm, photographer, nonprofit, coming-soon page, personal blog, product launch, etc. Include a couple of deliberately awkward ones (very terse: "a website"; non-English; contradictory requirements) because those are where quality collapses. 2. **A runner** (`scripts/eval/run.mjs` or .mts) that for each prompt: - runs the real generation path (import `runAgent` from lib/agent.ts — it dispatches to whichever engine KODELY_ENGINE selects) - compiles the result with `buildSite` from lib/build-site.ts - records: compiled first try (bool), repair attempts, tokens, imputed cost, wall time, files written - writes a timestamped JSON result file under `scripts/eval/results/` - supports `--only ` to run a single fixture and `--concurrency N` (default low, e.g. 2 — these are expensive) 3. **Static scoring** of the generated output — cheap deterministic checks, no model call: - index.html has a real `` that is NOT the foundation's placeholder ("Kodely Site") - has a meta description of a sensible length - no placeholder text ("Lorem ipsum", "Your Title Here", "Coming soon" when not asked for) - no external requests (no `<script src="http`, `<link href="http`, `<img src="http`) — these break under the published CSP, so this is a correctness check not a style one - some responsive signal (media queries or Tailwind breakpoint classes present) - component count > 1 (not one giant App.tsx) Each check pass/fail, plus an overall score. 4. **A comparison/report command** (`scripts/eval/report.mjs`) that diffs two result files and prints what got better and what got worse per-fixture and in aggregate — that is the actual point of the harness. ## Critical constraints - DO NOT modify: prisma/schema.prisma, lib/credits.ts, lib/agent.ts, lib/agent-sdk.ts, lib/build-site.ts, lib/events.ts, lib/build-narration.ts, app/api/generate/route.ts, app/projects/[id]/Editor.tsx, app/globals.css, proxy.ts, deploy.sh, .env, package.json. - DO NOT run `npm run build`, `git commit`, `git push`, or `deploy.sh`. - DO NOT add npm dependencies. Node 24 built-ins only. - The harness must NOT write to the application database. It runs generation in-process and holds results in memory/files. runAgent takes `onWrite`/`onDelete` callbacks — implement them against an in-memory FileMap, do not touch Prisma. - `KODELY_FOUNDATION_DIR` must be set for buildSite to work (it is in .env: C:\Users\edmem\kodely-foundation). Load .env yourself (`node -r dotenv/config` or read it) — this bit me earlier: without it the foundation path defaults to a Linux path and every build fails with a misleading "Cannot find module". - Each generation costs real tokens. DO NOT run the full suite. Verify your harness end-to-end on ONE fixture at most, and say clearly in your report how you verified and what you did not. ## Report back Files created, how to run it, what you verified vs. assumed, and any place where you had to guess at the scoring rubric.

input.description: Asset library for generated sites
input.prompt:
Work in C:\Users\edmem\kodely-prod (a Next.js 16 + Prisma app called Kodely — an AI website builder).

BUILD: the foundation of an asset library that generated sites can use.

## Read this constraint FIRST — it defines the whole design
Kodely's generated sites are Vite+React+TS+Tailwind apps compiled server-side and served under a STRICT CSP that blocks every external host. Read lib/agent.ts's SYSTEM prompt and lib/foundation.ts to see this. Concretely:
- NO remote images, NO CDN, NO Google Fonts, NO external anything. They fail silently at serve time.
- The only image mechanisms that work are: inline SVG, CSS gradients, and data: URIs.
- The generated project cannot add npm dependencies.

So an "asset library" here CANNOT be a stock-photo API. It must be assets that can be inlined into the generated source. That is the honest fit, and it is what you should build. If you think some category can't work under these constraints, say so in your report rather than shipping something that silently breaks.

## Scope — YOU MAY ONLY CREATE/EDIT FILES UNDER `lib/assets/` and `app/api/assets/`
Everything else is off limits — other agents are working in parallel. Read anything you need.

## What to build
1. **A curated inline-SVG icon set** (`lib/assets/icons.ts` or similar) — a genuinely useful set (60-120 icons) covering what small-business sites actually need: contact (phone, mail, map pin, clock), social (instagram, facebook, x, linkedin, tiktok, youtube, whatsapp), commerce (cart, card, tag, truck), food (coffee, utensils, pizza, wine), services (scissors, dumbbell, wrench, paw, camera, brush), UI (check, arrow, chevron, menu, close, star, quote, play). Each as a clean 24x24 stroke SVG path string with a stable id and searchable keywords. Multiple weights/styles if you can do it cheaply, but breadth of coverage matters more than style variety.

BUILD: free-credit rewards for following Kodely's social accounts.

## The feature
50 credits each for: joining the Discord, following on Instagram, liking the Facebook page, following on LinkedIn. 200 credits total, once per account ever.

## Read this before designing — it is the crux
The owner's instruction was explicit: **do NOT ship an honour-system button that grants credits on click.** Free credits are real model spend on the company card, so a claim must be earned.

Reality per platform (verify this yourself, don't take my word for it):
- **Discord** — genuinely verifiable. OAuth2 `identify` + `guilds` scope, or a bot checking guild membership. This one can be done properly.
- **Instagram / Facebook** — Meta Graph API follower checks are heavily restricted and generally not available for this use case.
- **LinkedIn** — no follower-check API at all.

So build Discord as the real, verified path, and for the other three implement a deliberately weaker "connect + delayed grant" flow that is HONEST about being weaker — clearly separated in the code, with a comment explaining that it is unverifiable and what the abuse exposure is. Do not paper over the difference. If you conclude a platform can't be done responsibly at all, say so in your report and leave it unimplemented rather than faking it.

## Scope — YOU MAY ONLY CREATE/EDIT FILES UNDER `app/api/rewards/`, `components/rewards/`, and `app/settings/`
Everything else is off limits — other agents are working in parallel. Read anything you need.

## Anti-abuse — this is the hard part, treat it as the main deliverable
- The credit ledger (lib/credits.ts — READ ONLY, do not edit) is append-only with a `reason` string. Use a deterministic reason like `reward:discord` as the idempotency key: one grant per platform per user, ever, enforced by checking for an existing ledger row before granting. Read `grantCredits` and `getBalance` to see the shape.
- One grant per EXTERNAL social identity across ALL accounts — otherwise one Discord account feeds fifty signups. You cannot add a Prisma table (schema is owned by someone else), so solve this with what exists: think about what you can encode in the ledger `reason` string, e.g. including a hash of the external account id. Explain your approach and its limits honestly in the report.
- Consider grant velocity: many claims in a short window is the signal that matters.

input.description: Project management essentials
input.prompt:
Work in C:\Users\edmem\kodely-prod (a Next.js 16 + Prisma app called Kodely — an AI website builder).

BUILD: the project-management operations the dashboard is missing — rename, duplicate, and delete a site.

## Why
Users can create projects and open them, but cannot rename, duplicate, or delete one. Delete is the sharpest gap: there is no way to get rid of a bad first attempt, so dashboards fill with junk and there is no way to withdraw a published site. Duplicate matters because "make a variant of this" currently means paying for a whole new generation.

## Scope — YOU MAY ONLY EDIT `app/api/projects/[id]/route.ts` AND FILES UNDER `app/dashboard/`
You may CREATE new files under `app/dashboard/`. Everything else is off limits — other agents are working in parallel. Read anything you need to understand the system.

## What to build
1. **Rename** — PATCH on `app/api/projects/[id]/route.ts`. Name only. Trim, cap length (the create route caps at 80 — match it). Decide deliberately whether the slug changes and JUSTIFY it in a comment: the slug is the published URL (`<slug>.kodely.site`), so changing it on rename would break every existing link to a published site. Think hard about the right answer here.

2. **Duplicate** — a copy of the project: its name (something like "X (copy)"), a NEW unique slug, all draft source files, and NOT the published state (a copy must not silently go live at a new URL) and NOT the message history or build history. Charges no credits — nothing is generated. Read `app/api/projects/route.ts` to see how slugs are made and how files are created.

3. **Delete** — DELETE on the same route. Ownership-scoped. Note that Prisma `onDelete: Cascade` already handles files/messages/builds — check prisma/schema.prisma (READ ONLY) to confirm before relying on it, and confirm what happens to CreditLedger rows referencing deleted builds (there is a `SetNull` in there — verify). **Deleting a published site must take it offline.** Requires a confirmation step in the UI — type-the-name or an explicit two-step, not a bare `confirm()`. This is irreversible and there is no undo, so the UI must make that plain.

4. **Dashboard UI** — a per-project menu on each row in `app/dashboard/page.tsx` (currently each project is a plain `<Link>`). Keep the existing visual idiom exactly: `rounded-xl border border-black/10 dark:border-white/10`, `text-sm`, restrained monochrome, no new colours except semantic red for delete. Keyboard accessible, visible focus state.

## Critical constraints
- **Ownership scoping is the security-critical part.** Every operation must scope by `userId` IN THE SAME QUERY as the id (the existing code does `findFirst({ where: { id, userId: user.id } })`) so a wrong-user id is indistinguishable from a nonexistent one. Never trust the route param alone. Read the existing GET handler in that file and match its auth idiom.
- DO NOT modify: prisma/schema.prisma, lib/credits.ts, lib/agent.ts, lib/agent-sdk.ts, lib/build-site.ts, lib/events.ts, lib/build-narration.ts, lib/auth.ts, app/api/projects/route.ts, app/api/generate/route.ts, app/api/projects/[id]/publish/route.ts, app/api/projects/[id]/export/route.ts, app/projects/**, app/settings/**, app/globals.css, proxy.ts, deploy.sh, .env, package.json.
- NOTE: `app/dashboard/page.tsx` was just modified — it now imports and renders a `CreditMeter` component and a Settings link. Read it fresh before editing and preserve those.
- DO NOT add npm dependencies.
- DO NOT run `npm run build`, `git commit`, `git push`, or `deploy.sh`.
- Run `npx tsc --noEmit` and `npx eslint <your files>`; your files must be clean. Pre-existing errors elsewhere (PromptHero.tsx, ThemeToggle.tsx and others have some) are NOT yours — leave them.
- You may test against the local Postgres (DATABASE_URL is in .env) but do NOT delete data you did not create.

## Report back
What you built, your slug-on-rename decision and the reasoning, what cascade behaviour you actually verified vs assumed, and how you tested.

Four agents are running; my own lane is finished for this pass. Here's where things stand.

## Live build progress — done

The gap was real and worse than the card suggested: on the SDK engine, files are diffed out of the working directory **after** `query()` returns, so every file event arrives in one burst at the end. The chat sat silent for the entire build. Separately, the Editor was discarding `status` events entirely — the "Build didn't compile — fixing it…" message has never been visible to anyone.

New [lib/build-narration.ts](lib/build-narration.ts) maps real tool calls to plain English, wired into both engines, deduped in the route so twelve consecutive `Read`s narrate once instead of stuttering.

I spot-checked the mapper against 17 inputs rather than trusting it, which caught three bugs:

- `CTASection.tsx` → "the cta section **section**" (stutter, and the initialism got lowercased) → now "the CTA section"
- The API engine passes project-relative paths, and my path normaliser only handled absolute ones — so `src/components/Testimonials.tsx` collapsed to "Testimonials.tsx" → now "the testimonials section"
- `FAQ` was being lowercased to "faq"

## Build animation — done

[BuildingOverlay.tsx](app/projects/[id]/BuildingOverlay.tsx) covers the preview pane while a build runs, since otherwise the iframe keeps showing the *previous* version, which reads as nothing happening. Your existing gradient `Mark` breathes at 3% scale, and a skeleton page (nav, hero, copy, CTA, three cards) fades in staggered with a sweep.

Deliberately **no progress bar** — we genuinely can't know what fraction is done, and a bar stalled at 80% is precisely what makes people reload mid-build.

I checked it in a real browser. First measurement said every block was stuck at `opacity: 0`, which looked like a serious bug — but `currentTime` was 0 on every animation, meaning the pane wasn't compositing frames. I forced the animations to their end state instead: all 11 blocks reach opacity 1, transform resets clean, colours resolve correctly. Not a CSS bug.

Also fixed along the way: your dev server was throwing `Both middleware file and proxy file are detected` and serving stale routes after the rename — it needed a restart, not just a reload.

## Four agents running

| Agent | Scope |
|---|---|
| Eval harness | `scripts/eval/` — ~30 golden prompts, static scoring, run-to-run comparison |
| Asset library | `lib/assets/`, `app/api/assets/` — inline SVG icons, flags, procedural patterns |
| Social rewards | `app/api/rewards/`, `components/rewards/`, `app/settings/` |
| Project management | `app/api/projects/[id]/route.ts`, `app/dashboard/` — rename, duplicate, delete |

Disjoint file sets, none touching the schema, credits, agent engines, or deploy. The last one has already landed a `ProjectRow` component on the dashboard.

Two constraints I gave them worth knowing about: the asset library **cannot** be a stock-photo API — your CSP blocks every external host, so it has to be inline SVG, CSS gradients, and data URIs or it silently breaks on publish. And the rewards agent was told not to ship an honour-system claim button; Discord is genuinely verifiable via OAuth, Instagram/Facebook/LinkedIn are not, and it has to be honest in code about which is which.

I'll integrate as they report, then build once and give you the full deploy sequence — still gated on `prisma db push` running before the code ships.

## 1. DISCORD — VERIFIABLE

- Authorize: `https://discord.com/oauth2/authorize` (`client_id`, `response_type=code`, `redirect_uri`, `scope`, `state`)
- Token: `POST https://discord.com/api/oauth2/token`, `Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded`
- Token-exchange body: `grant_type=authorization_code`, `code`, `redirect_uri` (plus client credentials)

**Scopes** (verbatim from the scopes table):

- `identify` — "allows `/users/@me` without `email`"
- `email` — "enables `/users/@me` to return an `email`"
- `guilds` — "allows `/users/@me/guilds` to return basic information about all of a user's guilds"
- `guilds.members.read` — "allows `/users/@me/guilds/{guild.id}/member` to return a user's member information in a guild"

**Both endpoints exist** ([docs.discord.com/developers/resources/user](https://docs.discord.com/developers/resources/user)):

`GET /users/@me/guilds` (scope `guilds`) returns an array of **partial** guild objects — fields: `id`, `name`, `icon`, `banner`, `owner`, `permissions`, `features`, and with `with_counts=true` also `approximate_member_count` / `approximate_presence_count`. **Yes, it includes the guild `id`**, so a client-side `.some(g => g.id === GUILD_ID)` works.

`GET /users/@me/guilds/{guild.id}/member` (scope `guilds.members.read`) returns a **guild member object** for the current user in that specific guild.

**Better fit: `guilds.members.read`.** Reasons: one request, no pagination, non-membership surfaces as an error rather than requiring you to scan a list, it returns `roles` and `joined_at` (so you can gate on role or tenure, and detect join-then-leave gaming via `joined_at`), and the consent screen asks for access to *one* server rather than "see all your servers" — materially better conversion and privacy posture.

**Pagination / rate-limit caveats on `/users/@me/guilds`:**
- `limit` **defaults to 200, max 200**; `before` / `after` are snowflake cursors. 200 is also the non-Nitro guild cap, so one page usually suffices — but a Nitro user can exceed it, and *that is exactly when a naive single-page check produces a false negative*. This is the strongest practical argument for the member endpoint.
- Global limit is 50 req/s ([rate-limits](https://docs.discord.com/developers/topics/rate-limits)); per-route limits must be read from `X-RateLimit-Limit` / `-Remaining` / `-Reset-After` / `-Bucket`, not hardcoded.
- Caveat not in the official docs, so treat as unconfirmed: there are long-standing reports ([discord-api-docs#670](https://github.com/discord/discord-api-docs/issues/670)) that `/users/@me/*` buckets are shared across *different* user tokens rather than per-token, which bites backend OAuth services at volume. Worth load-testing.

Note that post also says there is no longer an Instagram API group for *consumer-facing* apps at all — which is precisely the category your use case falls into.
- **Instagram API with Instagram Login / with Facebook Login** ([overview](https://developers.facebook.com/docs/instagram-platform/overview/)): permissions are `instagram_business_basic`, `instagram_business_content_publish`, `instagram_business_manage_comments`, `instagram_business_manage_messages` (+ `instagram_manage_insights`, `pages_show_list`, `pages_read_engagement` on the FB-Login variant). None expose a follow graph. These also authenticate *business/creator* accounts, not the ordinary consumer accounts your users would sign in with.
- **IG User node** ([reference](https://developers.facebook.com/docs/instagram-platform/instagram-graph-api/reference/ig-user/)): readable fields include `followers_count` and `follows_count` — **integers only**. There is **no `follows` / `followed_by` edge** returning which accounts are followed.

It is keyed on an IGSID from an existing conversation, requires `instagram_basic`, `instagram_manage_messages`, `pages_manage_metadata`, `pages_read_engagement` plus a Page token from someone with the MODERATE task. You cannot point it at an arbitrary web visitor who OAuth'd into your site.

**Verdict: "does user X follow account Y" is not answerable for a normal app.** No permission to apply for; the capability does not exist.

## 3. FACEBOOK — NOT VERIFIABLE IN PRACTICE

**The endpoint technically still exists.** `GET /v26.0/{user-id}/likes` is live in the current Graph API reference ([user/likes](https://developers.facebook.com/docs/graph-api/reference/user/likes/)), returns a list of Page nodes with `created_time`, read-only, and takes a `target_id` parameter (the "target node") — which is the documented way to test one specific Page rather than paging the whole list.

**But the permission gate is the blocker.** `user_likes` ([permissions reference](https://developers.facebook.com/docs/permissions/reference/user_likes)) requires App Review, and its **Allowed Usage** is enumerated narrowly: personalizing experiences by surfacing content matching user interests (content curation, sharing interests in dating/music apps), and parental-control/monitoring apps analyzing interests for safety concerns in under-18s. **A rewards or incentive gate is not among the approved use cases**, so a submission describing your actual use case should be expected to fail.

**Two further problems:**
1. Meta has moved Pages to the New Page Experience where **Followers replace Likes**. A Page under NPE may not have the Like signal you'd be querying at all.
2. `/{user-id}/likes` has always been prone to false negatives depending on the user's privacy settings — even when it works it is not a reliable gate.

**Policy — this is the real stopper.** Meta's developer policy on incentivization ([Platform Policy examples](https://developers.facebook.com/docs/apps/examples-platform-policy-4.4); fuller treatment at the [Incentivization Policies Deep Dive](https://developers.facebook.com/docs/development/terms-and-policies/incentivization-policy-deep-dive/), which currently 404s to automated fetches) permits incentivizing only a narrow set of actions — logging into your app with Facebook, checking in at your location, referral rewards for game installs — and **explicitly prohibits rewarding Page Likes or posting content**: don't incentivize people to post content to Facebook or Like a Page, or give the impression that doing so will be rewarded. Don't incentivize other actions."* Facebook's [Pages, Groups and Events Policies](https://www.facebook.com/policies/pages_groups_events/) reinforce it for promotions: a promotion must not require or incentivize participants to share, repost, or tag others.

**Note on sourcing:** several Meta policy pages returned Vietnamese-locale text or 404s to automated fetching. The clauses above are consistent across the pages that did resolve plus Meta's own search snippets, but I'd recommend one human read of the Incentivization Deep Dive page in a browser before you rely on the exact wording contractually.

**Sign In with LinkedIn / OIDC returns identity only** ([Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/linkedin/consumer/integrations/self-serve/sign-in-with-linkedin-v2)). Scopes are exactly `openid`, `profile`, `email`. `GET https://api.linkedin.com/v2/userinfo` returns: `sub`, `name`, `given_name`, `family_name`, `picture`, `locale`, `email`, `email_verified` (last two optional). Nothing about follows, connections, or company relationships. The docs also warn OIDC here "does not verify user identities and should not be marketed as such."

**All follower APIs are aggregate-only:**

- `organizationalEntityFollowerStatistics` ([docs](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/linkedin/marketing/community-management/organizations/follower-statistics?view=li-lms-2026-08)) returns counts bucketed by 7 demographic facets (geo, industry, function, seniority, staff-count-range, association type), capped at top 100 results per facet. No member identities. Requires `rw_organization_admin`, restricted to authenticated ADMINISTRATORs of that page. It no longer returns `totalFollowerCounts`.
- `GET /rest/networkSizes/urn:li:organization:{id}?edgeType=COMPANY_FOLLOWED_BY_MEMBER` ([Organization Lookup](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/linkedin/marketing/community-management/organizations/organization-lookup-api?view=li-lms-2026-08)) returns exactly `{"firstDegreeSize": 219145}` — a single total. Despite the tempting edge-type name, it is a count, not a relationship test. (Version note: `CompanyFollowedByMember` → `COMPANY_FOLLOWED_BY_MEMBER` as of v202305, not backward compatible.)

There is no endpoint enumerating follower identities and none testing a specific member against a page. Also flag: Marketing Version 202508 sunsets **August 17, 2026** — under a week from now — so anything built here needs current versioning immediately.

- **LinkedIn:** no incentivization clause surfaced in this research — but I did not audit the LinkedIn API Terms of Use or Professional Community Policies, so treat this as unresearched rather than cleared. Moot regardless, since the data isn't available.
- **Discord:** technically clean and I found no prohibition — but I did not review Discord's Developer Terms of Service or Developer Policy for incentivization language, so that should be checked before shipping. content.text:
All four agents are in, build is green, TypeScript clean, no new lint errors. Two findings change decisions you've already made, so those first.

## Facebook: I'd drop it

The rewards agent found that Meta's developer incentivization policy **explicitly prohibits rewarding people for Liking a Page** — "like our Facebook page for 50 credits" is close to a verbatim example of what's disallowed. The `user_likes` permission also has enumerated allowed uses that don't include incentives, and Pages on the New Page Experience report Followers rather than Likes anyway.

The code is written but stays **inert unless `KODELY_FACEBOOK_URL` is set**. I'd leave it unset. Worth noting the agent also flagged that several Meta policy pages served 404s or wrong-locale text to automated fetches, so have a human read the current wording before deciding — and the same caution applies to Instagram, same umbrella.

## The 50-credit grant is worth less than I told you

I wrote on your rewards card that the four social rewards were worth "roughly 1.4 extra builds." That was wrong. It relied on a ~144-credit build measurement; the eval harness just ran a real generation and it cost **472 credits**.

So 200 credits is about **0.4 of one build**, and your 750-credit signup grant covers under two. I've corrected the card and widened `estimateCredits` to 120–550 with the reasoning written in — two samples 3× apart is not a distribution, and quoting low is the exact failure the credits module exists to prevent. I also raised the "about N more builds" fallback to 400, skewed high deliberately: over-promising remaining builds is how someone hits zero mid-build.

Getting a real cost distribution is now the highest-value thing the eval harness can do.

## What the agents delivered

**Eval harness** — 30 fixtures, deterministic scoring, run-to-run diffing with `--fail-on-regression` for CI. It validated the rubric in both directions: the bare foundation scores 1/8, a hand-written good site scores 8/8. One real fixture ran green-first-try. **29 of 30 have never been generated** and the `api` engine path is untested. Full sweep is roughly 2 hours and ~14k credits, so it guards against >5 fixtures without `--yes`.

**Asset library, social rewards, project management** — all landed. Discord is genuinely verifiable (member-check endpoint, not guild-list scanning, which would false-negative for users in 200+ servers); Instagram/LinkedIn are self-declared with a 72h hold and the code says plainly that anyone can type any handle. Cross-account identity uses an HMAC of the external id in the ledger `reason`, keyed by a server secret — an unkeyed hash would let anyone with DB read access brute-force whether a given handle is your customer.

Project management verified cascade behaviour against the live Postgres rather than assuming: `CreditLedger` rows survive with `buildId: null`, so deleting a site doesn't un-charge the work. Slug never changes on rename — re-slugging would 404 every inbound link *and* release a globally-unique URL for someone else to claim.

## My lane — learning mode

Follow-up requests now get classified into intent buckets and both that and thumbs up/down surface on `/admin`. The top bucket is, in aggregate, what the first generation gets wrong most often.

Testing the classifier caught two real bugs: `\bcolou?r\b` doesn't match "colors" — the word boundary fails on the plural, silently mis-bucketing the most common visual request — and praise only matched when the *entire* message was praise, so "wow this is amazing" fell through. Now 27/27 including regression cases like "great, now make the colors warmer" correctly landing in `visual` rather than `praise`.

## Needs you

Nothing is committed or deployed. Before it can ship:

1. `prisma db push` on staging and prod **before** the code — `deploy.sh` doesn't run migrations, and this adds a table plus two columns
2. The admin promotion command from earlier (still blocked for me by the permission classifier)
3. `KODELY_REWARDS_ID_SALT` is **required** — without it no reward appears and nothing is ever granted. Plus the Discord client id/secret/guild id, and the redirect URI registered on the Discord app
4. `KODELY_ADMIN_HOST` and its DNS record, if you want the admin subdomain live

The Discord OAuth flow has never executed — there are no credentials here. Test it against a throwaway guild, both member and non-member, before announcing it.

## What I built

Five new files, all inside the allowed scope (`lib/assets/**`, `app/api/assets/**`). Nothing else was touched.

**`lib/assets/icons.ts`** — 147 icons on a 24×24 grid across 9 categories (contact 10, social 10, commerce 12, food 12, services 21, people 6, media 17, nature 8, UI 51). Three weights (`light`/`regular`/`bold`) come from a render-time `stroke-width` over one geometry, so styles cost zero extra bytes. Renderers: `iconSvg`, `iconJsx` (kebab→camel attribute rewrite), `iconDataUri`.

**`lib/assets/flags.ts`** — **I chose (c), both.** All 250 ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 countries (+EU) resolve to a flag emoji computed arithmetically from the two letters — no lookup table, complete by construction, and it's *text*, so it needs no asset at all. On top of that, 55 hand-authored SVG flags, each tagged `accuracy: "exact" | "simplified"` with a `note` naming exactly what's approximated. 42 are exact (band flags, Nordic crosses, Greece, Japan, India's 24-spoke chakra, the US 50-star grid, Turkey's crescent, South Africa's Y); 13 are explicitly simplified (UK's diagonal counterchange isn't reproduced; Brazil's stars/motto, Argentina's sun face, Spain's and Portugal's arms omitted; Canada's leaf is a hand-authored 11-point approximation). **Countries whose flags are mostly a detailed emblem — Mexico, Saudi Arabia, Sri Lanka, Bhutan — are deliberately absent from the SVG layer rather than shipped wrong.** They fall through to emoji. One honest caveat documented in the module: Windows Chrome/Edge render regional-indicator pairs as two grey letter boxes, so emoji flags are right for pickers and phone-code lists, not for a design leaning on the flag as an image.

**`lib/assets/patterns.ts`** — 30 named gradients (curated palette across warm/cool/vivid/nature/neutral/pastel/dark, each with a Tailwind arbitrary-value class), 6 mesh backgrounds, 3 feTurbulence grain textures as `data:` URIs, 12 section dividers on a stretched 1440×120 canvas with flip options, 12 pure-CSS repeating patterns, and deterministic initials avatars (FNV-1a → hue, so the same person gets the same colour every rebuild).

**`lib/assets/index.ts`** — `findAssets(query, {kind, limit, weight})` over all 461 entries with AND-ish multi-token scoring and a query-side synonym map covering trade vocabulary (`plumber`→wrench, `dentist`→tooth) and British spellings. Every match carries a paste-ready `source` plus a one-line `usage`. Also `getAsset`, `listAssets`, `listAssetIds`, `assetCatalogSummary`. Designed as the seam a future `search_assets` agent tool forwards straight through.

**`app/api/assets/route.ts`** — GET with `q` / `kind` / `limit` / `id`, gated with `requireUser().catch(() => null)` matching `app/api/projects/route.ts`. No `q` and no `kind` returns the catalogue summary rather than dumping 461 rendered assets.

## Provenance

All icon geometry is hand-authored from primitives (lines, circles, rounded rects, single arcs), with corner rounding delegated to `stroke-linejoin="round"` rather than drawn. No path data was copied from any icon library, free or licensed. The social marks are simplified generic renderings from the same primitives — not the trademark artwork; I noted in the module that commercial use should check each platform's brand guidelines. Flag geometry is generated from arithmetic in the file or authored from published construction specifications.

## Size

107 KB of source (icons 38.8, flags 26.3, patterns 22.7, index 16.5, route 3.0). Materialising the *entire* catalogue at once produces ~277 KB of strings, but that only happens on an unfiltered `listAssets()`; the API caps at 100 results and defaults to 24.

## Verified

`npx tsc --noEmit` and `npx eslint` both clean on my files. I rendered all 147 icons, all 55 flags, and every gradient/mesh/texture/pattern/divider/avatar into a browser and inspected them visually. Two real bugs found and fixed that way:

- `handshake` rendered as an unreadable knot — replaced with `bed` (hotels/B&Bs were an actual gap; "partnership" is served by `users`).
- `plus-grid` rendered blank — its CSS mask was misaligned, and worse, `mask-image` on a section would have clipped the section's own text. Replaced with `dots-offset`, which gets the same feel from backgrounds alone.

Also caught that `dividerSvg` emitted an inline `style` attribute, which is a string in HTML but must be an object in JSX — it would have broken on paste into a `.tsx`. input.prompt:
Work in C:\Users\edmem\kodely-prod (a Next.js 16 + Prisma app called Kodely — an AI website builder at kodely.me).

TASK: build the content pipeline for Kodely's SEO pages, and seed it with a first batch of genuinely accurate articles.

## Context
There is a `BlogPost` model in `prisma/schema.prisma` (READ ONLY) with: slug, title, metaDescription, category, targetKeyword, bodyHtml, publishedAt, updatedAt. `app/blog/` and `app/blog/[slug]/` already exist — read them first to see how posts are rendered and what shape `bodyHtml` is expected to be. There is also `seo-batch1.json` in the repo root worth reading for prior art on the intended format.

## THE HARD CONSTRAINT — read this twice
The project's planning board contains roughly 250 SEO article briefs, and **a large number of them describe features Kodely does not have.** Publishing an article that says Kodely does something it cannot is (a) a lie to a prospective customer, (b) an immediate bounce when they sign up and it isn't there, and (c) a refund request.

So: **before writing a single sentence about a capability, verify it in the code.** Ground truth lives in:
- `lib/agent.ts` — the SYSTEM prompt. This is the definitive statement of what generated sites can and cannot contain. Read it in full.
- `lib/foundation.ts` — the exact starting project and its dependencies.
- `lib/build-site.ts` — how sites are compiled.
- `app/api/site/[slug]/**` — how published sites are served, and the CSP they run under.
- `lib/credits.ts` — how pricing/credits actually work.
- `app/api/projects/[id]/export/route.ts`, `app/api/enhance/route.ts`, `lib/assets/` — recently added capabilities.

Things I already know are TRUE and are strong, honest angles: generated sites are real Vite + React + TypeScript + Tailwind apps (not HTML mockups); you are never charged for a build that fails to compile; you can export your full source as a zip; sites are compiled server-side and served static.

Things I know are FALSE right now — do NOT claim any of them: databases or any backend, user accounts/auth on generated sites, working contact forms that deliver mail, e-commerce/checkout, external API integrations, stock photography or remote images of any kind, custom web fonts, multi-page routing (it is a single-page app), or npm packages beyond react/react-dom.

If a topic cannot be written honestly, **do not write it** — list it in your report as "cannot be written truthfully until X ships". That list is genuinely valuable output; a short honest batch beats a long dishonest one.

## Scope — YOU MAY ONLY CREATE/EDIT FILES UNDER `scripts/seo/` AND `content/seo/`
Do NOT edit `app/blog/**` — read it to learn the render contract, but another agent may be in that area. Write your articles as data files plus a seeding script.

## What to build
1. **A seed script** (`scripts/seo/seed.mjs`) that upserts articles into the `BlogPost` table by slug — idempotent, safe to re-run, and with a `--dry-run` that prints what would change without writing. Load `.env` yourself for DATABASE_URL.
2. **10-15 genuinely accurate articles** as structured data files. Prioritise honest, high-intent topics: comparisons where you can only speak factually about Kodely's own side, "how to build X" guides where X is actually buildable (a restaurant landing page, a portfolio, a barber shop site), and explainers about how AI site generation works.
3. **A validator** (`scripts/seo/validate.mjs`) checking every article for: unique slug, title length under ~60 chars, metaDescription 50-160 chars, valid HTML that matches what `app/blog/[slug]` expects, no unclosed tags, and no external resource references.

## Writing standards
- `bodyHtml` is pre-rendered semantic HTML — check how `app/blog/[slug]/page.tsx` renders it and match exactly what it expects.
- Write for a real person deciding whether to use this, not for a keyword crawler. No "In today's digital landscape". No padding to hit a word count.
- Do not invent statistics, customer counts, testimonials, review scores, or awards. If you want a number, it must come from the code (e.g. actual credit costs from lib/credits.ts) — and read `SIGNUP_GRANT` and the `estimateCredits` comments carefully, because the real per-build cost is currently uncertain and being re-measured. Prefer not quoting a specific price at all over quoting one that will be wrong next week.
- When naming competitors, state only verifiable, non-disparaging facts, and prefer describing Kodely's own behaviour over characterising theirs.

## Critical constraints
- DO NOT modify: prisma/schema.prisma, anything under lib/, app/**, proxy.ts, deploy.sh, .env, package.json.
- DO NOT add npm dependencies.
- DO NOT run `npm run build`, `git commit`, `git push`, or `deploy.sh`.
- Run `npx tsc --noEmit` and `npx eslint <your files>`; your files must be clean.
- You may run your seed script against the local database in `--dry-run` mode freely. Only do a real write if you are confident it is idempotent, and do not delete rows you did not create.

## Report back
The articles you wrote and the specific code file that grounds each capability claim, the list of board topics that CANNOT be written truthfully today and what would need to ship first, and anything you found in the existing blog rendering that constrains the format.

Build green. Four agents still running; here's what landed while they work.

## Assets are now actually reachable by the builder

The asset library shipped as 461 assets that **nothing could reach** — no tool, no mention in the prompt. I wired it into both engines, which needed two different mechanisms:

- **API engine** gets a real `find_assets` tool (JSON Schema, no new dependency).
- **SDK engine** — the one you're running — gets the catalog written to `.kodely-assets/` in the working directory, with an `INDEX.md` it can Grep and per-asset files it can Read.

The SDK route isn't laziness: giving it a custom tool means an in-process MCP server, and the SDK's `tool()` helper needs zod — which is only a *transitive* dependency, not declared in `package.json`, and `package.json` is on your ship.sh forbidden list. Depending on a package that isn't declared is a silent breakage waiting for the next install.

The directory is dot-prefixed deliberately: `readFileTree` skips entries starting with `.`, so the catalog stays invisible to the diff that turns the working directory back into project files. Without that, every generated site would gain ~460 junk files. I verified that — the temp dir contains exactly `[".kodely-assets"]`.

I also extended the existing prompt-drift guard: `adaptPromptForSdk` now throws if *either* the tool contract or the new asset contract sentence goes missing, rather than silently telling the SDK agent to call a tool it doesn't have. That failure mode has already bitten this project once.

## A real search bug, found by testing

Searching **"french flag" returned French Guiana, French Polynesia, and French Southern Territories — not France.** Same for "british" (British Indian Ocean Territory) and "american" (American Samoa).

Cause: flag keywords derive from the country *name*, so "French Guiana" owns the literal token `french` at full score, while France could only be reached through a synonym — which is discounted *and* only consulted when the literal token scores zero. My first fix (query-side synonyms) didn't work for exactly that reason; I had to put demonyms on the country entry itself.

Now 12/12, and territory searches still work — "french guiana" still returns French Guiana, because it carries a second token only the territory matches.

## CSP finding worth keeping

I verified the asset agent's claim myself. The sandbox CSP is `default-src 'self'; ... img-src 'self' data:` with **no `font-src`** — so fonts fall back to `default-src 'self'`, which excludes `data:`. A base64 `@font-face` is blocked exactly like a remote font link.

The builder prompt said "no @import or `<link>` for web fonts", which is correct advice but incomplete reasoning — someone could reasonably conclude base64 was the workaround. Now stated explicitly, with the reason.

## In flight

Privacy/terms accuracy (the analytics I added aren't disclosed anywhere yet), admin user management, accessibility + the 12 lint errors, and SEO content grounded only in features that actually exist.

Still gated on you: `prisma db push` before any deploy, the admin promotion command, and `KODELY_REWARDS_ID_SALT`.

Also note: **`privacy@kodely.me` is not verified to exist.** It was in the old page and I kept it, but the only mailbox in code is `CONTACT_TO` (`hello@kodely.me`, `lib/mail.ts:24`). Confirm the alias is real, since it is now the stated route for account-deletion and rights requests.

I am not a lawyer and neither are you; this is written to be factually accurate about the code, not to be legally sufficient.

- **Legal basis / GDPR framing.** I made no GDPR, CCPA, SOC 2 or certification claims, and named no controller, no legal bases, no international-transfer mechanism (Anthropic and Stripe are US-based; a UK/EU operator needs SCCs or equivalent, and the policy currently says nothing).

## What I built

**`C:\Users\edmem\kodely-prod\app\admin\users\page.tsx`** — user list. Email (linked to detail), signup date, role, project count, build count with succeeded/failed split, current credit balance, lifetime credits spent, lifetime imputed cost. Search box matches email *or* name case-insensitively *or* an exact user id pasted from a log line. Sort by newest/oldest/email/project-count. Paginated at 25/page with prev-next links that preserve query and sort.

**`C:\Users\edmem\kodely-prod\app\admin\users\[id]\page.tsx`** — user detail. Six stat tiles (balance, lifetime granted, lifetime spent + 30-day window, builds, imputed cost, margin), an amber "Needs a look" banner, the credit statement, projects, build history, and the event journey.

**`C:\Users\edmem\kodely-prod\app\admin\users\ui.tsx`** — shared presentational helpers (`StatTile`, `Panel`, `TableFrame`, `Th`, `formatUsd`, `truncate`, `statusClass`, `reasonLabel`). Not a route; Next's generated `validator.ts` confirms only the two `page.tsx` files were registered as routes.

The ledger is the centrepiece: newest-first statement with date, decoded reason, the build it was charged against plus that build's status, signed delta in red/emerald, `balanceAfter`, and a thin balance-trajectory bar per row reusing the funnel-bar pattern from `/admin` — so "when did they run dry" is a glance rather than a column of numbers to diff. `reasonLabel` decodes the three encodings `reason` actually carries (`build`, `signup_grant`, `stripe:<session>`, and the `reward:<platform>:[pending:]<identityHash>` state machine from `app/api/rewards/_lib.ts`) so a 64-char hex blob never lands in the middle of a billing statement; the raw string stays on hover.

Authorization: `getAdminUser()` at the top of both pages with `notFound()`, matching the idiom and the comment in `app/admin/page.tsx`. Read-only throughout — no impersonation, no mutations, prompts truncated to 60 chars, errors to 70, no file contents anywhere.

## Avoiding N+1 on the balance lookup

`getBalance` reads `balanceAfter` off a user's newest ledger row. For a page of users that's one `findFirst` each. Instead I do it in a single pass with Postgres `DISTINCT ON`:

```sql
SELECT DISTINCT ON (l."userId") l."userId", l."balanceAfter"
FROM "CreditLedger" l
WHERE l."userId" IN (…)
ORDER BY l."userId", l."createdAt" DESC, l."id" DESC
```

`id DESC` is the tiebreak so two rows written inside the same millisecond resolve to the same row Prisma's `findFirst` would pick. I verified this against `getBalance`'s exact Prisma path for every user — identical results.

`Build` has no `userId` (it hangs off `Project`), so the per-user build rollup is one grouped join with `FILTER (WHERE status = …)` for the succeeded/failed split rather than a count per user. Spend and net-delta come from two `groupBy` calls with `userId IN (…)`. Total: **6 queries for the list page regardless of page size** — count, users, balances, builds, spent, net. No query runs inside a loop.

One deliberate limitation: I only offer **database-native** sorts. Balance, spend and build count are derived per-page, so offering them as sort options would silently sort 25 arbitrary rows instead of the table — worse than not offering it. That is commented in the file.

Free bonus from the same query set: the ledger is append-only and starts at zero, so `sum(delta)` must equal the newest `balanceAfter`. Comparing them costs one extra grouped query and surfaces a drifted ledger before a customer does — shown as a "Ledger drift" tile and a per-row `!`. The detail page does the same check row-by-row from data already in hand.

## What actually accumulates (verify each yourself before acting)
- `Event` (prisma/schema.prisma, lib/events.ts) — one row per user action, forever. Attached to a user id. Never deleted, and NOT deleted when a project is deleted. On user deletion the FK is `SetNull`, so rows are merely detached.
- `Session` — `SESSION_DAYS = 30` in lib/auth.ts is enforced at READ time only. Expired rows are never purged from the table; only explicit sign-out deletes one.
- `Build.filesSnapshot` — a full JSON copy of the source + build tree after EVERY successful build. This is by far the biggest storage item and it grows without bound per project.
- `Build` rows themselves, including `prompt` text.
- `CreditLedger` — survives project deletion by design (`buildId` becomes null). **This is an auditable financial record: it must NOT be pruned.** Treat it as permanently retained and say so.

## What to build
1. **`lib/retention.ts`** — a pure policy module: named retention rules, each with a target, an age threshold, and a clear comment justifying the number. Export a function per rule that COUNTS what would be affected, and one that DELETES. Keep counting and deleting separate — that separation is what makes a dry run trustworthy.
2. **`scripts/retention.mjs`** — the runner. **`--dry-run` MUST be the default.** Deleting requires an explicit `--apply`. Print a clear table of what would go, per rule, with row counts and (where you can estimate it) bytes reclaimed. Support `--only <rule>`. Load `.env` yourself for DATABASE_URL — see `scripts/eval/loader.mjs`, which already solves this and which you may import.
3. **Sensible default policy** — propose thresholds and justify each in comments. My starting suggestions, which you should challenge if you disagree: expired sessions purged immediately (they are already invalid, keeping them is pure liability); `filesSnapshot` cleared from all but the most recent N builds per project (the snapshot exists for rollback — old ones past a certain depth are dead weight, but check `app/api/projects/[id]/builds/**` to see how far back restore actually reaches before picking N); events older than ~12-24 months. Do not prune anything a product feature actually reads — verify by finding the readers first.
4. **A short `docs/retention.md`** documenting the policy in plain language, suitable for someone writing a privacy policy to quote.

- **`--dry-run` is the default. Never delete without `--apply`.**
- Deletes must be batched and bounded (e.g. `deleteMany` with a `take`-style loop), never one unbounded statement that locks a table.
- **Before pruning anything, find who reads it.** Grep for the field's readers. If a feature depends on it, either exclude it or raise the threshold, and say so in your report. Clearing `filesSnapshot` breaks build restore if you go too shallow — read `app/api/projects/[id]/builds/[buildId]/restore/route.ts` first.
- **Do NOT prune `CreditLedger`.** Ever.
- Test against the LOCAL database in dry-run only. **Do not run `--apply` against real data.** If you want to prove the delete path works, create your own throwaway rows and clean them up.
- DO NOT modify: prisma/schema.prisma, lib/events.ts, lib/credits.ts, lib/auth.ts, lib/agent.ts, lib/agent-sdk.ts, lib/build-site.ts, lib/assets/**, app/** (anything), proxy.ts, deploy.sh, .env, package.json, scripts/eval/** (read-only), scripts/seo/**.
- DO NOT add npm dependencies. DO NOT run `npm run build`, `git commit`, `git push`, or `deploy.sh`.
- Run `npx tsc --noEmit` and `npx eslint <your files>`; your files must be clean. NOTE: another agent is mid-edit in `components/marketing/HeroMock.tsx` so you may see errors there — those are NOT yours, ignore them.

Your proposed thresholds and the reasoning for each, what you found reads each field (and anything you therefore refused to prune), dry-run counts against the local database, and how someone should schedule this (cron line or similar) — note that `deploy.sh` does not currently run anything scheduled.

Two more agents landed. Here's what came out of them, including two real bugs in my own code.

## Two billing bugs, found by reading real data

**Zero-cost builds were charging 1 credit.** `creditsFor` floored at `Math.max(1, …)` so a build reporting 0 tokens and $0 cost still billed a credit. On the SDK engine, builds with missing telemetry produce exactly that — so this was systematic, not a one-off. There's a real ledger row in your local DB showing a charge for spend that provably didn't happen, inside the one module whose stated purpose is never doing that.

Fixed, and a zero charge now writes **no ledger row at all** — an entry that moves nothing is noise in a statement a customer may one day read to understand their bill. I also synced the eval harness's duplicated copy, which would otherwise have reported costs that disagree with what's actually charged.

**Failed builds recorded a blank model.** The model was only written on success, so every failed build had an empty Model column — making it impossible to attribute a spike in failures to a model change, which is exactly when you'd need to. Now written on both failure paths.

Also worth knowing from the same report: **8 of your 10 local builds failed**, nearly all on auth (`Not logged in`, `401 OAuth`), so the green-build-rate on `/admin` is currently computed off two successes. And `filesWritten: 9` appears on a FAILED build — it wrote files then died — so that field isn't a safe "did anything happen" signal.

## The privacy policy described a product that no longer exists

The agent verified each claim against code rather than taking my summary. It found the old policy omitted: the entire analytics stream, build ratings, per-build full file snapshots, social reward connections, the abuse scan (it claimed publishes were scanned *only* for secrets), the spend cap, and Discord as a data recipient.

It also corrected **me**: four names in my `EVENTS` constant were never actually emitted, so the policy would have described collection that doesn't happen. I've now wired the two billing ones properly and deleted the two landing ones with a note explaining why aspirational names aren't free. Verified by grepping every name — all 12 now fire somewhere.

One nuance now stated in the terms that wasn't before, and which will otherwise generate a dispute: **a run that fails to compile, self-repairs, then succeeds is charged once for the whole run including the repair.** The no-charge-on-failure promise is genuinely true — verified across all three failure paths — but it doesn't mean repairs are free.

I also deleted a script I'd duplicated: `scripts/promote-admin.mjs` already existed. Correcting my earlier instruction — that's the one to run, and I folded `--revoke` and an admin roster printout into it.

## Decisions that need you

**Two placeholders** are sitting in the legal pages because nothing in the codebase names them: the operating legal entity and registered address, and governing law/jurisdiction. Also — `privacy@kodely.me` is now the stated route for deletion and rights requests, but the only mailbox that appears in code is `hello@kodely.me`. Confirm that alias exists or the promise is empty.

**No retention job exists anywhere in the repo**, so the policy can currently only say "retained indefinitely" — including event rows with your user id attached. I've put an agent on building a real one (dry-run by default). Once it lands you can make an actual commitment instead.

**The SDK licensing point.** The agent escalated `KODELY_ENGINE=sdk` as its top item — a Claude subscription is licensed for individual use, and the file's own header says to switch back to `api` before opening up. You've already decided this twice for the testing period and I'm not relitigating it; I'm flagging it once as a launch blocker, not a testing-phase one.

Three agents still running: accessibility (mid-edit, currently the only thing failing typecheck), SEO content, and retention.

The answer is that it reaches back **forever** — `app/api/projects/[id]/builds/route.ts` lists every `SUCCEEDED` build with no `take`, and `Editor.tsx` renders all of them. So there was no existing depth to copy. 20 is a judgement call made deliberately deep, and I added the 30-day floor as the real safety: someone iterating hard can bury a checkpoint past rank 20 within hours, and losing rollback mid-session because you worked fast would be the worst possible failure of this job.

Concrete size data from your local DB: real snapshots measure **~105 kB each after TOAST compression**. The `Build` table is 296 kB for 10 rows while the entire `ProjectFile` table (127 files) is 512 kB — so one build's snapshot costs a fifth of all stored project files. Your read on this being the biggest item is correct.

**StripeEvent — I added a rule you didn't ask for.** `StripeEvent` grows one row per webhook forever and nothing prunes it. Stated risk, since it's billing-adjacent: those rows are the dedupe mutex (the webhook inserts before granting and relies on the P2002 conflict), so a deleted row means a redelivery could grant credits twice. Stripe abandons automatic retries within ~3 days, making 365 days a ~100x margin — but a **manual** dashboard resend of a >1-year-old event would no longer be deduped. Documented as such. If you'd rather not take that trade, delete the rule; it's self-contained.

## What reads each field, and what I refused to prune

- **`CreditLedger`** — never pruned, as instructed. Also load-bearing beyond the audit argument: `app/admin/users/page.tsx` derives live balances from it with a `DISTINCT ON ... ORDER BY createdAt DESC` query, so removing rows can change a displayed balance.
- **`Build` rows — refused.** Two unbounded readers: `app/admin/page.tsx` and `app/admin/users/[id]/page.tsx` both run `db.build.aggregate({_sum: {costMicros, creditsCharged}})` over *all* builds for lifetime unit economics. - **`Build.prompt` — refused.** Tempting redaction target, but it's the visible label of every checkpoint in the history panel (the list route selects it). Redacting would turn old checkpoints into unlabelled rows.
- **`Event`** — all aggregate readers in `lib/events.ts` take a `sinceDays` window and every `app/admin` caller passes 30. The unwindowed readers are a journey list capped at `take: 100` (unaffected) and a lifetime `db.event.count` on the admin user page, which **will report a smaller number** after a purge. Flagging that explicitly — it's a support-context stat, not a record, so I accepted it.
- **`FAILED` builds** never receive a snapshot (`app/api/generate/route.ts` only writes one on success), so the rule correctly ignores them.

## Dry-run results

Against `localhost:5432/kodely_personal`, all four rules return **0 rows** — the database is young (10 builds, 2 with snapshots, `Event` and `StripeEvent` empty), so nothing is yet eligible. I then deleted the fixtures and confirmed every table is back to its pre-test count.

## One thing I could not do

**`node scripts/retention.mjs --apply` was blocked by the permission system**, so the end-to-end delete path is unproven and I did not route around the denial. What I verified instead, all non-mutating: the `Prisma.DbNull` payload is accepted by `updateMany` at runtime (tested with `where: { id: { in: [] } }` — affects zero rows by construction), and the batch id-selection SQL (nested `Prisma.sql` fragment + window function + `ORDER BY`/`LIMIT`) parses and returns the right rows. That's every piece except the `deleteMany` calls themselves, which are standard `id: { in: [...] }` forms. If you want the full path proven, re-run the seed and `--apply` with permission granted.

## Scheduling

`deploy.sh` sets up no timers at all. Add a cron entry on the VM as `kodely` (prod is `/opt/kodely`):

```cron
15 4 * * * cd /opt/kodely && /usr/bin/node scripts/retention.mjs --apply >> /var/log/kodely-retention.log 2>&1
```

Do the first run by hand without `--apply` — the first enforcement after an unpruned period is the largest this job will ever do. Also note Postgres returns freed space to each table's free list, not the filesystem; autovacuum reclaims it, or `VACUUM` by hand (not `VACUUM FULL` on a live DB).

## Known gap worth a follow-up

Clearing a snapshot does **not** remove the checkpoint from the history panel — the list route never checks whether the snapshot survives, so a pruned checkpoint still displays and 404s with "Checkpoint not found." when clicked. The chosen depth puts these well past where anyone realistically clicks, so it's cosmetic, but the real fix is one line in `app/api/projects/[id]/builds/route.ts` (filter on `filesSnapshot: { not: Prisma.DbNull }`, or return a `restorable` flag). That's in `app/`, which was off-limits, so I documented it in section 5 of the doc rather than changing it.</result>

content.text:
Retention landed, and the lint count just hit **zero** for the first time — all 12 pre-existing errors cleared.

## Checkpoint bug, fixed and properly proven

The retention agent found that clearing old snapshots would leave dead restore points in the history panel — they'd still render, then 404 with "Checkpoint not found" when clicked. It couldn't fix it (`app/` was outside its scope), so I did.

Two things came out of verifying it. My first test was **worthless**: I compared the Prisma filter against raw SQL and got 2 = 2, but every build in the DB *had* a snapshot, so nothing proved it actually excludes nulls. Prisma's `DbNull` / `JsonNull` / `AnyNull` distinction is a well-known footgun and deserved a real test. I created one build with a snapshot and one without inside a rolled-back transaction: the first is visible, the second correctly excluded, and zero test rows survived.

I also bounded that query — it had no `take`, so a heavily-iterated project returned its entire build history on every panel open.

## Retention policy

| Rule | Threshold |
|---|---|
| Expired sessions | purged immediately — already invalid, pure liability |
| Build snapshots | cleared past newest 20 per project **and** older than 30 days |
| Events | 400 days (365 + reporting slack) |
| Stripe events | 365 days |

`--dry-run` is the default; deleting needs `--apply`. The agent seeded throwaway fixtures and confirmed the rules selected exactly the predicted rows, then removed them.

Two things it got right that I'd flag:

- **The snapshot rule needs *both* conditions.** Restore currently reaches back forever, so there was no existing depth to copy. Someone iterating hard can bury a checkpoint past rank 20 within hours — losing rollback mid-session because you worked fast would be the worst possible failure of a storage-cleanup job.
- **It refused to prune `Build` rows or `Build.prompt`**, having found unbounded readers: `/admin` aggregates lifetime cost over all builds, and the prompt is the visible label of every checkpoint. It only clears the `filesSnapshot` column.

Real numbers from your DB: snapshots are **~105 kB each compressed**. The `Build` table is 296 kB for 10 rows while all 127 project files total 512 kB — one snapshot costs a fifth of all stored project files.

It added a `StripeEvent` rule you didn't ask for and flagged the trade honestly: those rows are the webhook dedupe mutex, so pruning at 365 days means a *manual* dashboard resend of a >1-year-old event would no longer be deduped. Stripe abandons automatic retries within ~3 days, so it's a ~100× margin. Self-contained if you'd rather not take it.

**`--apply` was blocked by the permission system**, so the delete path itself is unproven. The agent didn't route around the denial, which was right. Everything up to the `deleteMany` calls is verified.

Nothing is scheduled — `deploy.sh` sets up no timers at all. There's a cron line in `docs/retention.md`, and the first run should be done by hand without `--apply`, since the first enforcement after an unpruned period is the largest this job will ever do.

Two agents still running: accessibility (lint already clear, presumably finishing the a11y pass) and SEO content.

## What the existing blog rendering constrains

Read off `app/blog/[slug]/page.tsx` and `app/globals.css` — I did not modify either.

- `bodyHtml` goes straight into `<div className="article-body">` via `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`. **Nothing sanitises it and nothing wraps it**, so the stored string must be a complete, well-formed run of block-level elements. Malformed markup breaks a live page's layout, which is why the seeder refuses to write invalid content rather than just warning.
- The page renders `post.title` as the one `<h1>`. An article shipping its own `<h1>` produces a second one — the validator rejects it.
- `.article-body` styles **only** `h2, h3, p, ul, ol, li, a, strong, code, table, th, td, blockquote`. Anything else renders unstyled — notably there is **no `<pre>` styling**, so code examples have to be `<blockquote>` or inline `<code>`. That's why every prompt example in these articles is a blockquote. No `<img>`, `<figure>`, `<hr>`, or `<h4>` support either.
- `readingTime()` strips tags with `/<[^>]+>/g`, so a literal `>` in text corrupts the word count. The validator rejects bare `>` and bare `&`.

- Related posts are `category`-matched, `take: 2`. Any category with only one article renders no related block, which is why I kept every category at 4+.
- The page's own CTA hardcodes "750 free credits" — consistent with `SIGNUP_GRANT`, but it's a second place that number lives.
- `metaDescription` is used raw as the meta description *and* as the card subtitle on the index, so it must read as plain prose with no markup.</result>

**Needs relaxed CSP or first-party script injection** — Google Analytics / GA4 / Meta pixel / Search Console verification-tag guides, Calendly or Google Maps embeds, YouTube embeds, live chat widgets, social feed widgets, Mailchimp forms, review-widget embeds.

**Needs `font-src` and hosted font files** — "custom fonts for your AI site", brand-typography guides.

**Needs a CMS or editor role** — "let your team update the site", non-technical content editing, staff logins.

**Needs npm packages** — anything about animation libraries, carousels, charts, date pickers, icon packs, routers.

**Needs the eval sweep in `scripts/eval` to finish** — any article quoting a per-build credit cost. `estimateCredits`'s own comment says two data points (144 and 472 credits) is not a distribution. `seo-batch1.json` already ships "a typical first build runs roughly 100–150 credits", which is now wrong by roughly 3x at the top end; I'd treat that as a correction to make, not just a topic to avoid.

**Needs `estimateCredits` wired into the UI** — any "see the cost before you build" angle.

**Not blocked, but needs correcting before publishing** — `seo-batch1.json`'s `kodely-vs-rocket-new` and `kodely-vs-lovable` both state "Export / download code — Not yet". That shipped: `app/api/projects/[id]/export/route.ts`. Their comparison tables understate the product.

**Borderline, writeable with the barber-shop treatment** — vertical pages like dentists/chiropractors/gyms/accountants are fine *if* scoped to a one-page credibility site with link-out CTAs. They become lies the moment they imply appointment booking or patient forms, which is the default shape of that keyword's intent. `website-builder-for-dentists` and `website-builder-for-chiropractors` in batch1 are worth re-reading with that in mind.

**One thing I could not verify either way** — whether the agent can produce a working favicon (it can only write text files; `readDistTree` in `lib/build-site.ts` filters to text extensions and does include `.svg`, and `public/` copying is untested). I avoided the topic rather than guess.

## What the existing blog rendering constrains

Read off `app/blog/[slug]/page.tsx` and `app/globals.css` — I did not modify either.

- `bodyHtml` goes straight into `<div className="article-body">` via `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`. **Nothing sanitises it and nothing wraps it**, so the stored string must be a complete, well-formed run of block-level elements. Malformed markup breaks a live page's layout, which is why the seeder refuses to write invalid content rather than just warning.
- The page renders `post.title` as the one `<h1>`. An article shipping its own `<h1>` produces a second one — the validator rejects it.
- `.article-body` styles **only** `h2, h3, p, ul, ol, li, a, strong, code, table, th, td, blockquote`. Anything else renders unstyled — notably there is **no `<pre>` styling**, so code examples have to be `<blockquote>` or inline `<code>`. That's why every prompt example in these articles is a blockquote. No `<img>`, `<figure>`, `<hr>`, or `<h4>` support either.
- `readingTime()` strips tags with `/<[^>]+>/g`, so a literal `>` in text corrupts the word count. The validator rejects bare `>` and bare `&`.
- The blog index is `force-dynamic` and the post page is `force-static` with `revalidate = 3600` — a seeded change takes up to an hour to appear on the post page.
- Related posts are `category`-matched, `take: 2`. Any category with only one article renders no related block, which is why I kept every category at 4+.
- The page's own CTA hardcodes "750 free credits" — consistent with `SIGNUP_GRANT`, but it's a second place that number lives.

## Never invent facts about a real business
"Specific copy" means specific to the SUBJECT, not invented details about a
real business. Never fabricate: street addresses, phone numbers, email
addresses, opening hours, prices, staff names, years in business, customer
counts, awards, certifications, review scores, or testimonials.

These end up on a real business's public website. An invented phone number is
a real number belonging to somebody else; invented opening hours send real
customers to a closed door; an invented testimonial is a fabricated
endorsement. This outranks the "no placeholder text" rule above — when you
don't know a fact, that rule does not license you to make one up.

Use a clearly-bracketed placeholder instead: [your phone number],
[your address], [your opening hours]. A bracket is an obvious prompt to fill
something in; a plausible-looking invention is one nobody notices before
publishing. Invent freely for anything that is genuinely a design choice —
headlines, section copy, taglines, colour, imagery.

## Never build something that only pretends to work
There is no backend, so anything needing a server cannot function. Do not
build a contact form, booking form, newsletter signup, login, cart or checkout
that appears functional — a form that silently discards a real enquiry is
worse than no form.

Where the brief asks for one, use a real alternative that works with no
server: a mailto: link, a tel: link, or a prominent [link to your booking
system]. If you show such a control as a visual element, its label must make
the destination obvious ("Email us", "Call now"), never "Submit" or "Send".

content.text:
The SEO agent surfaced the most consequential finding of the session, and it isn't about content.

## Your builder invents facts about real businesses

The agent tried to write "Kodely won't invent your address or prices" — then discovered that rule lives only in `ENHANCE_SYSTEM`, **not** in the builder's prompt. The builder is instead told *"Real, specific copy… never placeholder headings"*, which actively pushes it to fabricate.

That means a generated restaurant site can ship with an invented phone number, invented opening hours, invented prices, and invented testimonials — on a real business's public website. An invented phone number is a real number belonging to someone else. Invented hours send real customers to a closed door.

I've added two guardrails to `lib/agent.ts`, written to outrank the no-placeholder rule explicitly, since that rule was the thing licensing the invention:

- **Never invent facts about a real business** — addresses, phone numbers, hours, prices, staff names, awards, testimonials. Use `[your phone number]` instead: a bracket is an obvious prompt to fill in, a plausible invention is one nobody notices before publishing. Design choices — headlines, copy, colour — stay free.
- **Never build something that only pretends to work.** No fake contact/booking/checkout forms. A form that silently discards a real enquiry is worse than no form. Use `mailto:`/`tel:` links, labelled so the destination is obvious.

Verified the SDK prompt adapter still swaps correctly against the real system prompt — 7/7, including that both new guardrails survive the swap.

## 56 blog posts are live, and I checked rather than assumed

The agent's report implied several live pages overclaim. I fetched them. **`build-a-online-store-with-ai` is actually honest** — it explicitly says there's no working cart, payments, or order database. Good thing I looked.

Two real issues though:

**Live and wrong now:** every batch-1 post says *"A typical first build runs roughly 100–150 credits."* Your two measurements are 144 and 472. The first sits inside that range; the second is over 3× its top end. We don't know the real distribution, so publishing *any* range is premature — and on a product whose headline promise is no bill shock, an understated public cost figure is the worst thing to be wrong about.

**Breaks the moment you deploy:** several posts say *"there's no zip or full-project download."* That's **accurate today** — export is built but undeployed. Shipping it turns a true statement into a false one, and the two head-to-head comparison pages both list "Export / download code — Not yet". Those content edits have to go out *with* the deploy, not after.

Blog content lives in the `BlogPost` table on prod, not the repo, so that's a DB update on the box. Carded as urgent.

## Also from that agent

It caught that `estimateCredits` **has zero callers** — nothing surfaces a cost estimate before you build, so it had to retract that claim from three articles. It wrote 17 articles grounded in specific files, and produced a genuinely useful inventory of which board topics *can't* be written truthfully yet, grouped by what would have to ship first — backend, form delivery, image upload, multi-page routing, custom domains, relaxed CSP, `font-src`.

Build is green, TypeScript clean, and lint is at **zero** — the accessibility agent cleared all 12 pre-existing errors. That agent is the only one still running.
