Work in C:\Users\edmem\kodely-prod (a Next.js 16 + Prisma app called Kodely — an AI website builder).

BUILD: a template / starter-prompt gallery.

## Why
The product opens on an empty prompt box. "Describe the site you want" is the blank-page problem — the single biggest drop-off in this category. A gallery of concrete starting points converts "I don't know what to type" into one click. It also steers people toward prompts the builder is actually good at, which raises first-build quality without touching the model.

## The hard constraint — read it before designing
Generated sites are single-page Vite+React+TS+Tailwind apps served under a strict CSP with **no backend of any kind**. Read `lib/agent.ts` (the SYSTEM prompt, in full) and `lib/foundation.ts` before writing a single template.

That means a template must NOT promise: working contact/booking forms, accounts or logins, carts or checkout, databases, external API calls, remote or stock images, custom web fonts, or multiple pages/routes. A "Booking site" template that implies real bookings is a lie that produces an angry customer. Templates for those verticals are fine ONLY if scoped to a one-page credibility site with `mailto:`/`tel:` link-out CTAs — and the template's own description must be honest about that.

Note also: `lib/agent.ts` was just given two new rules — never invent facts about a real business (use bracketed placeholders like `[your address]`), and never build a control that only pretends to work. Your template prompts should be written to cooperate with those rules, not fight them.

## Scope — YOU MAY ONLY CREATE/EDIT FILES UNDER `lib/templates.ts`, `app/templates/`, AND `components/templates/`
Everything else is off limits — other agents are running in parallel. READ anything.

## What to build
1. **`lib/templates.ts`** — 18-24 templates. Each with: stable id, name, short honest description, category, and a **full, well-crafted starter prompt** (the thing that actually goes in the box). The prompt is the product here — write each one the way an expert user would: audience, purpose, tone, the sections wanted, and bracketed placeholders for facts only the owner knows. Cover the verticals the builder genuinely does well: restaurant/cafe, barber/salon, personal portfolio, photographer showcase (gallery of *placeholder* imagery — be honest that they can't upload photos yet), tradesman, gym/studio, law/accountancy, wedding/event info page, nonprofit, coming-soon/waitlist, SaaS landing page, product launch, personal blog-style single page, link-in-bio, agency, consultant, band/musician, local services.
2. **A gallery page** `app/templates/page.tsx` — browsable, filterable by category, each card showing name + description + a preview of the prompt. Clicking a template starts a project with that prompt prefilled.
3. **The hand-off mechanism** — read `lib/pending-prompt.ts` and how `components/marketing/PromptHero.tsx` and `app/(auth)/**` already move a pending prompt through signup into a new project (`PENDING_PROMPT_KEY`). Reuse that exact mechanism rather than inventing a second one. Signed-in and signed-out users must both work.

## Critical constraints
- DO NOT modify: prisma/schema.prisma, anything else under lib/ (including agent.ts, credits.ts, events.ts, assets/**, pending-prompt.ts — read them, don't edit), app/api/**, app/projects/**, app/dashboard/**, app/settings/**, app/admin/**, app/legal/**, app/blog/**, app/page.tsx, app/globals.css, components/marketing/**, proxy.ts, deploy.sh, .env, package.json.
- If the hand-off genuinely requires a change outside your scope, DO NOT make it — describe exactly what you need in your report instead.
- DO NOT add npm dependencies. DO NOT run `npm run build`, `git commit`, `git push`, or `deploy.sh`.
- Match the existing marketing visual idiom exactly — read `app/pricing/page.tsx` and `components/marketing/**` first. Restrained, monochrome with the brand gradient as accent, `rounded-2xl border border-black/10 dark:border-white/10`.
- Accessibility: the public pages just went through an a11y pass. Match that bar — a `<main id="main-content">` landmark, a `SkipLink` (see `components/marketing/SkipLink.tsx`), real labels on the filter controls, visible `focus-visible:` states, no keyboard traps, and no horizontal scroll at 380px.
- **A known constraint you must respect: white text on the brand gradient fails contrast (worst 1.81:1). Do not add new white-on-gradient text.** Use the existing neutral button treatments instead.
- Run `npx tsc --noEmit` and `npx eslint app lib components`; BOTH must be clean — the repo is currently at zero lint errors and must stay there.

## Report back
The templates you wrote, which verticals you scoped down for honesty and how, the hand-off mechanism you used, anything you needed outside your scope, and what you verified.

input.description: Transactional email notifications
input.prompt:
Work in C:\Users\edmem\kodely-prod (a Next.js 16 + Prisma app called Kodely — an AI website builder at kodely.me).

BUILD: transactional email notifications.

## Why
Kodely sends exactly one email today — the contact form (`lib/mail.ts`, `app/api/contact/**` — read both first). A user who runs out of credits, or whose build failed, or who signed up and never came back, hears nothing. The highest-value one by far is **low credits**: hitting zero mid-session with no warning is the exact bill-shock/dead-end experience this product positions against.

## Scope — YOU MAY ONLY CREATE/EDIT FILES UNDER `lib/notifications/` AND `app/api/notifications/`
Everything else is off limits — other agents are running in parallel. READ anything, especially `lib/mail.ts`, `lib/credits.ts`, `lib/events.ts`, `prisma/schema.prisma`.

## What to build
1. **`lib/notifications/templates.ts`** — plain-text-first email templates (with a simple, inlined-CSS HTML alternative; no remote images, no tracking pixels). Start with these four:
   - **Welcome** — what they can build, what a credit is, link to get started.
   - **Low credits** — fires when the balance drops below roughly two builds' worth. Must state the balance and roughly how many builds that is, and link to top up. Read `averageBuildCredits` in `lib/credits.ts` — per-user measured average is what the UI already uses, so the email must agree with the meter or it undermines it.
   - **Build failed** — reassure explicitly that they were NOT charged (that is genuinely true; verify in `app/api/generate/route.ts`), and say what to try.
   - **Site published** — the URL, and what to do next.
2. **`lib/notifications/send.ts`** — the dispatcher. Reuses the existing transport in `lib/mail.ts` (do not build a second one). Must be **fire-and-forget and non-blocking**: an email failure must never fail a build, a publish, or a signup.
3. **`app/api/notifications/run/route.ts`** — a cron-triggered endpoint for the digest-style ones (low credits). **Protect it with a shared secret from the environment** (`KODELY_CRON_SECRET`), compared in constant time; an unauthenticated endpoint that emails your entire user base is a gift to an attacker. Return 404, not 401, on a bad secret.

## The hard problem: DO NOT SEND DUPLICATES
There is **no schema change available to you** — `prisma/schema.prisma` is owned by someone else and off limits. So you cannot add a `sent_emails` table. Solve idempotency with what exists.

Strong hint: `lib/events.ts` has an append-only `Event` table with a closed `EVENTS` vocabulary — **read it, but you may not edit it**, so you cannot add an event name either. Work out what you CAN query to determine "have we already told this person this?" — e.g. deriving state from `CreditLedger`, `Build`, `Project.publishedAt`, and existing `Event` rows. If you genuinely cannot make a given email idempotent without a schema change, **do not send it** — implement it, leave it disabled behind a clear guard, and say exactly what schema you would need in your report. I will add it.

Emailing someone "you're running low" every hour is worse than never emailing them at all.

## Critical constraints
- **Never email anyone content that isn't theirs**, and never put credentials, tokens, session ids, or prompt text in an email.
- **No unsubscribe mechanism exists.** These must all be genuinely transactional (triggered by the user's own account state), never marketing. Do not build a re-engagement or drip campaign — that needs consent tracking we don't have. Say so in your report if you're tempted.
- DO NOT modify: prisma/schema.prisma, lib/mail.ts, lib/credits.ts, lib/events.ts, lib/agent.ts, lib/agent-sdk.ts, anything else under lib/ outside lib/notifications/, app/api/** outside app/api/notifications/, app/**, proxy.ts, deploy.sh, .env, package.json.
- DO NOT add npm dependencies (nodemailer is already present).
- DO NOT run `npm run build`, `git commit`, `git push`, or `deploy.sh`. **Do not actually send email to any real address.**
- Run `npx tsc --noEmit` and `npx eslint app lib components`; BOTH must be clean — the repo is at zero lint errors and must stay there.
- You may query the local Postgres read-only to check your idempotency queries. Do not modify data.

## Report back
The four templates, exactly how you made each one idempotent (or why you disabled it), the env vars needed, the cron line to schedule it, what you verified vs. assumed, and any schema you'd want me to add.

input.description: Security audit of the app
input.prompt:
Work in C:\Users\edmem\kodely-prod (a Next.js 16 + Prisma app called Kodely — an AI website builder at kodely.me). This is the owner's own application and this is an authorized internal security review.

TASK: a read-only security audit. **You are writing findings, not fixes.**

## Scope of what to examine
Everything under `app/`, `lib/`, `proxy.ts`, `prisma/schema.prisma`, `middleware`-equivalents, and `scripts/`. Focus on:

1. **Authentication & session handling** — `lib/auth.ts`. Session token generation, hashing, expiry enforcement, cookie flags (`httpOnly`/`sameSite`/`secure`/`domain`), fixation, and whether sign-out truly invalidates. input.description: Marketing copy accuracy audit
input.prompt:
Work in C:\Users\edmem\kodely-prod (a Next.js 16 + Prisma app called Kodely — an AI website builder at kodely.me).

TASK: audit every capability and pricing claim on the marketing pages against what the code actually does, and fix what's wrong.

## Why this matters now
A parallel effort just found that published blog content overstates the product in several places, and that the one public per-build credit figure ("roughly 100–150 credits") is contradicted by measurement. The marketing pages have never been checked the same way. A claim on the pricing page is a promise attached to a payment.

## Ground truth — verify every claim against these, do not trust the copy
- `lib/agent.ts` — the SYSTEM prompt. **The definitive statement of what a generated site can contain.** Read it in full. Note it was just given two new rules (never invent business facts; never build a control that only pretends to work).
- `lib/foundation.ts` — the starting project and its only dependencies.
- `app/api/site/[slug]/**` — `SANDBOX_CSP`. No external hosts at all. There is no `font-src`, so even a base64 `@font-face` is blocked.
- `lib/credits.ts` — `MICROS_PER_CREDIT`, `SIGNUP_GRANT`, `estimateCredits` (**note: it has ZERO callers — no cost estimate is shown in the UI today**), `averageBuildCredits`, the spend cap.
- `lib/stripe.ts` — the real credit packs and prices.
- `app/api/generate/route.ts` — the no-charge-on-failure behaviour, and the repair loop.
- `app/api/projects/[id]/export/route.ts` — zip export. **Built but NOT yet deployed.**
- `lib/site-seo.ts` — what SEO handling actually happens.
- `app/api/projects/[id]/publish/route.ts` — publishing only ever returns `<slug>.kodely.site`. **No custom domains.**

**Known-false things to hunt for:** working contact forms, bookings, accounts/logins on generated sites, carts/checkout, databases, external API integrations, stock or uploaded images, custom web fonts, multi-page sites, custom domains, npm packages beyond react/react-dom, or any "see the cost before you build" claim.

**A specific number to check everywhere:** `SIGNUP_GRANT` is 750 and appears hardcoded in several places (`app/pricing/page.tsx`, `app/(auth)/signup/page.tsx`, `app/blog/[slug]/page.tsx`'s CTA). Find every literal copy and make each one derive from the constant, so it can never drift.

**On per-build cost: publish no number.** Measurements so far are 144 and 472 credits — a 3x spread on two samples. `estimateCredits`'s own comment says that is not a distribution. If any page states or implies a per-build cost, remove the figure rather than replacing it.

## Scope — YOU MAY ONLY EDIT: `app/pricing/**`, `app/page.tsx`, `components/marketing/TrustBento.tsx`, `components/marketing/FeatureVisuals.tsx`, `components/marketing/WhatPeopleBuild.tsx`
READ anything. If a false claim lives in a file outside this list, DO NOT edit it — report the exact file, line and claim instead.

## Critical constraints
- **This is a correctness pass, not a rewrite.** Keep the voice, structure and design. Change a sentence when it is untrue or unsupportable; do not restyle, restructure, or "improve" copy that is accurate.
- Do not weaken genuinely true and valuable claims. Real strengths, all verifiable: sites are real Vite+React+TS+Tailwind apps rather than HTML mockups; a build that fails to compile is never charged; credits are metered from real token usage against a published rate; there is a user-settable spend cap; published sites get real title/meta/OG handling.
- **Do not add new white text on the brand gradient** — it fails colour contrast (worst 1.81:1) and that is a known accepted issue; don't make it worse.
- The public pages just passed an accessibility review — preserve `<main id="main-content">` landmarks, `SkipLink`, form labels, `aria-*`, and `focus-visible:` styles. Do not regress them.
- DO NOT modify: prisma/schema.prisma, anything under lib/, app/api/**, app/blog/**, app/legal/**, app/templates/**, app/projects/**, app/dashboard/**, app/settings/**, app/admin/**, app/globals.css, other files under components/marketing/, proxy.ts, deploy.sh, .env, package.json.
- DO NOT add npm dependencies. DO NOT run `npm run build`, `git commit`, `git push`, or `deploy.sh`.
- Run `npx tsc --noEmit` and `npx eslint app lib components`; BOTH must be clean — the repo is at zero lint errors and must stay there.

## Report back
Every claim you found that was false or unsupportable, with file:line and what you changed it to; every hardcoded 750 you replaced; false claims you found OUTSIDE your editable scope (file, line, exact text); and any claim you were unsure about and why.

`C:\Users\edmem\kodely-prod\lib\zip.ts:61-67`:

    .replace(/\\/g, "/")
    .split("/")
    .filter((segment) => segment !== "" && segment !== "." && segment !== "..")

I need to be honest about what "get this board done" realistically means here: of the 728 cards, roughly 253 are SEO content pieces, 99 are competitor research teardowns, and many others are strategic decisions only the user can make, like pricing tiers or brand direction. A significant chunk of the Builder/Editor cards also depend on backend systems that intentionally don't exist yet, like a visual database editor or auth and payments builders.

So full completion isn't realistic, but there's still a large amount of genuinely actionable work. I'm mapping out disjoint file territories for a dozen or so new agents to run alongside the three already in progress, covering things like admin RBAC and audit logging, a projects registry with moderation and takedown tools, a support inbox, system health monitoring, a blog/SEO CMS, feature flags, and builder features like responsive preview and a command palette — while watching for file conflicts between agents touching shared areas like the project builder.

I'm realizing most of the builder/editor cards collide on the same Editor.tsx file, so I should consolidate those into one agent handling multiple cards rather than splitting them across agents and risking serialization conflicts. I'm also mapping out territories for billing/pricing UX, onboarding flows, a second batch of SEO content, competitor research synthesis, a status page with incident runbooks, and deciding that i18n for generated sites is really a prompt change I should handle myself rather than delegate.

Now I'm finalizing roughly twelve agents with clean, non-overlapping territories: separate admin agents for RBAC/audit logs, sites registry/takedown, feedback inbox, content CMS, feature flags, and system health, plus one dedicated agent owning the entire editor UX bundle to avoid file conflicts.

Adding billing UX, onboarding, SEO content batch, competitor research synthesis, and ops/status page agents brings the total to twelve new plus three already running, fifteen overall. I'm noting several of these will need new database tables, starting with the audit log schema.

Since I own the schema, I should add the needed tables upfront rather than having agents request them mid-flight — AdminAuditLog, FeatureFlag, and ModerationFinding. input.prompt:
Work in C:\Users\edmem\kodely-prod (Next.js 16 + Prisma, an AI website builder called Kodely).

BUILD: an admin audit log, and surface it.

## Why
Admin surfaces show cost, margin, customer prompts and personal data. There is currently no record of who looked at what. "Which admin viewed this account" has no answer today.

## Schema already exists — use it, do not change it
`AdminAuditLog` in prisma/schema.prisma (READ ONLY): `id, actorId, actorEmail, action, targetType, targetId, meta Json?, createdAt`, indexed on `[actorId, createdAt]`, `[action, createdAt]`, `[targetType, targetId]`. Append-only by convention.

## Scope — YOU MAY ONLY CREATE/EDIT: `lib/admin-audit.ts`, `app/admin/audit/**`
Do NOT edit `app/admin/page.tsx`, `app/admin/layout.tsx`, or `app/admin/users/**` — other work owns those. READ them to match idiom (especially `getAdminUser()` from lib/auth.ts and the table/stat-tile patterns in `app/admin/page.tsx`).

## Build
1. **`lib/admin-audit.ts`** — a `recordAdminAction()` helper and a closed `ADMIN_ACTIONS` vocabulary (dotted, past-tense: `user.viewed`, `site.taken_down`, `flag.changed`). Model it on `lib/events.ts` (READ ONLY) — same discipline: closed name set, small non-PII `meta`, never prompt bodies or generated content. Unlike `track()` in events.ts, decide deliberately whether an audit write should be fire-and-forget or awaited, and justify it in a comment — a dropped analytics event is a gap in a chart, a dropped audit row is a gap in an accountability record.
2. **`app/admin/audit/page.tsx`** — a readable log: when, who, what action, what target (linked where it makes sense), meta. Filter by actor and by action, paginated, newest first. Match the existing admin visual idiom exactly (`rounded-xl border border-black/10 dark:border-white/10`, `text-sm`, `tabular-nums`, monochrome).
3. Call `getAdminUser()` at the top of every page you create and `notFound()` if null — the layout gates the section, but Next's docs say a layout must not be the sole authorization boundary.

## Also produce (do not implement)
A short section in your report listing every existing admin surface that SHOULD be recording an action but currently isn't, with file paths — so whoever owns those files can add the calls. Do not edit those files.

## Constraints
- DO NOT modify: prisma/schema.prisma, anything under lib/ except lib/admin-audit.ts, app/api/**, app/admin/page.tsx, app/admin/layout.tsx, app/admin/users/**, app/projects/**, app/dashboard/**, app/settings/**, app/legal/**, app/blog/**, app/globals.css, proxy.ts, deploy.sh, .env, package.json.
- No new npm dependencies. Do NOT run `npm run build`, `git commit`, `git push`, or `deploy.sh`.
- Do NOT add white text on the brand gradient — it fails contrast and that is a known accepted issue.
- `npx tsc --noEmit` AND `npx eslint app lib components` must BOTH be clean. The repo is at zero lint errors and must stay there. Other agents are running in parallel, so if you see errors in files you did not touch, they are not yours — leave them.
- Local Postgres is available (DATABASE_URL in .env). Read-only, plus rows you create and clean up yourself.

## Report back
What you built, your fire-and-forget vs awaited decision and why, the list of surfaces that should be logging but aren't, and what you verified.

input.description: Feature flags and kill switches
input.prompt:
Work in C:\Users\edmem\kodely-prod (Next.js 16 + Prisma, an AI website builder called Kodely).

BUILD: runtime feature flags and kill switches.

## Why
Every behaviour change currently requires a deploy, and `deploy.sh` on this project has a history of shipping stale code. There is no way to turn off generation, publishing, or rewards in an incident without a code push. A kill switch that needs a deploy is not a kill switch.

## Schema already exists — use it, do not change it
`FeatureFlag` in prisma/schema.prisma (READ ONLY): `key (@id), enabled, description, rolloutPct (0-100, ignored when enabled is false), updatedAt, updatedBy`.

## Scope — YOU MAY ONLY CREATE/EDIT: `lib/flags.ts`, `app/admin/flags/**`
Do NOT edit anything else under lib/ or app/. READ freely — `lib/events.ts` for the closed-vocabulary pattern, `app/admin/users/page.tsx` for query and visual idiom, `lib/auth.ts` for `getAdminUser()`.

## Build
1. **`lib/flags.ts`**
   - A closed `FLAGS` constant naming every flag that exists, with a one-line comment each. Free-text flag keys rot exactly like free-text event names.
   - `isEnabled(key, userId?)` — resolves `enabled` plus `rolloutPct`. **Bucket by a hash of `userId + key`**, so a given user's answer is stable rather than flickering between requests, and two different flags at 50% don't hit the same half of users. Explain the hashing choice in a comment.
   - **Caching is the crux.** A DB read per flag check on every request is unacceptable, but a stale cache makes a kill switch useless in the moment you need it. Pick a short TTL (seconds), justify the number in a comment, and make sure a flag flip takes effect within it. Note in your report that this is per-process, so a multi-process deploy converges within one TTL rather than instantly.
   - **Fail-safe direction matters and differs per flag.** A kill switch that fails OPEN during a DB outage is useless; a feature gate that fails CLOSED breaks the product for everyone. Support both, make the default explicit per flag, and write down the reasoning.
   - Seed sensible flags: kill switches for generation, publishing, signups, and rewards; plus a gate or two for new features.
2. **`app/admin/flags/page.tsx`** — list flags, toggle, set rollout percentage, show who changed it and when. Match the admin visual idiom exactly. `getAdminUser()` at the top, `notFound()` if null.

## Also produce (do not implement)
In your report: the exact call sites where each kill switch SHOULD be checked (file paths and a one-line description), so whoever owns those files can wire them. Do not edit those files.

## Constraints
- DO NOT modify: prisma/schema.prisma, anything under lib/ except lib/flags.ts, app/api/**, other app/admin/** subtrees, app/projects/**, app/dashboard/**, app/settings/**, app/globals.css, proxy.ts, deploy.sh, .env, package.json.
- No new npm dependencies (use node:crypto for hashing). Do NOT run `npm run build`, `git commit`, `git push`, or `deploy.sh`.
- No new white-on-brand-gradient text (fails contrast; known accepted issue).
- `npx tsc --noEmit` AND `npx eslint app lib components` must BOTH be clean. Parallel agents are running — errors in files you did not touch are not yours.
- Local Postgres available; clean up any rows you create.

## Report back
The flags you seeded, your caching TTL and hashing decisions with reasoning, the per-flag fail-open/fail-closed defaults, the call sites that need wiring, and what you verified.

input.prompt:
Work in C:\Users\edmem\kodely-prod (Next.js 16 + Prisma, an AI website builder called Kodely).

BUILD: four Builder/Editor UX improvements. They are bundled into one agent because they all touch `app/projects/[id]/Editor.tsx`, and parallel edits to one file would collide.

## Read first
`app/projects/[id]/Editor.tsx` in full, plus `BuildingOverlay.tsx` and `BuildRating.tsx` beside it, and `app/api/generate/route.ts` for the SSE event shapes (`text`, `progress`, `status`, `file`, `done`, `error`). Recent work added: live progress narration, a build overlay, thumbs up/down, a zip download, an Enhance flow, and a low-credit warning. **Preserve all of it.**

## Build, in this priority order
1. **Stop / cancel a running build.** The route already aborts cleanly when the client disconnects (`AbortController`, `cancel()` on the stream, and a FAILED build recorded with `creditsCharged: 0`). Expose that as a real Stop button. Verify against the route what actually happens to credits on abort and make the UI tell the truth about it.
2. **Responsive preview with device frames.** Desktop / tablet / mobile widths for the preview iframe. Generated sites are prompted to work down to 380px, so this is how anyone would ever check that. Keep it simple — width constraints and a label, not a skeuomorphic phone.
3. **Command palette + keyboard shortcuts.** Cmd/Ctrl-K opens it. Actions from what already exists: switch Preview/Code/History, publish, download zip, focus the prompt box, open settings. Must be fully keyboard operable, trap focus while open, close on Escape and restore focus.
4. **Connection-loss recovery.** If the SSE stream dies mid-build (network drop, laptop sleep), the UI currently just stops. Detect it and tell the user plainly what happened and what state their project is in. **Do not invent a resume capability that does not exist** — check what the server actually does on disconnect before writing any message.

## Scope — YOU MAY ONLY CREATE/EDIT FILES UNDER `app/projects/[id]/`
Everything else is off limits. READ anything.

## Constraints
- **Do not regress the accessibility work.** The app just passed an a11y pass: visible `focus-visible:` states, real labels, `aria-*` on stateful controls, no keyboard traps, no horizontal scroll at 380px. Match that bar in everything you add.
- **No new white text on the brand gradient** — it fails contrast (worst 1.81:1), a known accepted issue. Use the existing neutral button treatments.
- Match the existing visual idiom exactly: `rounded-md`/`rounded-lg`, `text-xs`/`text-sm`, monochrome, `border-black/10 dark:border-white/10`.
- DO NOT modify: prisma/schema.prisma, anything under lib/, app/api/**, app/dashboard/**, app/settings/**, app/admin/**, app/globals.css (if you need CSS, use Tailwind utilities or report what you need), proxy.ts, deploy.sh, .env, package.json.
- No new npm dependencies. Do NOT run `npm run build`, `git commit`, `git push`, or `deploy.sh`.
- `npx tsc --noEmit` AND `npx eslint app lib components` must BOTH be clean. Parallel agents are running — errors in files you did not touch are not yours.
- A dev server may be on http://localhost:3003. **The Browser pane may not composite frames**, so CSS animation `currentTime` can read 0 and screenshots can time out — verify DOM and computed styles programmatically instead.

## Report back
Each of the four, what you verified about server behaviour (especially credits on abort and what really happens on disconnect), anything you deliberately did not build because the capability does not exist, and how you tested.

input.prompt:
Work in C:\Users\edmem\kodely-prod (Next.js 16 + Prisma, an AI website builder called Kodely).

BUILD: a real billing and credits area for customers.

## Why
A user can see a balance and click "Top up". They cannot see where their credits went. The whole product positions against bill shock, and the ledger — which is append-only and auditable by design — is invisible to the person it is about.

## Read first
`lib/credits.ts` (the whole anti-bill-shock contract, `MICROS_PER_CREDIT`, `SIGNUP_GRANT`, `getBalance`, `spentInWindow`, `getSpendCapStatus`, `averageBuildCredits`, `estimateCredits`), `lib/stripe.ts` (`CREDIT_PACKS`, `billingEnabled()`), `app/dashboard/page.tsx`, `components/CreditMeter.tsx`, `app/dashboard/TopUpButton.tsx`, `app/settings/page.tsx`, and `app/admin/users/[id]/page.tsx` — that last one already renders a ledger statement well, and the customer-facing version should be at least as clear.

## Scope — YOU MAY ONLY CREATE/EDIT: `app/dashboard/billing/**`, `app/dashboard/TopUpButton.tsx`
Do NOT edit `app/dashboard/page.tsx`, `app/dashboard/ProjectRow.tsx`, `app/settings/**`, `components/CreditMeter.tsx`, or anything under lib/ or app/api/. READ them.

## Build
1. **`app/dashboard/billing/page.tsx`** — the customer's own credit statement. Every ledger entry: date, what it was for, signed amount, running balance. Decode `reason` into plain English — it carries `build`, `signup_grant`, `stripe:<session>`, and a `reward:<platform>:[pending:]<hash>` state machine (see `app/api/rewards/_lib.ts`). **Never show a raw hash to a customer.** Link a build charge to the project it belongs to. Paginated.
2. **Spend summary** — balance, spent in the last 30 days, and the user's own measured average per build (`averageBuildCredits`). If a spend cap is set, show progress against it.
3. **Honest cost information.** `estimateCredits()` exists and has ZERO callers. Its own comment says the two measurements so far (144 and 472 credits) are not a distribution. If you surface an estimate anywhere, present it as a wide range with that uncertainty stated — **do not present a precise-looking number**, and do not quote a single "typical build costs X" figure.
4. **`TopUpButton.tsx`** — it currently only appears when `billingEnabled()`. Make the billing page degrade honestly when Stripe is unconfigured: show the statement, and say top-ups are unavailable rather than rendering a button that 503s.

## Constraints
- **Read-only on money.** Do not write to `CreditLedger`, do not grant or deduct anything, do not create Stripe sessions beyond what `TopUpButton` already does.
- **Do not restate the no-charge-on-failure promise unless you verify it** in `app/api/generate/route.ts`. It is true — confirm it yourself before writing it down. Note that a run which fails, self-repairs, then succeeds IS charged once for the whole run including the repair; if you mention repairs, say that accurately.
- Match the dashboard's visual idiom exactly: `rounded-xl border border-black/10 dark:border-white/10`, `text-sm`, `tabular-nums` on figures, monochrome.
- Preserve the accessibility bar: real labels, `focus-visible:` states, `<main>` landmark if you add a page shell, no horizontal scroll at 380px.
- **No new white text on the brand gradient** (fails contrast; known accepted issue).

BUILD: a support inbox — customer feedback, plus per-user operator notes.

## Why
Build ratings (thumbs up/down, with a reason on thumbs-down) are being collected as `Event` rows and are aggregated into a satisfaction percentage on `/admin`, but nobody can read the individual ones. ## Schema already exists — use it, do not change it
`SupportNote` in prisma/schema.prisma (READ ONLY): `id, userId, authorEmail, body, createdAt`, relation to `User` with cascade delete, indexed `[userId, createdAt]`.

## Read first
`lib/events.ts` (READ ONLY) — the `EVENTS` vocabulary, `buildRatings()`, and the `Event.props` shape. Ratings are stored as `build.rated` events with props `{ buildId, projectId, rating: "up"|"down", repairAttempts, model, reason? }` where `reason` is one of a fixed list (`looks-generic`, `wrong-content`, `layout-off`, `missing-something`, `broken`, `other`) — see `app/api/feedback/route.ts`. Also read `app/admin/users/[id]/page.tsx` for query patterns and visual idiom, and `lib/auth.ts` for `getAdminUser()`.

## Scope — YOU MAY ONLY CREATE/EDIT: `app/admin/feedback/**`
Do NOT edit `app/admin/page.tsx`, `app/admin/layout.tsx`, `app/admin/users/**`, `app/admin/sites/**`, `app/admin/audit/**`, `app/admin/flags/**`, or anything under lib/ or app/api/.

## Build
1. **Feedback inbox** — individual `build.rated` events, newest first, filterable by rating and by reason. For each: who, which project/build, the reason given, the model, and `repairAttempts`. **The question worth answering on this page: are the thumbs-down builds the ones that needed a repair pass?** Make that visible — it is the difference between a quality problem and a reliability problem.
2. **Reason breakdown** — counts per reason, so the most common complaint is obvious at a glance.
3. **Per-user support notes** — read and write `SupportNote`. An add-note form storing `authorEmail` from the current admin. Notes are operator-written, never shown to the customer.
4. `getAdminUser()` at the top of every page, `notFound()` if null.

## Important cautions
- **The `Event` table is currently EMPTY** and ratings only started being collected very recently. Build a genuine empty state and say clearly in your report that this is unpopulated, so nobody reads an empty page as "everyone is happy".
- Support notes are subject to a data-subject access request. Put a short, visible line in the note UI reminding the operator to write only what they would stand behind if the customer read it. That is a real constraint, not decoration.
- Truncate anything long. Do not dump prompts or generated file contents.

What you built, what the repair-vs-rating correlation view shows, the empty-table caveat, and what you verified.

## What I built

**`C:\Users\edmem\kodely-prod\lib\templates.ts`** — 23 templates (`id`, `name`, `description`, `category`, `prompt`) across 7 categories: Food & drink (restaurant, coffee shop, food truck), Beauty & wellness (barbershop, hair/beauty salon, gym/studio), Local services (tradesperson, local service business), Professional services (law firm, accountant, consultant, agency), Personal & creative (portfolio, photographer, band/musician, one-page blog, link-in-bio), Startup & product (SaaS landing, product launch, coming-soon/waitlist), Events & causes (wedding, event/conference, nonprofit). Each prompt states audience, purpose, tone, an ordered section list, and bracketed placeholders, then explicitly names the link-out CTA and the no-photos reality.

**`app\templates\page.tsx`** — server component; `getCurrentUser()` → `signedIn`, `force-dynamic`, `SkipLink` + `<main id="main-content" tabIndex={-1}>`, marketing shell (Aura/Nav/Reveal/Footer), pricing-page idiom (`rounded-2xl border border-black/10 dark:border-white/10`, neutral buttons, gradient only as `brand-gradient-text` and icon accent — no new white-on-gradient text). A three-item "ground rules" band states the honest limits once, up front: one page/no backend, real links not fake forms, your facts stay bracketed.

**`components\templates\TemplateGallery.tsx` + `TemplateCard.tsx`** — search box (real `<label>`, sr-only), a genuine radio group in a `fieldset`/`legend` for category filter (arrow-key nav, `peer-focus-visible:` outline, per-category counts), `role="status"` live region for result count and the "starting" state, and cards showing category, name, description, a one-line prompt preview, plus a `<details>` holding a **labelled, editable textarea of the full prompt** — so bracketed details can be filled in before building.

## Verticals scoped down for honesty
Restaurant/cafe/food-truck: no reservation or ordering form → `tel:`/`mailto:`/`[link to your booking system]`; food-truck schedule stated as hand-edited, no map embed. Barber/salon/gym: no booking engine or payments; button label must say "Call to book" rather than "Book now". Tradesperson/local services: explicitly no quote form ("a form that quietly loses an emergency call-out is worse than none"). Law/accountancy: no intake form, no client portal, no invented bar/SRA numbers, case results or testimonials. Photographer: card description says outright you cannot upload photos yet; the prompt asks for a designed placeholder-tile grid with captions instead of stock/remote images. Band: no embedded player — link out to streaming. Blog: no comments/newsletter/search; posts live in the page. Coming-soon: the prompt names the trap and forbids the email field, substituting `mailto:` with a prefilled subject or a link to Tally/Google Form. SaaS/product launch: no signup/cart — links to the real app or store; any UI shown must read as an illustrative mock. Wedding/event/nonprofit: RSVP, tickets and donations all link out; nonprofit prompt bans invented impact numbers specifically.

## Hand-off
Reuses `lib/pending-prompt.ts` exactly — no second mechanism. On click: write the (possibly edited) prompt to `PENDING_PROMPT_KEY`, clear `PENDING_PROMPT_IMAGE_KEY` (so a reference image attached on the home page earlier in the session can't ride along). Signed out → `router.push("/signup")`, where the existing "picking up where you left off" panel and `destinationAfterAuth()` in the signup/login submit handlers (and `/continue` for Google OAuth) take over. Signed in → call `destinationAfterAuth()` directly, then push its result. Either way `app/projects/[id]/Editor.tsx` auto-fires the prompt on mount. The button stays locked after click so a double-click can't create two projects.

Side effect worth knowing: `destinationAfterAuth` derives the project name from the first 60 chars of the prompt, so template-started projects are named e.g. "Build a one-page website for [your restaurant's name], a…". Giving them the template's name would need a change to `lib/pending-prompt.ts` (out of my scope), and would also only fix the signed-in path — the signed-out path goes through the auth pages' own call. I left it consistent rather than forking the mechanism.

## Needed outside my scope
**Nothing links to `/templates` yet.** `components/marketing/MarketingNav.tsx` (`LINKS` array) and `MarketingFooter.tsx` are off limits. To make the page reachable, add `{ href: "/templates", label: "Templates" }` to `LINKS` in MarketingNav, and ideally a footer link plus a "Not sure what to type? Browse templates" link under `PromptHero` on `app/page.tsx`. Without that, the page is only reachable by direct URL.

## Verified
`npx tsc --noEmit` clean, `npx eslint app lib components` clean (both exit 0). Rendered the page against the running dev server: all 23 cards present, category radios exposed with accessible names, filtering works (Startup & product → 3 cards, live region reads "Showing 3 of 23 templates"). At a 375px viewport `scrollWidth === clientWidth` (375) — no horizontal scroll — including with all 23 prompt textareas expanded. `git status` shows only `app/templates/`, `components/templates/`, `lib/templates.ts` as new; no other file modified by me. I did not run a build, commit, push, deploy, or add any dependency.</result>

RESEARCH TASK for Kodely, an AI website builder (codebase at C:\Users\edmem\kodely-prod). Deliverable is a plan, not code.

## The idea to work out
The owner wants a higher tier — "Kodely Pro" / "Super" — that generates **full applications**, not just marketing sites: CRMs, booking systems, inventory trackers, client portals. Crucially, they want **pre-built foundations for these app types** so generation is easy AND **credit-cheap**, because generating a whole app from scratch every time is expensive.

That last point is the real thesis and you should test it: a foundation that carries most of the app means the model writes less, which cuts cost per build. Quantify that where you can.

## Start by understanding what exists — this is not greenfield
Read carefully and let it constrain everything:
- `lib/foundation.ts` — the current starting project. Note how small it is and that it ships ONLY react + react-dom.
- `lib/agent.ts` — the SYSTEM prompt. Read in full. Note the hard constraints.
- `lib/build-site.ts` — how sites compile: ONE locked pre-installed dependency tree, symlinked, never `npm install` per generation, 60s timeout.
- `app/api/site/[slug]/**` — `SANDBOX_CSP`. `default-src 'self'`, `connect-src 'none'`. **No external requests at all.** No backend, no database, no auth, no persistence.
- `lib/credits.ts` — how cost works. Measured builds: 144 and 472 credits.
- `prisma/schema.prisma` — how Kodely itself stores things today.

**The blocker is architectural, not a prompt problem.** A CRM needs data that persists, users who log in, and queries. Today a generated site is static files under a CSP that forbids network calls. Do not hand-wave this.

## What to research and decide
1. **What "full app" minimally requires** — persistence, auth, server logic, file storage — and the realistic options for each. Consider seriously: client-only apps with IndexedDB/localStorage (real for a single-user tracker, useless for a shared CRM); a Kodely-hosted backend-as-a-service; per-project database provisioning; embedding something like SQLite/PGlite. Give each a verdict with reasoning, not a list.
2. **What the CSP would have to become**, and what that costs in safety. `connect-src 'none'` is currently what stops a generated site phoning home. Note the existing published security audit at `docs/security/audit-2026-08.md` if present.
3. **The foundations themselves** — propose 4-8 concrete app foundations (CRM, booking/scheduling, inventory, client portal, invoicing, simple e-commerce, internal admin tool, event management). For each: what ships pre-built vs what the model generates, the data model, and **an estimate of credits saved versus generating from scratch, with your reasoning shown**.
4. **Dependency implications** — `build-site.ts` uses one shared locked tree. What would foundations need added, and what does that do to build time and the security posture?
5. **Pricing/packaging** — the tier only makes sense if it covers its cost. Read `lib/credits.ts` and `lib/stripe.ts`. Where does a Pro tier sit? What is the honest margin story given a real build measured 472 credits?
6. **Competitive reality** — research what Lovable, Bolt.new, Replit, v0, Base44 and Rocket.new actually deliver for full-stack app generation, how they handle backend/database/auth, and what they charge. Use WebSearch/WebFetch. Be concrete and cite. Note where their approach is available to Kodely and where it is not.

## Deliverable
Write a JSON array to `C:\Users\edmem\AppData\Local\Temp\claude\C--Users-edmem-OneDrive-Desktop-Kodely\eb67eaec-3d5e-420f-a5fc-4419d7203aa9\scratchpad\cards-pro.json`.

Each element: `{"title": "...", "description": "...", "type": "FEATURE"|"CHORE"|"IDEA"|"BUG", "priority": "LOW"|"NORMAL"|"HIGH"|"URGENT", "labels": ["..."]}`

Aim for **25-40 cards** forming a real plan: the architectural decisions that must be made first (as decision cards stating the options and your recommendation), the foundations, the infrastructure, pricing, and the risks. Titles are short and concrete. Descriptions carry the actual thinking — a card that just restates its title is worthless. Where something is genuinely blocked on a decision only the owner can make, say so in the card and give a recommendation.

Sequence matters: make it obvious what has to happen before what.

## Constraints
- **Write ONLY the JSON file above.** Do not modify any code, schema, config, or the board database. This is research.
- Do not invent competitor pricing or capabilities — verify with WebSearch/WebFetch, and if you cannot verify something, say so in the card rather than asserting it.
- Be honest about cost. If your credit-saving estimate is a guess, label it a guess and show the arithmetic.
- Do not run `npm run build`, `git commit`, `git push`, or `deploy.sh`.

## Report back
Your architectural recommendation and why, the credit-saving thesis and whether it holds up, the top 3 decisions the owner has to make before any of this can start, and how many cards you wrote.

input.prompt:
RESEARCH TASK for Kodely, an AI website builder (codebase at C:\Users\edmem\kodely-prod). Deliverable is a plan, not code.

## The idea to work out
A **prompt wizard** that helps someone assemble a great prompt instead of staring at an empty box. The owner wants it to cover: styling direction, colour scheme, **logo upload**, a **reference site** they like, and **their current site** (to carry over content or branding).

## Start by understanding what exists — several of these are already partly solved or blocked
Read carefully:
- `lib/agent.ts` — the SYSTEM prompt in full. Note two rules just added: never invent facts about a real business (use bracketed placeholders), and never build a control that only pretends to work.
- `lib/enhance.ts` + `app/api/enhance/route.ts` — auto-enhance ALREADY EXISTS: a rough prompt expands into a spec under five fixed headings. The wizard must build on this, not duplicate it.
- `lib/templates.ts` and `app/templates/` — a 23-template starter gallery just shipped (may still be in progress). Same point: complement, don't duplicate.
- `components/marketing/PromptHero.tsx` — the current prompt box, including an image-attach path that downsizes client-side to a data URL, and voice input.
- `lib/pending-prompt.ts` — how a prompt survives signup into a new project.
- `app/api/site/[slug]/**` — `SANDBOX_CSP`. **Generated sites cannot load remote images, custom web fonts, or make any external request.**
- `lib/assets/` — 461 inlinable assets (icons, flags, gradients, patterns, avatars) the builder can already use.
- `lib/credits.ts` — cost model. Measured builds: 144 and 472 credits.

## The hard parts you must resolve, not gloss
1. **Logo upload.** Generated sites are text files under a CSP with no remote hosts. A logo would have to be inlined as SVG or a data URI, and it passes through the model's context as tokens. Work out what is actually feasible: SVG upload (small, inlinable), raster (how big before it wrecks cost?), or a Kodely-hosted asset with a CSP change. Give a recommendation with numbers.
2. **Reference site.** Fetching a URL to analyse it means server-side fetching of an arbitrary user-supplied URL — SSRF risk. Read `docs/security/audit-2026-08.md` if it exists. What can be extracted safely and legally? Copying a competitor's design is also a legal and ethical question worth naming.
3. **Their current site.** Same fetching concerns, plus: what is genuinely worth carrying over — text content, colour palette, logo, business facts. This one interacts with the "never invent facts" rule: importing real facts from a real site is the *legitimate* way to fill those brackets.
4. **Colour scheme / styling.** Cheapest and safest of the four. How should choices be expressed to the model so they actually change the output? Note `lib/agent.ts` warns against generic "AI purple" — read what it says about the quality bar.
5. **Not forcing it.** There is a board card "Never force the wizard — raw box stays the default". Respect that: design the wizard as optional, skippable, and fast.

## Also research
How Lovable, Bolt.new, v0, Wix ADI, Durable, Framer AI and Base44 onboard a new user — what they ask, in what order, how many steps before first output, and what they do with a logo or a reference URL. Use WebSearch/WebFetch. Be concrete, cite, and say where you could not verify.

## Deliverable
Write a JSON array to `C:\Users\edmem\AppData\Local\Temp\claude\C--Users-edmem-OneDrive-Desktop-Kodely\eb67eaec-3d5e-420f-a5fc-4419d7203aa9\scratchpad\cards-wizard.json`.

Each element: `{"title": "...", "description": "...", "type": "FEATURE"|"CHORE"|"IDEA"|"BUG", "priority": "LOW"|"NORMAL"|"HIGH"|"URGENT", "labels": ["..."]}`

Aim for **20-35 cards**: the wizard flow itself step by step, each input type with its technical approach and its risks, how it hands off to the existing enhance path, security cards for the fetching problems, and the measurement (does the wizard actually improve first-build quality? — note `scripts/eval` exists as a harness). Descriptions must carry real reasoning; a card restating its title is worthless.

## Constraints
- **Write ONLY the JSON file above.** No code, schema, config, or board-database changes. This is research.
- Do not invent competitor behaviour — verify or say you could not.
- Do not propose anything that violates the CSP without explicitly flagging it as requiring a CSP change and what that costs.
- Do not run `npm run build`, `git commit`, `git push`, or `deploy.sh`.

## Report back
The wizard flow you recommend and how many steps, your verdict on each of the four hard inputs (logo, reference site, current site, styling), the SSRF mitigation you'd require, and how many cards you wrote.

Two new stages created, ten agents running. But the security audit found something that outranks all of it.

## Two critical holes — verified, then fixed

**Your live build engine gave a user prompt unrestricted shell access.**

`lib/agent-sdk.ts` passed `allowedTools: [..., "Bash", ...]` on the belief it was a whitelist. I checked the SDK's own type definitions rather than take the finding on trust, and they say verbatim: *"List of tool names that are auto-allowed without prompting for permission… **To restrict which tools are available, use the `tools` option instead.**"*

So it was an **auto-approve** list. Every other tool stayed available, and Bash was pre-approved. `cwd` is not a jail, and the prompt is verbatim user input from the generate route.

There's no Options-level `tools` field, so I enforced it two ways: `disallowedTools` strips them from the model's context, and a `canUseTool` allow-list denies anything not explicitly permitted — meaning a tool added by a future SDK version is denied by default rather than silently allowed. Bash is gone; the prompt now tells the agent it can't delete files and to de-reference a component instead.

I also caught a bug I introduced doing it: `updatedInput: {}` in the allow branch would have replaced every tool's real input with an empty object.

**The second one affects both engines**, so switching back to `KODELY_ENGINE=api` would not have helped. `normalizePath` accepted `vite.config.ts`, and `build-site.ts` spawned vite with `{ ...process.env }` — handing anything in that config your `DATABASE_URL`, OAuth and Anthropic tokens, session secret, and Stripe keys. One successful config write was enough to exfiltrate every credential the app holds. The only thing preventing it was a sentence in the system prompt, which isn't an access control.

Fixed in two layers: `isProtectedPath()` blocks writes to build configs, `package.json`, tsconfig, dotfiles and `node_modules` — on both the API tool path *and* the SDK write-back diff — and the vite child now gets a minimal environment instead of inheriting yours.

**Two still open, and they need you:** generated sites are reachable at `kodely.me/api/site/<slug>/` as first-party content (phishing, not account takeover — `httpOnly` and `connect-src 'none'` hold), and there's no rate limiting on login or signup because all three limiters key on `userId` and can't apply pre-auth. Both carded as urgent.

**The highest-value thing you can check:** confirm `KODELY_ENGINE` on `/opt/kodely`. The audit could only see your local `.env`.

## Board

New stages at positions 6 and 7: **Kodely Pro — Full Apps** and **Prompt Wizard**. Two research agents are filling them — they'll produce 45–75 cards between them, and I'll insert those once they report.

I gave both agents the constraint that matters: a CRM needs persistence, auth and queries, and generated sites are currently static files under `connect-src 'none'`. That's architectural, not a prompt problem, so the Pro research has to solve it rather than assume it away. Same for the wizard — logo upload and reference-site fetching both collide with the CSP and with SSRF risk.

Also worth flagging on your ask: **"conserve credits" is the strongest part of the Pro idea** and I asked for it to be quantified rather than asserted. Here's where things stand. Ten agents have run this round; five have reported.

## Transactional email — built, and it caught a bug in my code

The agent found that **"crossed from fine to low" doesn't work as a trigger** here. Your signup grant is 750 and my fallback average is 400, so `buildsLeft = 1` for a brand-new account — meaning the low-credit warning would have *never fired* for exactly the people it exists for, because they're never on the "fine" side to begin with.

It solved that with a graded state (`ok → low → spent`), diff-tested against my meter's rule across 2,600+ balance/average combinations with zero mismatches, and simulated a whole 750-credit tank at five different build costs: always 1–2 emails, never a stream.

That surfaced a real bug I'd introduced: **every brand-new account rendered amber** the moment they signed up. A warning at full balance isn't a warning, it's noise, and it trains people to ignore the real one. I've split the count from the alarm — "About 1 more build" stays accurate at 750, but the colour now waits until the tank is actually draining. Verified across ten realistic balance/average pairs.

Its two asks are done: `lib/mail.ts` now exports a generic `sendMail` (I put `from` *after* the spread so a caller can't override the envelope sender — the version I first wrote contradicted its own comment), and `EmailLog` is in the schema and pushed, which turns at-most-once into exactly-once.

Worth knowing before you enable it: `KODELY_CRON_SECRET` is required or the endpoint 404s, `KODELY_NOTIFY_ALLOWLIST` should be set to your own address first, and **staging must not run the cron** — the published-site URLs it builds point at the prod wildcard.

## Template gallery — built, but unreachable

23 templates, each scoped honestly (the photographer one says outright you can't upload photos yet; coming-soon forbids the email field and substitutes a `mailto:`). Verified at 375px with no horizontal scroll.

**Nothing links to `/templates`.** `MarketingNav` and `MarketingFooter` were outside that agent's scope, so the page only exists by direct URL. That's a one-line addition I'll make once the marketing files are free.

## Board

Two new stages live at positions 6 and 7 — **Kodely Pro — Full Apps** and **Prompt Wizard** — with research agents filling them.

## Still running

Editor UX, admin audit log, sites registry, feature flags, billing UX, support inbox, and the two research agents.

Lint is at 4 errors, all in `CommandPalette.tsx` and `Editor.tsx` from the Editor agent's in-flight work. I've messaged it rather than editing files it's actively in — with a specific warning not to trade a lint error for a hydration error, since that's happened in this app before.

# 1. LOVABLE (lovable.dev)

**Backend / database — FIRST-PARTY, built on Supabase's open-source foundation**
- Lovable Cloud is the default built-in backend: database, storage, auth, realtime, functions. "Lovable's built-in backend (Cloud) is enabled by default, so most projects never need a separate Supabase account." — https://docs.lovable.dev/integrations/supabase
- It "utilizes Supabase's open-source foundation," so it is first-party-branded but Supabase-derived under the hood. — https://docs.lovable.dev/features/cloud
- Connecting your own Supabase project remains available as an optional path for infra ownership. — https://docs.lovable.dev/integrations/supabase

**Auth**
- Configured directly through Lovable, including social login providers; docs state configuring auth through Lovable "works on the built-in backend only." If you bring your own Supabase project, you configure auth in the Supabase dashboard instead. — https://docs.lovable.dev/integrations/supabase
- Cloud includes user authentication with sign-in methods such as Google OAuth. — https://docs.lovable.dev/features/cloud

**Server vs client-only / hosting**
- Real server-side backend, not client-only. Apps are hosted on Lovable's servers in one of three regions (Americas, Europe, Asia Pacific), chosen at Cloud setup and **not changeable afterward**. — https://docs.lovable.dev/features/cloud
- Lovable manages both frontend and backend on its own infrastructure, with custom domains, automatic SSL, and global delivery. Code is exportable via Git sync; you can self-host part or all of the stack. — https://docs.lovable.dev/tips-tricks/deployment-hosting-ownership
- Generated apps are "standard Vite + React projects" (client-rendered frontend + backend services). — https://docs.lovable.dev/tips-tricks/deployment-hosting-ownership
- *Unverified:* the specific claim that every publish deploys as an edge Worker with pre-rendered routes came from a third-party blog, not Lovable docs.

**Templates / starters — YES, explicitly**
- "Design templates": Design → Use a template. "A design template is a Lovable project that has been marked as reusable," and using one **copies the entire project codebase into the new project**. — https://docs.lovable.dev/features/business/design-templates
- Public template gallery at https://lovable.dev/templates (websites, portfolios, etc.)
- *Note:* I found no official Lovable statement framing templates as a **cost/credit-reduction** mechanism. That framing is verified for Bolt (below), not Lovable. Treat "Lovable uses templates to reduce generation cost" as unverified.

**Pricing — metered in CREDITS**
- Free: 5 build credits/day, capped at 30/month; plus 20 Cloud credits/month and 4 AI credits/month. — https://lovable.dev/pricing and https://docs.lovable.dev/introduction/subscription-plans
- Pro: **from $25/month for 100 credits**, scaling up to **$2,250/month for 10,000 credits**. — https://docs.lovable.dev/introduction/subscription-plans
- Business: **from $50/month for 100 credits**, scaling to **$4,300/month for 10,000 credits**; adds SSO, restricted projects, data opt-out, design templates. — https://docs.lovable.dev/introduction/subscription-plans
- Enterprise: custom contract; excludes the standard Cloud/AI grants. — https://docs.lovable.dev/introduction/subscription-plans
- Annual pricing (~$21/mo Pro, ~$42/mo Business) appeared in search snippets but I could **not** confirm it on an official page — **unverified**.
- Metering unit detail: Default Mode credit cost **varies by task complexity** (examples cited: 0.50–1.70 credits per message); Plan Mode is a flat 1 credit/message. Monthly credits expire 2 months after issue; annual credits expire 1 month after the period ends; top-up credits last 12 months. Credits are non-refundable and not redeemable for cash. "Plans are priced by the credits they include, not by seats" — workspaces support unlimited members on all plans. — https://lovable.dev/pricing

**Credit-burn incidents**
- No official Lovable incident disclosure found. Complaints are third-party/anecdotal: bug-fix loops consuming credits, and users reporting no visibility into cost before a message runs. — https://dev.to/momen_hq/the-hidden-costs-of-vibe-coding-a-practical-look-at-lovables-credit-usage-3cec
- Specific figures circulating ("30 credits for one bug fix", "65–75% bug-loop rate") come from blog/marketing content with no primary source — **unverified**.

---

# 2. BOLT.NEW (StackBlitz)

**Backend / database — first-party branded "Bolt Database", powered by Supabase**
- Supabase's own launch post states plainly: "every project in Bolt Cloud that needs a backend is powered by Supabase." Published **September 30, 2025**. Includes Postgres, auth/user management (incl. SAML/SSO), S3-compatible file+video storage, Edge Functions, Realtime APIs. Notes Bolt had already connected apps to **over 600,000 Supabase backends**. — https://supabase.com/blog/bolt-cloud-launch
- Bolt's own docs present it as first-party: "Create and manage databases in Bolt without the need for third-party tools," with unlimited databases, built-in auth management, file storage, server functions. Connecting your own Supabase project is offered as an **alternative** ("Use Supabase instead of Bolt database"). Unpublished projects auto-pause after ~6+ days of low usage. — https://support.bolt.new/cloud/database
- Bolt Cloud also involves a Netlify partnership for hosting per third-party reporting — **partially unverified** (Netlify is confirmed as an optional publish target in Bolt's own docs: https://support.bolt.new/integrations/netlify).

**Auth — built-in, Supabase-backed**
- Native email/password signup and **Google SSO**. Leaked-password protection via HaveIBeenPwned enabled by default; customizable email templates; built-in password reset. Docs acknowledge "Bolt Database email templates are powered by Supabase technology." — https://support.bolt.new/cloud/database/authentication

**Server vs client-only / hosting**
- **Two distinct runtimes.** During *generation/preview*, the app runs client-side in StackBlitz **WebContainers** — a full Node.js runtime executing inside the browser tab (filesystem, terminal, package manager, dev server all client-side). — https://github.com/stackblitz/bolt.new
- When *published*, apps use Bolt's built-in hosting by default, with Netlify as an optional alternative target. Backend logic runs as real server/edge functions on the Supabase-powered Bolt Cloud. — https://support.bolt.new/cloud/hosting and https://support.bolt.new/integrations/netlify

**Templates / starters — YES, and explicitly framed as a token-saving mechanism**
- This is the strongest public statement of the three. Bolt's blog recommends templates "to save tokens." — https://bolt.new/blog/top-5-bolt-new-templates-to-jumpstart-your-next-project
- Official token-efficiency doc: Bolt processes fewer tokens with less context; recommends cleaning unused files, splitting large files, and using Discuss Mode to plan before building. — https://support.bolt.new/best-practices/maximizing-token-efficiency
- Reported behavior that you can build on a template **without consuming tokens until you make changes** came from third-party coverage — **unverified** against Bolt docs.

**Pricing — metered in TOKENS (LLM tokens, not credits)**
From https://bolt.new/pricing:
- Free: **$0** — 300,000 tokens/day, 1,000,000 tokens/month, 10MB file uploads, up to ~333k web requests. No rollover.
- Pro: **$25/month** — starting at 10,000,000 tokens/month, **no daily limit**, tokens roll over, 100MB uploads, up to 1M web requests.
- Teams: **$30/month per member** — same token allowances as Pro plus workspace collaboration.
- Enterprise: custom pricing and custom token allowances.

Token mechanics (https://support.bolt.new/account-and-subscription/tokens):
- Critical cost driver, in Bolt's own words: "most token usage is related to syncing your project's file system to the AI: the larger the project, the more tokens used per message." Cost scales with **codebase size**, not interaction count.
- Free tokens reset the 1st of each calendar month, no rollover. Paid tokens are retained for **two months** from issue; rollover tokens are consumed **oldest-first**.
- Pro subscribers can buy non-expiring "token reloads." Exact reload dollar prices — **unverified**.

Hosting limits (https://support.bolt.new/cloud/hosting/plans):
- Free hosting: up to 10 GB bandwidth + 333,333 requests/month, hard traffic ceiling (~10,000–15,000 monthly visits).
- Pro hosting: up to 30 GB bandwidth + 1M requests/month, with pay-as-you-go overage. Pro hosting is included with every paid Bolt subscription. **No separate dollar price is published for hosting tiers.**

**Token-burn incidents**
- A Hacker News "Ask HN" post reports a user losing 10M tokens with an unresolved support response: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=46321594 — this is a **single user account, not a confirmed platform incident**. No official StackBlitz incident disclosure found. Bolt's refund policy being discretionary is reported third-party — **unverified**.

---

# 3. REPLIT / REPLIT AGENT

**Backend / database — first-party, migrated OFF Neon**
- Important and easy to get wrong: Replit Database is now "a fully-managed SQL database" that is Replit's own managed solution. The docs note that **prior to December 4, 2025**, the development database "was hosted on Neon and has a few crucial differences." So the widely-repeated "Replit is powered by Neon" claim is **outdated** for current production. — https://docs.replit.com/cloud-services/storage-and-databases/sql-database
- Includes **20GB of free storage for every Replit App**; every Replit app comes with a database by default. — same URL
- Agent provisions schema and wires an ORM automatically when asked to add a database. — https://docs.replit.com/cloud-services/storage-and-databases/sql-database

**Auth — first-party "Replit Auth"**
- Agent-only: "Manual implementation is not supported, as Agent handles all the complexity for you." Triggered by saying "use Replit Auth" in a prompt. — https://docs.replit.com/replit-workspace/replit-auth
- End users sign in with existing Replit accounts; login methods include Google, GitHub, X, Apple, and Email. Underlying vendors named in docs: Firebase, Google Cloud, reCAPTCHA, Stytch, Clearout. — same URL
- Auth pane provides user management; auto-creates user entries in your database.

**Server vs client-only / hosting — real servers, priced separately from Agent**
Replit is the clearest "real server" of the three, and notably **hosting is billed separately from Agent usage** (https://docs.replit.com/billing/deployment-pricing):
- Autoscale (default/recommended): **$2.00/month base + $0.60 per million compute units + $0.40 per million requests**; scales to zero when idle.
- Reserved VM: **$15.00/mo** (shared 0.5 vCPU / 2GB), **$35.00** (dedicated 1 vCPU / 4GB), **$50.00** (2 vCPU / 8GB), **$130.00** (4 vCPU / 16GB).
- Scheduled: $2.00/month + $0.60/M compute units; scheduler free.
- Static: hosting free, **$0.05/GB** data transfer.
- Replit's own cost examples: small business site (~75k monthly requests) ≈ $2.39/mo; API service (300k requests) ≈ $4.50/mo.

**Templates / starters — YES**
- Custom Templates: Enterprise admins create pre-configured starting points that appear directly in the Agent input box. "When a builder selects a custom template, Agent forks it and uses the template's configuration, instructions, and skills to guide all subsequent work." — https://docs.replit.com/teams/custom-templates
- Public gallery: https://replit.com/gallery
- No official statement framing templates as a **cost-reduction** measure — **unverified**.

**Pricing — metered in "effort-based" CHECKPOINTS/credits**
From https://replit.com/pricing:
- Starter (Free): $0, free daily usage, create projects and publish **1 live project**, built-in database access.
- Core: **$25/mo, or $20/mo billed annually**; includes **$25 toward most powerful models**, 2 parallel agents, unlimited workspaces, badge removal.
- Pro: **$100/mo, or $95/mo billed annually**; includes **$100 toward most powerful models**, 10 parallel agents, up to 15 collaborators + 50 viewers, 28-day database rollback, premium support.
- Enterprise: custom; SSO/SAML, single-tenant, static outbound IPs.
- The official pricing page does **not** publish specific credit counts for free daily usage — **unverified**.

Effort-based pricing mechanics (https://replit.com/blog/effort-based-pricing, published **June 18, 2025**, updated July 2, 2025):
- Old model: flat **$0.25 per checkpoint**. Small edits cost $0.25; large tasks fragmented into multiple $0.25 checkpoints.
- New model charges by "effort" measured in **time and computation**. Simple changes cost **less than $0.25**; complex tasks bundle into one checkpoint that "may cost more than $0.25." "Cost will reflect the true scope of the Agent's work."
- Two user-facing effort dials: "High power model" and "Extended thinking."
- Rollout: immediate for new users, from **July 1, 2025** for existing Core and Teams subscribers. (Note: some third-party pages misdate this as 2026 — the primary source is 2025.)
- Third-party figures like "simple edits 5–20 credits, complex features 150–300+ credits" are **unverified** against Replit docs.

**Surprise-bill incidents — THIS IS THE BEST-DOCUMENTED CASE OF THE THREE, with official admission**
Replit publicly acknowledged the problem (https://replit.com/blog/effort-based-pricing-recap):
- Replit stated "the transition to the new pricing model did not meet our standards for how we like to roll out major changes."
- **July 11 billing incident**: between 11:26 AM and 5:43 PM PDT, "checkpoint charges were being incorrectly computed and were often much larger than they should have been," affecting **~6% of paying users**. Automatic refunds/credits were issued for the full cost of affected checkpoints, no user action required.
- Replit gave **$10 in free credits to all members** who used the new pricing model.

Subsequent Agent 3 backlash (mid-September 2025), per https://www.infoworld.com/article/4059876/replit-update-sparks-developers-dissatisfaction-over-pricing.html:
- Users reported consuming "a third of their monthly budget in one night." Root cause cited: Agent 3's increased autonomy triggering unnecessary refactoring on minor edits.
- CEO Amjad Masad acknowledged the Agent 3 issues and said the company was "actively trying to fix them." InfoWorld did **not** publish specific dollar amounts.
- Larger figures circulating in search summaries (one user charged $1K in a week; another $1,982 in 24 days; another ~$700/month) trace to a Register article at https://www.theregister.com/software/2025/09/18/replit-infuriating-customers-with-surprise-cost-overruns/ which **returned HTTP 404 on direct fetch** — I could not verify these numbers against the primary source. Treat as **unverified**.
- A Trustpilot reviewer reported ~$500/week and being charged for agent idle/freeze time — single anecdote, **unverified**: https://www.trustpilot.com/review/replit.com

# CROSS-CUTTING NOTES

**The three metering units are genuinely different, which makes direct comparison misleading:**
- Lovable = **credits** (variable per message, 0.50–1.70 typical in Default Mode)
- Bolt = **LLM tokens** (scales with codebase size, since the filesystem is re-synced to the AI each message)
- Replit = **effort-based checkpoints** (time + computation, price revealed *after* the checkpoint is charged)

**All three are Supabase-adjacent except Replit.** Lovable Cloud and Bolt Database are both Supabase-powered but first-party-branded. Replit is the only one running its own database stack (and moved off Neon in December 2025).

**Only Bolt has an official public statement tying templates to cost reduction** ("save tokens"). Lovable and Replit both ship templates that fork/copy an entire project codebase, but neither publicly frames this as a generation-cost lever.

**Hidden-cost asymmetry:** Replit bills app hosting separately from Agent credits (Autoscale/Reserved VM line items), while Lovable and Bolt bundle hosting into the plan with bandwidth/request caps. A Replit user's true monthly cost is plan + agent effort + deployment.

# 1. Lovable (lovable.dev)

**First-run shape — freeform box, then a design fork (2 interaction steps to first output)**
- Landing page is a single freeform prompt box labelled "Ask Lovable to create…"; you can type before signing up, then sign in. There is no wizard. ([getting-started](https://docs.lovable.dev/introduction/getting-started))
- Docs state: "There is nothing to install and nothing to configure." First version "takes a few minutes." ([getting-started](https://docs.lovable.dev/introduction/getting-started))
- **But Lovable does interpose a design step.** "Design guidance" shows **three rendered design directions** on "a first message that asks for anything with a UI." User picks one, and may refine the chosen direction **up to six times** before submitting. ([design-guidance](https://docs.lovable.dev/features/design-guidance))
- So: prompt → 3 previews → pick/refine → build. It is **skipped** when the prompt already specifies fonts/colours/branding, for games and low-UI functional requests, and for projects already using a design template or design system. Deliberate skip = "include a detailed visual brief directly in your prompt." ([design-guidance](https://docs.lovable.dev/features/design-guidance))

**Style/colour up front:** Yes — via the three-preview picker above (rendered previews, not chips/dropdowns/theme sliders). Additionally a **design system picker at project-creation time**: design systems are "a regular Lovable project that is marked as a design system," selectable when creating a new project. ([design-systems](https://docs.lovable.dev/features/design-systems))

**Logo upload:** Yes. Images can be attached to chat via drag, paste, or Chat actions → Attach; limits 20 MB free / 256 MB paid / 1 GB Enterprise. ([chat](https://docs.lovable.dev/features/projects/chat)) Handling: Lovable reads the image and you instruct placement (e.g. replace the navbar logo). Persistent assets go into the repo `public` folder when GitHub/GitLab is connected and are referenced by path; files over 10 MB can't be committed and Lovable "moves the files to Lovable's CDN and updates your code." Externally hosted images can be used by pasting the URL in chat. ([using-images](https://docs.lovable.dev/tips-tricks/using-images))

**Reference URL / site import:** Yes, but the only precisely documented mechanism is the **Build with URL API**. Hash-fragment params: `prompt` (required, up to 50,000 chars), `images` (public JPEG/PNG/WebP URLs), and `html` — "a publicly accessible web page URL. Lovable fetches the page and uses it as a reference for layout, content, and styling." Up to **10 combined images + pages**; non-public refs are "silently drop[ped]" and the app still builds from the prompt. Signed-out users authenticate first, references preserved. Changelog dates the `html=` capability to **Jun 16, 2026**. ([build-with-url](https://docs.lovable.dev/integrations/build-with-url), [changelog](https://docs.lovable.dev/changelog))
- Whether pasting an arbitrary URL into ordinary chat triggers the same server-side fetch: **UNVERIFIED**.
- Full content migration of the user's own existing site: **UNVERIFIED** — no documented crawl-and-migrate feature; Figma import and GitHub import are the documented inbound paths. ([figma](https://docs.lovable.dev/integrations/figma))

**Prompt enhance:** **Not documented.** The chat docs enumerate the input's affordances (Build/Plan toggle, dictation Option+V, "Add reference" @-picker, screenshot capture, annotation drawing tools, plus-menu) and contain **no enhance/improve-prompt button**. ([chat](https://docs.lovable.dev/features/projects/chat)) A "Prompt enhancer" item exists on Lovable's public feedback board (feedback.lovable.dev/p/prompt-enhancer) — I could not fetch it (DNS failure), so its status is **UNVERIFIED**. Design guidance appears to occupy this role instead. Treat "Lovable has one" in the brief as unconfirmed.

**Cost:** Free = **5 build credits/day** (reset 00:00 UTC), capped at **30/month**, plus 20 Cloud credits and 4 AI-gateway credits monthly. Plan-mode chat = **1 credit per message**. Build mode is variable: simple styling edit ≈ **0.50**, component removal ≈ **0.90**, auth ≈ **1.20**, "landing page with images" ≈ **2.00** credits. Top-ups $0.30/credit (Pro), $0.60 (Business). **Design guidance adds no extra cost** — "uses standard chat messages and does not add additional credit costs." ([credits-and-usage](https://docs.lovable.dev/introduction/credits-and-usage), [design-guidance](https://docs.lovable.dev/features/design-guidance))
